title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Today

The backsliding story: how democracies slide toward authoritarianism — Bermeo’s typology, the third wave, and three cases
The international dimension: what other states do to prop autocracies up, punish them, or help them along
Closing the module: the two-problems spine, one last time, and where that leaves you reading the news


This is the module’s last lecture and it does double duty as both new content and a course finale. Last week closed the breakdown story (what replaces a fallen autocracy); this week asks the reverse question — how a democracy slides toward authoritarianism, using the same toolkit this module has spent eleven weeks building — and then widens the lens to the international dimension: autocracies and backsliding democracies alike are shaped by what other states do to them, not just by what happens at home. The last part of the lecture is not new material at all; it is the whole course, reassembled around Svolik’s two problems, before the send-off.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Whose module does this properly?
Last week closed the breakdown story — what replaces a fallen autocracy. Today’s is the mirror question. Full disclosure first, because it matters for your reading and your essays:

Classical democratization theory — modernization, Lipset, the conditions under which transitions consolidate — belongs to Michelle D’Arcy’s Democracy & Development A, same semester, same cohort. She does that canon properly; we won’t duplicate it here.


What’s ours: present-tense autocratisation — backsliding, happening now, to regimes that started as democracies. That’s the rest of today.

Guard rail — PLAN-MT2026.md §3, binding. This slide exists specifically to say the boundary out loud, on-screen, as instructed — not just to observe it silently in the syllabus. Keep it short and factual, not apologetic; the pivot line (“what’s ours: present-tense autocratisation”) is the one that matters.


Say this straight, one breath, then move.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Modern autocrats don’t storm the palace
text:
Modern autocrats don’t storm the palace


Modern autocrats rarely seize power in a single coup. They erode democracy gradually, from the inside, often through means that are — on paper — legal.



No tanks. No single dramatic moment. Just a thousand small, individually defensible steps.

Bermeo’s argument (required reading) is a claim about how the mode of regime change has itself changed. The classical image of authoritarian takeover — a coup, tanks in the street, a general on television — is not what most present-day backsliding looks like. Instead an elected leader uses genuinely legal powers, one at a time, each individually defensible as ordinary politics, to remove the checks that would otherwise constrain them. No single step looks like an attack on democracy; the cumulative effect is one.


The pivot that makes this urgent: coups as the mode of regime change → slow legal capture as the modal one today.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Bermeo’s typology: the old menu

Open coups — tanks, a general on television, power seized by force overnight
Promissory coups — the military intervenes “to restore democracy,” then doesn’t leave, or leaves on its own schedule


Bermeo’s point: both are becoming rare. There’s a third item on the menu — and it’s the one doing almost all the work today.

Let the room feel the gap before naming the third form (next slide).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
…and the modal path today
Executive aggrandizement: the elected executive dismantles checks on their own power, piece by legal piece — courts, electoral rules, media, civil society.

“Executive aggrandizement” is Bermeo’s term for the third and now-dominant form of backsliding: it is done by an executive who already won an election legitimately, using powers that office genuinely carries — appointing judges, proposing legislation, issuing decrees — stretched to remove the checks that would otherwise limit a second, third, or indefinite term. It is the hardest of the three forms to see happening in real time, because each individual step (a court appointment, a redrawn electoral map, a media-licensing decision) can be defended as ordinary, even routine, governance.


It’s the hardest to see happening, because each individual step can be defended as normal politics.

Key move: not “backsliding replaced coups” but “the menu shifted” — courts and elections are cheaper and more legitimating than tanks (callback Weeks 5-6).


Prior-exposure flag (brief §“Prior exposure”). This cohort took Comparative Politics A/B, whose Week 6 (“Regime Change”) already introduces “democratic decline,” “autocratization,” and “illiberal democracy” by name, with Hungary, Poland, India and Brazil name-checked. So the facts of backsliding are not new to this room. What’s new is applying this module’s toolkit — elite-control vs. mass-control — to diagnose which moves in the playbook are doing which job. Say this out loud rather than re-teaching backsliding as if it were a fresh discovery; it isn’t, and pretending otherwise wastes the room’s patience.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How much do you actually need to steal a democracy?
text:
How much do you actually need to steal a democracy?

A supermajority — control of the legislature, not just the executive
The power to amend the constitution
Enough loyal bodies to fill every institution you’re packing


That is not a mood — it’s an election result you have to win first.

Bermeo’s gradual, legal, individually-defensible steps are real, but they don’t happen for free. Executive aggrandizement requires the entry conditions listed above, and all three are expensive: winning them takes a genuine, large-scale electoral victory, not just an election win. The “gradual slope” description is about method; this slide is about what has to be true before the first step on the slope is even available.


Source: Waller, Statecraft 10 Sep 2026 — “The part that they don’t tell you is that for all of that to happen, you have to have supermajorities in the institutions… You need to be able to make constitutional changes… that actually takes a lot of work, and polarization prevents that from happening.”


A complication, not a contradiction — say so explicitly (Bermeo = the steps once on the slope; Waller = what it costs to get on it). Cold-call: “Hungary’s playbook is widely described as easy to copy — why so rare?”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Pluralism by default
Autocratisers don’t run as extremists. Russia, Turkey, Hungary — each leader won their first majorities as centrists: stability, consensus, the average person. The ideology came later.

So why doesn’t every polarised democracy autocratise, if the playbook is this well known?
Way’s answer: some societies are too internally divided — ethnically, linguistically, ideologically — for any one leader to build the supermajority the previous slide requires. Division blocks consolidation, not just backsliding


Pluralism by default (Way): a society can be too fractured for full authoritarian control to consolidate, even when a leader wants it — the divisions that make governing hard also make total capture hard. Way’s motivating cases are post-Soviet states (Ukraine in the 1990s–2000s, Moldova) that never fully autocratised despite trying. It is a disagreement with, not a replacement for, the “gradual slope” story: it explains why some countries never get far enough onto the slope to matter.


Proposed reading (recommended, not on _course.yml — Noah’s call): Way, Lucan A. 2015. Pluralism by Default: Weak Autocrats and the Rise of Competitive Politics. Johns Hopkins University Press.


Source: Waller, Statecraft 10 Sep 2026 — “these leaders portray themselves essentially as centrists… at least for their first few elections, that’s usually borne out”; and on Way’s book, applied by Waller to the US case as an argument that American diversity makes aggrandisement structurally hard.


Don’t resolve for the room — let Bermeo’s sequence and Way’s entry-conditions sit together as two true things about different stages.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Same present tense, different labels

Backsliding / autocratization — a democracy losing quality, still contested, not yet gone
Competitive authoritarianism — Week 2’s category: elections are real but structurally rigged against the opposition
Consolidated autocracy — no meaningful contest left at all


These three labels mark points on the same slope rather than separate categories. Backsliding describes a democracy that is losing quality — courts less independent, media less free, elections less level — while still holding genuinely contested elections that an incumbent can lose. Competitive authoritarianism, the category this module met in Week 2, describes a regime that has slid further: elections happen and are not entirely fake, but the playing field is tilted so consistently that the incumbent’s defeat becomes very unlikely rather than merely less likely. Consolidated autocracy is the far end, where no meaningful contest remains at all. The interesting analytical work — and most of the disagreement among scholars — happens in placing a specific country at a specific moment on this slope, not in disputing that the slope exists.


Shared vocabulary before the cases — reused on the Venezuela and US slides. Two minutes, not more.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
A third wave — of autocratization

The number of liberal democracies worldwide has been falling for over a decade
Lührmann & Lindberg: a “third wave of autocratization” is underway — the mirror image of Huntington’s democratic waves
Most of it runs through elected incumbents using legal tools, not through coups


Callback to Week 1’s opening stat (share of world under autocracy) — full circle.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Spine callback: elite tool, or mass tool?
text:
Spine callback: elite tool, or mass tool?
The backsliding playbook is the same toolkit as the rest of the module — now aimed at a democracy from the inside.

Capture the courts, the electoral commission, the referees — elite control: neutralise the people who could rule against you
Tilt the electoral field (recall Week 6’s menu of manipulation) — both: reshapes who competes (elite) and how votes convert to seats (mass)
Muzzle media and civil society (recall Weeks 8–9) — mass control: cut off the information citizens need to coordinate opposition
Demonise the opposition as illegitimate enemies — mass control: legitimation, aimed at your own base, not at elites


Discussion, 2 minutes, with your neighbour: pick one Hungarian move from the case study coming up and decide — elite tool or mass tool? Then we’ll cold-call three pairs.

Actually run the 2 minutes — don’t skip because it’s the last week. Cold-call 2-3 pairs and let disagreement stand; several genuinely split elite/mass.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Hungary: the completed playbook


IMG orban.jpg (reused, credits in w12img/CREDITS.md) · .img-right reserves a column so it can’t collide with the incremental list.

Since 2010, Fidesz has run the “gradual, legal” playbook to (near) completion, in full public view:

A two-thirds supermajority — won in 2010, 2014, 2018 and 2022 — used to rewrite the constitution
Court-packing and jurisdiction-stripping — the referees replaced, not abolished
Electoral boundaries and rules redrawn to entrench the incumbent
Independent media bought out or starved of advertising; a university (CEU) driven out of the country


Every step, individually, had a legal justification. That’s the point — this is what “legal, gradual, from the inside” looks like when it’s finished.

Fidesz’s constitutional supermajorities — 2010, 2014, 2018, and 2022 — are the mechanism behind everything else on this slide: Hungary’s constitution requires a two-thirds parliamentary majority to amend it, which Fidesz has repeatedly won under an electoral system it also redrew. The Central European University’s relocation from Budapest to Vienna, completed in 2019 after a 2017 law targeting foreign-accredited universities, is often cited as the single most visible individual episode in the sequence — a globally ranked university driven out of an EU member state through ordinary legislative process.


Hungary is the exemplar because it’s done. Ask: at what point does a backsliding democracy stop being a democracy? No clean answer — sit in it.


Election years verified 2026-09-16: Fidesz–KDNP won two-thirds parliamentary majorities in the 2010, 2014, 2018 and 2022 Hungarian elections (widely reported; e.g. Reuters/AP election-night coverage each cycle). CEU relocation: completed 2019, following the 2017 “Lex CEU” legislation. Warn-off note, borrowed from the Build-a-Regime essay spec (PLAN-MT2026.md §4): if students reach for “the Hungary playbook” as a template in their essays, that’s the easy, well-worn answer — worth flagging here too, not just in the notes, since this is where they’ll first hear the phrase.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Which stage is Hungary at?
Backsliding democracy, competitive authoritarianism, or consolidated autocracy — using the ladder from two slides ago, where would you place Hungary today, and why?

Genuine cold-call — 2-3 students commit to a rung and defend it with evidence. V-Dem codes Hungary “electoral autocracy” — reveal after they answer.


Third built-in discussion device (brief requires at least three: this cold-call, the pair-discussion on the spine-callback slide, and the straw poll on the US slide). Never titled by its mechanism — the question is the title.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Venezuela: competitive authoritarianism, completed
Levitsky & Way’s own textbook case of competitive authoritarianism — and then it stopped being competitive.

Chávez (1999–2013): elections that were real but tilted — state resources, media access, and the courts all favoured the incumbent, but opposition victories still happened
Maduro (2013–): the 2017 Constituent Assembly sidelines the elected legislature; the 2018 and 2024 elections are widely assessed as neither free nor fair


The line from “hybrid regime” (Week 2) to “the real thing” isn’t instant. It’s a slope, and Venezuela shows how far down it goes.

Nicolás Maduro’s National Constituent Assembly, elected in a July 2017 vote whose result was disputed even by the firm that supplied the voting technology, was used to sideline the opposition-controlled National Assembly and rewrite the constitution outside the normal legislative process. The 2018 presidential election was boycotted by major opposition parties and widely rejected internationally; the 2024 election, in which the opposition-aligned candidate is generally understood to have won based on independently collected vote-tally receipts, saw Maduro’s government declare victory without releasing detailed results — the clearest recent illustration of a regime abandoning even the pretence of competitiveness.


Callback to Week 2/6. Point: “competitive authoritarian” isn’t a stable resting place — it can keep eroding. Pairs with Hungary: same direction, different speed.


2017 Constituent Assembly election and 2018/2024 election disputes: widely reported (Reuters, AP, Carter Center/EU observer statements). Verified 2026-09-16 as broadly-agreed facts, not a specific disputed figure — the exact vote-count claims from 2024 remain contested, which is itself worth saying out loud rather than picking a side on stage.


IMAGE — a photo of a Caracas protest or the National Assembly building, Wikimedia Commons. Or pair with w12img/hungary-indices.png’s chart style: a V-Dem trajectory chart for Venezuela specifically, if time allows generating one with scripts/make_chart.py.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How do we know it’s happening — before it’s finished?
text:
How do we know it’s happening — before it’s finished?
V-Dem doesn’t wait for a regime to fully collapse to call it. It scores dozens of components — judicial independence, media freedom, clean elections — every year, for every country.

A backsliding country shows up as a downward slope across several components at once, years before anyone declares the regime “gone.”

V-Dem’s method is what makes present-tense claims about backsliding more than journalistic impression: rather than a single up-or-down democracy score, it tracks dozens of disaggregated components (judicial independence, freedom of expression, clean elections, and more) every year for essentially every country in the world, built from expert coding rather than a single analyst’s judgement. A country that is backsliding typically shows a simultaneous downward slope across several of these components — courts and media weakening together, for instance — well before any single dramatic event would prompt a headline. That’s the evidential basis behind calling Hungary an “electoral autocracy” years before anyone would have called it a coup.


Keep brief. Point: “backsliding” is a measured claim, not a vibe — V-Dem’s disaggregated components are how you’d defend it in an essay.


IMAGE — a V-Dem component radar/line chart for one backsliding country (Hungary works well, ties back to the earlier slide), Source: V-Dem’s own country graphs at v-dem.net.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The United States debate
 

IMG levitsky.jpg / ziblatt.jpg — the authors of the recommended reading, stacked in the .img-right reserved column so they can’t collide with the list. Reused from the Intro pool (credits w12img/CREDITS.md). Delete both image lines to drop them.

Apply the same toolkit to a case much closer to home — and disagree about the verdict, not the tools.

If you were coding the US the way V-Dem codes any other country: what would you look for? (courts, electoral administration, media independence, legitimation rhetoric)
Levitsky & Ziblatt’s warning signs (recommended reading): rejection of democratic rules of the game, denial of opponents’ legitimacy, toleration of violence, willingness to curtail rivals’ civil liberties
Where scholars actually disagree: not on whether the indicators exist somewhere in US politics, but on their severity, direction, and whether “consolidated” democracies are actually as backsliding-proof as we assumed


Ask the room, show of hands: “on the ladder from two slides ago, where would you currently place the US?” — not to resolve it, but to surface how split the room is before you say anything else. Keep the follow-up strictly analytical: ask why they voted that way, in terms of which indicator, not which side.


Most delicate slide — deliver dry. “You have a toolkit; apply it, disagree about the verdict, not the tools.” Keep off named politicians. If heated: redirect to “which indicator are you weighing more heavily.”


Framing flag for Noah, not a content suggestion. The brief asks this be handled “analytically, not polemically.” Current draft frames it as “apply the tools, disagree about the verdict” — but you know this room and this year better than a draft can; recalibrate the specific indicator list and the poll question close to delivery, since “consolidated democracy” comparisons age fast and get more or less loaded depending on what’s in the news that week. Unverified/flag: some recent V-Dem editions have classified the US below “liberal democracy” on certain sub-indices — check the exact current V-Dem classification before stating it on-slide rather than asserting it from memory.


Proposed reading (recommended, not on _course.yml — Noah’s call): Linz, Juan J. 1990. “The Perils of Presidentialism.” Journal of Democracy 1(1): 51–69. For the dual-legitimacy point — a separately elected president and legislature each claim a mandate, and the president’s claim (the whole country voted) reads as superior, which is what produces attempts to override the legislature. Source: Waller, Statecraft 10 Sep 2026.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The line worth remembering

CC: this is the deck’s one big-quote slide (brief requirement). Draft sentiment below is a paraphrase of Bermeo’s core claim, not a verbatim quotation — I don’t have reliable access to the exact printed wording. Noah: swap in the actual verbatim line from “On Democratic Backsliding” (2016) before this goes in front of a room — pull it directly from the PDF along with the page number for the citation.


Backsliding today rarely looks like the fall of a regime. It looks like the regime rules getting rewritten by the people who are supposed to be bound by them.
— paraphrased from Bermeo, “On Democratic Backsliding” (2016) — verify wording


If the real quote isn’t swapped in, say so out loud rather than presenting the paraphrase as verbatim.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Where do new regimes get their models?
text:
Where do new regimes get their models?
Not always invented at home. Gunitsky’s argument: regime type can diffuse — spread by example — or be actively promoted by a dominant outside power.

After a hegemonic shock — a war or a collapse that reorders who’s on top globally (1918, 1945, 1991) — the winning power’s own regime type suddenly looks more attractive, and sometimes gets pushed directly
1989–91: the Soviet collapse briefly made liberal democracy the only model with any prestige left — hence the wave of “formal trappings of democracy” adopted even by regimes with no intention of holding real power


Gunitsky’s distinction is between diffusion (other countries copy a regime type because it now looks successful or legitimate, with no one pushing) and promotion (a dominant power actively exports its own institutions, sometimes by force, sometimes by conditioning aid and alliances on it). His empirical claim is that both spike together after a hegemonic shock — a war or collapse that suddenly reorders which great power is on top — because the shock does two things at once: it makes the winner’s regime type look more successful, and it temporarily lowers the political cost of the winner intervening to install it. The 1989–91 Soviet collapse is his central case: for a few years, adopting some democratic trappings was almost obligatory even for regimes with no real intention of becoming democracies, precisely because there was, briefly, no rival great-power model left standing.


Keep moving — scene-setting for “is now a shock moment?” next.


IMAGE — a simple timeline: 1918 (US/Wilson), 1945 (US/USSR split), 1991 (US unipolar moment) marked as hegemonic-shock years, with a note on the wave of regime changes that followed each. Build with a plain timeline graphic, not a chart.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Is now a shock moment?
Gunitsky’s theory says regime models spread fastest right after the global pecking order visibly changes. Does that describe the 2020s?

Genuine open question — cold-call or pair-discuss a minute. No textbook answer. If the room reaches “autocratic powers’ model looking newly attractive” — draw it out, don’t feed it.


cc: contested, not settled. Whether the 2020s constitute a “hegemonic shock” in Gunitsky’s sense (US relative decline, China’s rise, the war in Ukraine) is a live debate among IR scholars, not an established fact — present it as the discussion question it is, not as a conclusion.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Propping up your friends
Not every regime survives on its own resources. Some are kept alive by an outside patron.

Recall two cases from last week: Assad’s Syria, propped up for over a decade by Russia and Iran despite total isolation elsewhere; Belarus, backstopped diplomatically and materially by Russia through the 2020 crisis
The literature sometimes calls this a “black knight” — an authoritarian patron that substitutes for the Western aid or investment a regime under sanction or isolation would otherwise lose


Both Syria and Belarus were used last week as cases about elite cohesion — this week’s addition is naming the outside factor that let each regime’s elite stay cohesive in the first place. An external patron can supply the hard-currency and diplomatic cover a sanctioned or isolated regime would otherwise be starved of, which is what lets its elites keep believing the regime can survive and keep their side of the bargain. Cutting off a black knight patron — not just imposing sanctions yourself — is often the more decisive lever, which is exactly why sanctions regimes that don’t also target the patron tend to underperform.


Say “remember Assad, remember Belarus” out loud — this is a callback, not new material.


cc: unverified attribution. “Black knight” as a term for an authoritarian patron-state is used in some of the democracy-promotion/sanctions literature (e.g. work on Russia’s regional role) but is not in Noah’s own MSc reading list — verify the standard citation (candidates: Tansey, Koehler & Schmotz 2017; Bader, Grävingholt & Kästner 2010 on “authoritarian gravity centres”) before presenting the term as settled vocabulary rather than a useful label.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Do sanctions work — and work how?
text:
Do sanctions work — and work how?
The intuitive theory: cut off resources, the regime falls. The evidence is messier.

Escribà-Folch & Wright: sanctions can force a regime to choose between patronage spending and repression — cut off the money for buying loyalty, and some regimes repress more, not less
Peksen & Drury: sanctions can hand a regime a ready-made justification for cracking down — “emergency measures against foreign interference”


Escribà-Folch and Wright’s mechanism runs through the regime’s own survival calculus rather than through the population’s suffering: sanctions reduce the resources available for patronage, and a regime that can no longer pay its coalition risks losing it — so some regimes substitute repression for spending, using coercion to hold the same coalition together more cheaply. Peksen and Drury’s finding sits alongside this rather than contradicting it: an externally imposed sanctions regime also supplies a rhetorical resource, letting the government frame domestic crackdowns as a defensive response to foreign pressure rather than as ordinary repression. Read together, both papers are cautions against treating sanctions as a straightforwardly pro-democratic tool.


Real question: “if designing sanctions on an autocracy, what are you trying to break — money, military, or story?” No clean answer — let it sit.


IMAGE — a simple two-column diagram: “sanctions cut resources” → [“patronage falls” → “repression substitutes”] vs. [“regime concedes”], to visualise the fork the printnote describes. Illustrative, not data-driven.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Can international institutions save a democracy?
text:
Can international institutions save a democracy?
Sometimes — but not by stopping a coup.

Poast & Urpelainen: IOs are good at helping an already-transitioning democracy consolidate — building institutional capacity, raising the cost of backsliding
They’re much worse at preventing reversals outright — an IO can’t stop tanks in the street, and does best with governments that were never military-led to begin with


Poast and Urpelainen’s distinction matters because it cuts against a common assumption — that joining the EU, NATO, or a regional bloc is itself protective against authoritarian reversal. Their finding is narrower and more useful: international organisations help consolidate democracies that are already on a transitional path, mainly through institutional capacity-building, but they have little power to actually stop a coup or a military takeover once one is underway, and the consolidation effect is weakest for regimes that transitioned out of military rule in the first place. Hungary’s own EU membership is the uncomfortable test case for the room to notice on their own: membership plainly did not prevent the backsliding covered earlier this lecture.


Ask “why didn’t EU membership stop any of what we just covered?” — let the room work toward the answer (capacity-building, not coercion).


Source: Poast & Urpelainen 2015, from Noah’s own MSc week 5 reading list.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Reach doesn’t stop at the border
text:
Reach doesn’t stop at the border
Recall Week 9: exile used to mean safety from your own government. It increasingly doesn’t.

Transnational repression — surveillance, intimidation, and even assassination attempts reaching dissidents abroad, tracked by Freedom House’s own dataset
The international dimension isn’t only about what outside states do to a regime — it’s also what a regime does from home, to people outside it


Week 9 covered transnational repression as an extension of a regime’s domestic surveillance and control toolkit — the same logic, aimed past its own borders at exiled dissidents, journalists, and diaspora communities, including cases documented as close to home as Dublin. This week’s point is the mirror image of the rest of today’s international-dimension material: so far the theme has been outside actors acting on a regime (patrons, sanctions, institutions); transnational repression is the regime acting outward, which is why “the international dimension” cuts both ways rather than being a one-way story of the world constraining autocrats.


Brief callback — don’t re-run Week 9. One line: “the border doesn’t protect you from your own government the way it used to.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: The whole term in one slide
text:
The whole term in one slide
Back to Week 1’s opening cold-call — Russia. Hungary. Singapore. Mexico (1990s). The United States. Which is a democracy? You’ve spent twelve weeks building the toolkit that actually answers it.

Every autocrat faces two problems (Svolik) — power-sharing with elites, control of the masses — and every week was a tool for one or both
Russia, Hungary, Singapore: contested or clearly autocratic on most measures, by most measures you now know how to apply
Mexico (1990s): the classic hybrid case — competitive authoritarianism before the term existed
The United States: still contested, on purpose — you just spent the last twenty minutes disagreeing about it, and that disagreement is the answer


The five-country cold-call from Week 1 was never meant to be answered on the spot — it was meant to sit unresolved for the whole term. By this point in the course you have the vocabulary to do more than guess: Russia and Hungary read as autocratic or backsliding-to-completed by essentially every standard measure this module has covered; Singapore is a genuine hard case, a long-ruling dominant party with real elections and real constraints that most scholars still code as not fully democratic; Mexico under the PRI (pre-2000) is the textbook competitive-authoritarian case that gave the category its name; and the United States is the one the module deliberately leaves open, because the honest answer is that reasonable people using the same indicators currently disagree about it — which is itself evidence that “consolidated democracy” was never as permanent a status as it sounded.


Say explicitly: “Week 1, five countries, one question — remember your first guess?” The real send-off — don’t rush past it. Tight on time? This slide absorbs the next one, not the reverse.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
This week in autocracy


Noah: two or three stories from this week. One line each — headline, country, and the concept it illustrates (elite problem or mass problem?). This slide is the same shape every week, same slot, right after the plan.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Recall Week 3
Svolik’s power-sharing problem: the allies strong enough to help you rule are strong enough to remove you. Autocrats can’t fully trust the inner circle because the inner circle is exactly who could replace them.

The military is the sharpest version of that problem there is. It is, quite literally, the only actor in the regime with organised, standing violence.

Svolik’s power-sharing problem, from Week 3: an autocrat needs strong allies to help run the regime, but any ally strong enough to be useful is also strong enough to be a threat. There is no institutional fix that removes this tension entirely — only different ways of managing it. The military is the sharpest instance of the problem because it is the one actor inside the regime that holds organised, standing violence. A minister who turns disloyal can be sidelined with a phone call; a general who turns disloyal has tanks.


Put “Svolik” and “power-sharing” on screen — same commitment problem, same inner-circle logic, but now the currency is tanks, not cabinet posts.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Elite tool or mass tool?
The spine question, every week:

Is this an elite-control tool, or a mass-control tool?


Coups and coup-proofing are elite-control, full stop — the army isn’t the mass public, it’s the most dangerous member of the ruling coalition. Everything this week is about managing that relationship.


Contrast: Week 9 propaganda = mass-control; Week 5 patronage = mostly elite-control
Coups are the extreme case — failure means the regime ends that afternoon

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Key term: coup d’état

Coup d’état: the sudden, illegal seizure of state power by a small group — usually from inside the regime’s own military or security apparatus — typically without mass participation.


Note what this isn’t: not a revolution (no mass mobilisation), not a civil war (no sustained fighting), not an election. It’s fast, small, and insider-led.

A coup d’état is distinguished from other ways regimes change hands by three features together: it is illegal (it bypasses whatever succession rule the regime formally has), it is carried out by a small group rather than a mass movement, and that group is typically already inside the state’s own coercive apparatus — the military or security services — rather than an outside challenger. This is what separates a coup from a revolution (which mobilises large numbers of ordinary people) and from a civil war (which is sustained armed conflict rather than a single, fast seizure).


Not everyone took second-year Comparative — don’t assume the term’s already precise. Thirty seconds, move on.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The coup trap
The dictator’s grim arithmetic:

You need a strong, capable military to deter rivals, rebels, and foreign threats
A strong, capable military is also the best-equipped actor to depose you
The stronger and more competent you make it, the more dangerous it becomes to you personally


There is no version of this where you get a powerful army that can’t turn on you. You’re always trading one risk for another.

Let this sit — it’s the whole week in one slide. Everything after is different regimes managing a problem with no clean solution.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Who actually removes dictators?
Ask the room to guess before you reveal.


Not mass uprisings — those get the headlines but are comparatively rare
Not, usually, foreign invasion or assassination
Mostly: insiders. Coups — by the military or by regime elites — are the modal way an autocrat loses power historically


Let the room guess before revealing — most picture crowds in a square, not insiders.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: 45% of authoritarian regimes since 1945 began with a coup
text:
45% of authoritarian regimes since 1945 began with a coup
Geddes, Wright & Frantz’s dataset of 280 autocratic regimes, 1945–2010: coups are the single most common route to power — ahead of popular revolution, ahead of foreign imposition.

Geddes, Wright and Frantz’s dataset covers 280 autocratic regimes that took power between 1945 and 2010. Their headline finding is that 45% of these regimes originated in a coup — militaries and political parties are the actors most likely to seize power this way. Contrary to the popular image of coups defending narrow economic elites or growing out of popular uprisings, GWF find many coups instead grow out of grievances inside the military itself — officers excluded from promotion on grounds like ethnicity, for instance.


Say the number, then pause. Measures regime origin, not how sitting dictators lose power — but same underlying picture either way.


Verified 2026-09-16: 45% figure and the “militaries and parties are the groups most likely to seize power” framing from a Foreign Affairs review of Geddes, Wright & Frantz, How Dictatorships Work — https://www.foreignaffairs.com/reviews/paths-power. This resolves the earlier flag on this slide asking for the exact percentage; the figure is GWF’s own dataset statistic (280 regimes, 1945–2010), not a secondary estimate. Note the measure is regime origin, not leader exit within an existing regime — accurate framing above, worth restating verbally if you want to be precise with the room.


Noah: if you’d rather cite the number straight from the book (you’ll have it to hand; I worked from a review, not the primary text), swap the citation — the figure itself checks out but the primary source is better than mine.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Coup-proofing: the menu
Quinlivan’s (required) toolkit, drawn from Middle Eastern cases:

Counterbalancing — multiple, overlapping security forces that watch each other, none strong enough alone to move against the ruler
Loyalty over merit — promote kin, co-ethnics, members of the ruler’s sect or region into command
Rotation — move officers before they can build a personal power base
Praetorian guards — a pampered elite unit whose privileges depend entirely on the ruler personally, not on the state
Paying the praetorians — expensive perks are the price of the loyalty premium


Quinlivan draws his toolkit from Middle Eastern cases: Saddam Hussein’s Iraq (a Republican Guard, a regular army, and a Special Republican Guard, plus multiple intelligence services, all watching each other), the Saudi National Guard as a deliberate counterweight to the regular military, and Syria under the Assads. The pattern across all of them is redundancy and rivalry built in by design, not the result of incompetence — an autocrat pays a real price in coordination and efficiency to buy a coup-proof structure.


IMAGE — diagram: a counterbalancing org chart — regular army, presidential/ republican guard, internal security/intelligence services, all reporting separately to the ruler and each watching the others. Saddam’s Iraq is the cleanest worked example if you want one specific case rendered. Build for w10img/ (matplotlib, following the pattern of the Intro deck’s list-experiment-diagram.png / this course’s own truth-funnel.png).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Worked example: Saddam’s Iraq, applied
Every item on the menu, in one regime:

Republican Guard (loyalty-vetted), regular army, and a Special Republican Guard (Saddam’s own tribe and clan) — all separately commanded
Multiple, overlapping intelligence services watching the military and each other
Command rotated and fragmented deliberately, so no single officer ever controlled enough force to act alone


Saddam Hussein’s Iraq is the cleanest single-regime illustration of Quinlivan’s whole toolkit operating at once. Below the regular army sat a loyalty-vetted Republican Guard, and below that a Special Republican Guard recruited disproportionately from Saddam’s own tribe and clan network — three tiers of force, each a check on the one below and above it. Layered over all three were multiple, overlapping intelligence and security services, which watched the military as closely as they watched the public. Command was kept deliberately fragmented and rotated, so that no single officer ever controlled enough combined force to act alone. The redundancy bought coup security; it is also a large part of why the Iraqi military that this system produced performed so poorly once it actually had to fight, in 1991, 2003, and again against ISIS in 2014.


Sets up the next slide — ask them to predict, from this structure alone, how well they’d expect this army to fight.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The cost of coup-proofing
A coup-proofed army is loyal. Is it any good at fighting?

Cronies over competent officers. Fragmented, duplicated command chains. Weapons and fuel deliberately hoarded away from units the ruler doesn’t fully trust. Every design choice that buys loyalty also degrades battlefield performance.

Cold-call: “If you were building a military purely to never coup you, what would you sacrifice?” Let them generate the Quinlivan list before revealing.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The trade-off, cashed out

Iraq, 2014 — Mosul fell to a much smaller ISIS force almost overnight; a military hollowed out by decades of coup-proofing and patronage-based promotion collapsed rather than fought
Iran — the regular Artesh sits alongside the separately-commanded IRGC, a parallel force built explicitly to counterbalance the army, not to maximise national defence capability
Russia — Rosgvardia (National Guard) and, until 2023, Wagner both existed partly as counterweights to the regular military and the FSB — redundancy bought at the cost of a coherent chain of command


Three regions, one mechanism. In Iraq, a military hollowed out by decades of coup-proofing and patronage-based officer promotion collapsed in 2014 when a much smaller ISIS force took Mosul almost without a fight. Iran runs its regular army, the Artesh, alongside a separately-commanded Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps built explicitly as a counterweight rather than to maximise national defence capability. Russia’s National Guard (Rosgvardia) and, until 2023, the Wagner Group both existed partly as counterweights to the regular military and the FSB — redundancy bought at the price of a coherent chain of command, a price that showed up vividly in June 2023 (see the case slide below).


Say “same tool, different countries” out loud. Optional 4th beat: 2022 Ukraine invasion — keep tight, not the week to relitigate the war.


The Iraq/Mosul citation (Hoekstra 2020, “How Mosul Fell: the Role of Coup-Proofing in the 2014 Partial Collapse of the Iraqi Security Forces”) isn’t on the current reading list — found it in the Chicago-Zakharov syllabus dump, it’s a clean, short, exactly-on-point case study. Worth adding as a recommended reading rather than required; flagging rather than deciding.


Currency check: confirm the Rosgvardia/Wagner framing is still accurate and not overtaken by events by delivery time (2026) — this is a fast-moving case, see the Wagner slide below for the fuller currency flag.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: A coup is a coordination game
text:
A coup is a coordination game
Most coup plotters can’t actually defeat the whole armed forces by force. What they need instead is for everyone else to believe the coup has already succeeded — because then it has.


Officers who are lukewarm, or opposed, defect to the winning side the moment they think it’s already won
Nobody wants to be the last loyalist standing against a fait accompli
So plotters don’t need to win a fight — they need to win the belief


This is the coordination-game framing developed by Naunihal Singh in Seizing Power (not currently on this module’s reading list — see the cc below). It reframes the whole topic: a coup is not primarily a military contest, it is an information contest about who is going to win, because most actors’ best individual move is simply to go along with whoever is about to be in charge. Officers who are lukewarm or even opposed to a coup will defect to the winning side the moment they believe it has already won, because nobody wants to be the last loyalist standing against what looks like a fait accompli.


Naunihal Singh’s Seizing Power: The Strategic Logic of Military Coups (2014) is the natural anchor for this slide and isn’t currently assigned — flagging as a strong recommended-reading candidate (Ch. 2 specifically) rather than adding it to required, since Quinlivan + GWF already carry the required load this week.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Why the radio station?

The cliché of coup footage — plotters seizing the state broadcaster first — isn’t decoration. It’s the whole strategy.

Controlling the airwaves lets plotters announce victory and make it common knowledge: not just “we believe we’ve won,” but “everyone knows that everyone knows we’ve won.” That’s what makes defection rational for everyone watching, all at once.


Coups that fail to make this common knowledge fast enough often collapse in hours — not because they lacked force, but because uncertainty never resolved in the plotters’ favour.

IMG ostankino-tower.jpg (Moscow’s TV tower — reused as a generic “seize the broadcaster” stand-in, not tied to a specific coup attempt) · delete the image line to drop it · edit width/position to move. .img-right reserves a column so it can’t collide with the slide’s three fragments.


The seized TV or radio station in coup footage is not a symbolic afterthought — it is the actual mechanism of a coup succeeding. Controlling the airwaves lets plotters announce victory and turn it into common knowledge: not merely that plotters believe they have won, but that everyone watching knows that everyone else watching knows the plotters have won. That shared, public belief is what makes defection rational for every wavering officer simultaneously, rather than each having to guess what everyone else will do. Coups that fail to establish this common knowledge quickly enough often collapse within hours — not for lack of force, but because the uncertainty about who has actually won never resolved in the plotters’ favour.


Invite examples from the room: 1991 Soviet coup against Gorbachev — plotters held the airwaves but failed to project confidence; Yeltsin on the tank undid the common-knowledge claim.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
You’ve just seized the palace
It’s 6am. The president is in custody. You control the palace and one TV station.
What are your first three phone calls?

Cold-call after the pair discussion. Let the room generate answers first — likely: army/security heads, state media, a foreign patron or rival to pre-empt. Redirect to the coordination logic: every answer resolves uncertainty for someone still deciding.


Discussion device #2 — 2-minute pair discussion (build-brief requirement): before the cold-call reveal, have students turn to a neighbour for 90 seconds and each draft their own list of three calls, then take 2–3 pairs’ answers before you steer. Cheap, works well on a “what would you actually do” premise, and buys you a genuine discussion moment inside the lecture with no tutorial to lean on.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Egypt, 2013: the military as regime-owner
Not a coup against the regime — the military was already the regime, stepping back into the driver’s seat.

On 3 July 2013 the armed forces removed an elected president (Morsi), suspended the constitution, and installed an interim leadership headed toward one of their own (Sisi) — a return to form for an institution that has run Egypt, directly or from just behind the curtain, since 1952.

On 3 July 2013 Egypt’s armed forces, led by General Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, removed elected president Mohamed Morsi from power and suspended the constitution, installing judge Adly Mansour as interim president before Sisi himself later won the presidency outright. The framing worth stressing is that this was not a coup against an otherwise-stable civilian order — the military has run Egypt, directly or from just behind an elected front, in every regime since the Free Officers’ 1952 revolution. 2013 briefly interrupted that pattern (an elected Muslim Brotherhood government) and then the military simply reasserted the ownership it had never really given up.


IMAGE — Tahrir Square crowds, July 2013, or a photo of Sisi. Wikimedia Commons search “Egyptian protests July 2013” or “Abdel Fattah el-Sisi”. .absolute bottom-right, ~24% width.


Date verified 2026-09-16: 3 July 2013, Sisi removes Morsi, suspends constitution, installs Adly Mansour as interim president. Source: contemporary reporting summarised via web search (multiple outlets agree on the date and sequence); primary citable source for the slide itself would be Brownlee, Masoud & Reynolds or similar academic account if you want one on-slide.


Contrast with Wagner (next): here the military was always the regime’s true owner reasserting itself, not a coup-proofing tool turning risky.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Russia, 2023: Wagner and the counterbalance that talked back
text:
Russia, 2023: Wagner and the counterbalance that talked back
A private military company, built partly as a counterweight to the regular army and security services, marches on Moscow — and gets within hours of a real confrontation before standing down.

The textbook irony: coup-proofing tools (parallel, personally-loyal armed structures) are themselves a coup risk once they get powerful enough to have their own interests.

On 23 June 2023 Wagner Group leader Yevgeny Prigozhin declared a “march for justice” after accusing the Russian military leadership of attacking his own forces. Wagner units took control of the southern city of Rostov-on-Don and a column advanced north toward Moscow, getting to within roughly 200km of the capital. On 24 June, with Belarusian mediation, Prigozhin ordered the column to stand down and return to camp, saying he wanted to avoid Russian bloodshed; he went into exile in Belarus. Two months later, on 23 August 2023, Prigozhin was killed along with other senior Wagner figures when his private jet crashed. The episode is the clearest possible illustration of coup-proofing’s own risk: a parallel, personally-loyal armed structure built to counterbalance the regular military is itself a coup risk once it becomes powerful enough to have interests of its own.


Fact-checked 2026-09-16 against three sources and confirmed as accurate: Al Jazeera timeline, Washington Post visual timeline, Wikipedia, Wagner Group rebellion. Sequence: rebellion declared 23 June 2023; Wagner took Rostov-on-Don and a column advanced toward Moscow the same day; stand-down and Belarus exile 24 June; Prigozhin killed in a plane crash 23 August 2023 (exactly two months later). All dates and the outcome match across sources.


Noah: this is your case to build out — you know the Prigozhin mutiny far better than any generic account I could draft. The verified sequence above is solid to build on (Wagner’s creation as a Ministry of Defence rival → the June 2023 march on Moscow → the negotiated stand-down → Prigozhin’s death two months later) — your own read on what it reveals about coup-proofing’s limits is the thing worth real slide-time, more than my summary.


IMAGE — Wagner convoy on the M4 highway, or a Prigozhin photo. Wikimedia Commons search “Wagner Group Rostov-on-Don 2023” turns up press photos of the occupied military HQ. .absolute, bottom-right.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Kadyrov: the deal that bypasses the state
text:
Kadyrov: the deal that bypasses the state
Wagner was a coup-proofing tool that turned into a coup risk. Chechnya shows the other failure mode: a personal deal that replaces the state entirely.

Ramzan Kadyrov governs Chechnya as a personal patron-client arrangement with Putin, not through the normal institutions of the Russian Federation
The FSB is not permitted to operate inside Chechnya — cc: from the episode, verify — part of the informal deal that keeps it quiet
The wider pattern: regional strongmen running their own militias, not just Chechnya


The Wagner mutiny is one failure mode of coup-proofing — a parallel force built as a counterweight that became a coup risk once it had interests of its own. Kadyrov’s Chechnya is a different one: not a formal institution at all, but a personal patron-client bargain between Kadyrov and Putin that substitutes for the normal chain of command entirely. Kadyrov runs Chechnya as something closer to a fiefdom, with his own armed forces answering to him personally, and the deal that keeps this arrangement stable and quiet is reported to include the FSB staying out of Chechnya altogether. The broader worry this points to is that governors and state-owned companies elsewhere in Russia have also built up their own militias — an unresolved question of how many more personal baronies like this one exist.


Pair with the Wagner slide — same country, same logic (informal deals substituting for institutions), different shape. FSB-in-Chechnya claim is reported, not settled.


Source: Waller, Statecraft, 10 Sep 2026 — “Kadyrov and Putin have a personal patron-client relationship that bypasses all the institutions of the Russian Federation… the FSB is officially not allowed to investigate or engage in any activities inside of Chechnya.” Also: “a variety of governors and large state-owned companies have their own militias now.” cc: from the episode, verify on the FSB-Chechnya claim specifically — reported by Waller, not independently confirmed here.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Latin American juntas: when the military is the regime
text:
Latin American juntas: when the military is the regime
The 20th-century classic: the armed forces don’t just threaten the regime, they are the regime — ruling directly, often as an institution rather than a single strongman.

Links straight back to Week 2’s typology: military regimes are their own category precisely because “who removes the dictator” and “who the dictator is” collapse into the same actor.

Chile under Pinochet, Argentina’s military juntas, and Brazil’s 1964–1985 military governments are the standard examples of a military regime proper — the armed forces ruling directly, often as an institution with its own internal command rather than as personal instruments of a single strongman. Military regimes also tend to be the least durable authoritarian type: officers frequently want to return to the barracks once order is restored, which is a very different survival logic from personalist or single-party regimes that cling to power indefinitely.


IMAGE — a Latin American junta photo (Pinochet-era Chile is the most recognisable). Wikimedia Commons search “Chilean military junta 1973” or “Pinochet”. .absolute, bottom-right, ~24% width.


Pick your case live (Chile, Argentina, Brazil). Bridge: military regimes tend to be the least durable type — callback to Week 2’s survival data.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Why don’t generals want the job?
text:
Why don’t generals want the job?
Running a country isn’t in a general’s skill set — and it isn’t what they signed up to lose their reputation over.

Generals don’t actually like to rule whole countries — it’s complicated, and not what they’re trained for
If it goes wrong, it went wrong on their watch, in uniform — they’d rather hand the economy back to civilians before that happens
Coups beget coups. Each one lowers the bar and normalises the next


Not a Latin American quirk: interwar Europe and 19th-century Iberia (Spain, Portugal) show the same pattern of coup after coup after coup.

Two reasons generals hand power back. First, running a country is a genuinely different skill from running an army — managing an economy, a bureaucracy, a society that isn’t hierarchical the way a barracks is — and most officers know it. Second, and just as important, is blame: a junta that stays in charge owns whatever goes wrong next, in a way that damages the military’s own institutional standing, not just the individual ruler’s. Ideological juntas are the exception — where officers are committed communists or socialists (a Cold War pattern), they tend to build a party and transition into a party regime instead of handing back. The other regularity worth naming: coups beget coups. Once a country crosses that line once, the bar for the next one is lower, and the pattern repeats. None of this is a Latin American or African peculiarity — interwar Europe had plenty of coup governments, and 19th-century Iberia (Spain, Portugal) saw the same cycle.


Ask the room to guess why before revealing — most say “the economy tanks” before “the blame,” which is the sharper point. Interwar/Iberia line stops this reading as a Latin American/African stereotype.


Source: Waller, Statecraft, 10 Sep 2026 — “Generals don’t actually like to rule whole countries… they don’t want to be blamed for bad economic progress… they would like to go back to the barracks”; “Coups tend to lead to more coups”; and on scope, “Europe had plenty variations on the coup format of government in the interwar period, or if you look at coups in Iberia in the 19th century.” Paraphrased above, not quoted verbatim.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Three cases, one mechanism
Egypt, Wagner, and the Latin American juntas look like three unrelated stories. They’re the same elite-control problem, three ways.

Egypt: the military never stopped owning the regime — the least surprising failure mode
Wagner: a coup-proofing tool became the coup risk — the most ironic failure mode
Latin America: the military is the regime, formally — the most durable-looking, and (per the callback above) usually the least durable


Egypt, the Wagner mutiny, and the Latin American military juntas look like three unrelated stories, but they are the same elite-control problem worked out three different ways. In Egypt the military never actually stopped owning the regime behind whatever civilian front was in place, so 2013 was less a coup than a reassertion. In Russia a coup-proofing tool — a parallel, personally-loyal armed structure — itself became a coup risk once it grew powerful enough to have its own interests, the sharpest irony of the three. In classic Latin American juntas the military simply is the regime, formally and openly, which looks like the most durable arrangement on paper but, per the civil-military slide above, tends to be the least durable in practice.


Say out loud: still the elite-control question from the top, now three cases. Ask which one they find most surprising.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Civil–military relations, generally

Every dictatorship — not just military ones — has to keep the generals onside; it’s a standing management problem, not a one-off event
The trade-off scales down too: even routine promotion and procurement decisions balance competence against loyalty
In a genuine crisis, the army’s choice — shoot, or defect — is often the single most decisive variable in whether a regime survives (hold that thought for Week 11)


Every dictatorship, not only formally military ones, has to keep the generals onside as a standing management problem rather than a one-off event. The same competence-versus-loyalty trade-off that shapes grand coup-proofing strategy also scales down into routine, unglamorous decisions — who gets promoted, which unit gets the new equipment. Barany’s argument (recommended reading) is that in a genuine crisis moment, the army’s choice between firing on protesters and standing down or defecting is often the single most decisive variable in whether a regime survives — more decisive, usually, than the size of the crowd in the street.


Whether the army fires or stands down usually decides the outcome more than crowd size. Say explicitly: this bridges into next week.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The succession problem, named
A coup is one way the top job changes hands. Death or incapacity is another — and personalist regimes handle it badly.


Personalist rulers often deliberately avoid naming a strong successor — a credible heir is also a credible rival
So when the leader dies suddenly, there’s frequently no agreed answer to “now what?”
Brownlee’s work on hereditary succession: dynastic transfer (son inherits) is one solution regimes reach for precisely because it forecloses an open contest


Personalist autocrats frequently avoid naming a strong, credible successor, for the same reason they avoid building a strong, capable military without hedging against it: a credible heir apparent is also a credible rival, someone around whom disgruntled elites could rally before the incumbent is even gone. The result is that when a personalist leader dies suddenly or becomes incapacitated, there is often no agreed answer to who takes over, which is itself a moment of acute regime vulnerability. Jason Brownlee’s work on hereditary succession treats dynastic transfer — engineering the succession so a son or close relative inherits — as one deliberate solution to this problem, precisely because it forecloses an open contest for power rather than leaving the outcome to be settled by whoever moves fastest.


Keep tight. Throughline: coup-proofing and succession-proofing are the same problem — stopping who could replace you — at two different moments.


Noah: your call on how much time this segment gets, or whether it survives your edit pass at all — it’s flagged as optional for exactly that reason.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Case: North Korea’s three generations

The clearest dynastic succession anywhere in a nominally single-party state.

Kim Jong-un inherited in 2011 from his father, Kim Jong-il — who had inherited in 1994 from his father, Kim Il-sung, the regime’s founder. Three generations, no open contest, ever.

IMG kim-succession.jpg (Kim Jong-un, 2019) · delete the image line to drop it · edit width/position to move. .img-right reserves a column. Dates verified 2026-09-16: Kim Jong-un succeeded Kim Jong-il December 2011; Kim Jong-il succeeded Kim Il-sung 1994. Well-documented, uncontested facts.


North Korea’s three generations of Kim rule are the clearest example anywhere of dynastic succession inside a nominally single-party, non-monarchical state. Kim Jong-un inherited power in 2011 from his father Kim Jong-il, who had himself inherited from his own father, Kim Il-sung, the regime’s founder, in 1994. At no point across three transfers was there an open contest for the top job.


One case, one point: the fix for “no successor without a rival” is often a blood relative — no independent legitimacy to build.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Case: Azerbaijan’s electoral dynasty
Same solution, a very different-looking regime type.

Ilham Aliyev succeeded his father Heydar Aliyev as president in 2003 — via a formally competitive election whose outcome nobody seriously expected to go any other way.

Pairs with the Kim slide — single-party and formally electoral states, same fix. Wry aside spot: “competitive” is doing a lot of work there.


IMAGE — Aliyev-specific photo would be stronger than the generic crown-prince-alt.jpg stand-in this deck’s w10img/ folder holds (it’s Mohamed bin Zayed of the UAE, not Aliyev — a placeholder, not a match). Wikimedia Commons search “Ilham Aliyev” for a proper photo.


Verified 2026-09-16: Ilham Aliyev succeeded his father Heydar Aliyev as President of Azerbaijan in October 2003. Well-documented, uncontested fact — not separately footnoted as load-bearing in the way the Wagner/Egypt/GWF numbers are, but flagging that it was checked.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Coup or crumble?
If Country X’s ageing, personalist leader died in office tomorrow with no named successor — coup, dynastic handover, elite power-sharing deal, or chaos?

Pick a live, ambiguous case at delivery time (a personalist leader currently in poor health or advanced age is the sharpest version of this question) and poll the room before revealing any expert forecasting.

The question text above is written out in full and ready to use as-is with a generic “Country X,” or swap in a real, current example at delivery time for extra bite.


Straw poll, show of hands. Reinforces: even experts struggle to predict this.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How would we know a coup was coming?
text:
How would we know a coup was coming?
Political risk analysts and intelligence services try. What would the signal even look like?


Officer transfers or purges just before a rumoured date — a ruler pre-empting, or plotters consolidating?
Unusual troop movements, especially units converging on the capital
Elite-communication silence — sudden radio silence from a faction that’s usually chatty is itself a signal


Anticipating a coup is structurally hard for the same reason the coordination-game framing above makes coups themselves hard to predict: the signals analysts look for — unexplained officer transfers or purges, unusual troop movements toward the capital, a faction of the regime going unusually quiet — are ambiguous by design, because a ruler managing a coup risk and plotters preparing one can produce very similar-looking noise.


cc: unverified. This slide states plausible categories of early-warning signal drawn from the political-risk literature in general terms, not a specific dataset or forecasting model with a citable accuracy record — treat as a discussion prompt, not an evidenced claim, until a source is attached.


Keep short and open — coup forecasting is genuinely hard and often wrong.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Propaganda & Censorship



Controlling minds without controlling anyone’s beliefs

IMG ostankino-tower.jpg — Ostankino Tower, Moscow (CC BY-SA 4.0, Sergey Pesterev), copied from the Intro module’s Backsliding deck (w09-lec13-img/) — full credit in w08img/CREDITS.md. Stands in for Moscow’s TV infrastructure; delete background-image= and background-opacity= from the heading to drop it.


Welcome back from reading week. Pivot: money (Week 5) → minds. Three puzzles: (1) terror → spin, (2) why lie when nobody’s fooled, (3) why censor coordination, not complaint.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Today

Two cases first: a fifty-year gap in Soviet/Russian TV, same job
Fear vs. spin dictators (Guriev & Treisman) — and the elite twist
Propaganda nobody believes — signalling, not persuasion
Censoring coordination, not complaint


Two hours, one underlying argument: authoritarian information control has changed its tools over the twentieth and twenty-first centuries — from overt terror to information manipulation — but not its goal, which is to manage what the public and the elite believe about the regime’s popularity and competence. The first half asks why regimes bother producing propaganda that persuades nobody; the second half asks why they censor some speech and not other speech. Both halves turn out to run on the same logic: information control is never really about truth, it’s about behaviour.


Fast. First back from reading week — one line: “Week 6 was the last co-optation week; today, controlling what people believe.”


Revision log, 2026-09-16
