title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
This week in autocracy


Noah: two or three stories from this week. One line each — headline, country, and the concept it illustrates (elite problem or mass problem?). This slide is the same shape every week, same slot, right after the plan.


Five minutes, no more. Ask the room first: “what happened this week that belongs in this module?” — then show yours. The point is the habit: by teaching week 12 they should be bringing the stories, not you.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Exhibit A: the weather report that wasn’t
text:
Exhibit A: the weather report that wasn’t
Rozenas & Stukal (2019, Journal of Politics) coded years of Russian state-TV economic news. Their finding: coverage of the economy gets systematically rosier exactly when the real economy is doing worse.

Not blanket lying — managed lying, tuned to conditions. That precision is the whole puzzle of this lecture.

Rozenas, Arturas, and Denis Stukal. 2019. “How Autocrats Manipulate Economic News: Evidence from Russia’s State-Controlled Television.” Journal of Politics 81(3). It is not on the required reading list but is a genuinely useful citable anchor: the authors show that Russian state television’s coverage of the economy is more positive, relative to real conditions, the worse the real economy is actually performing — the opposite of what a naive “just tell people good news” model predicts, and consistent with a regime managing perceptions strategically rather than lying at random.


Don’t name Guriev & Treisman yet — let the puzzle land. Shows information control is calibrated, the thread the whole lecture pulls on.


Verified 2026-09-16 (web search): Rozenas, A. & Stukal, D. 2019, “How Autocrats Manipulate Economic News: Evidence from Russia’s State-Controlled Television,” Journal of Politics 81(3) — citation and core finding confirmed against the published abstract. Mining note: this framing borrows from Noah’s own MSc syllabus (POP88264 2025, “Hybrid Regimes and Electoral Authoritarianism” week). Also checked POU44172 Russian Politics HT2027/slides/ for ready-made Russian-TV material: the closest hit is Jade McGlynn’s “defensive consolidation” quote in week10/week11 (propaganda produces varied, often lukewarm reactions, not uniform belief) — genuinely useful for this week’s “propaganda isn’t really about persuasion” argument, but flagging before reusing: the same JS cohort could well be sitting in Russian Politics this term too, so repeating McGlynn there and here needs Noah’s sign-off on whether that’s a problem or a deliberate reinforcement.


Noah: your own line here about watching Russian state TV do this in real time — the module’s told from the inside, this is where that voice belongs.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Soviet television, 1975
State media as the only source. Total narrative monopoly, mandatory belief, an enormous ideological apparatus behind it.

The USSR ran a genuine information monopoly: no legal alternative media, no foreign broadcasts reaching most citizens undisturbed (jamming stations existed specifically to block them), and belief in the official line was, at least outwardly, mandatory rather than optional. This is the “fear dictator” information regime at its most complete.


Keep short — the contrast with the next slide is the point.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Russian television, 2026
State media dominant but not exclusive — VPNs exist, Telegram exists, everyone half-knows the news is managed.

IMAGE — a Channel One / Rossiya-1 studio still next to a phone showing a Telegram channel, side by side: the two information regimes in one frame. Source: Wikimedia Commons (search “Rossiya 1 studio” / “Channel One Russia”) for the studio half; a generic Telegram-app screenshot for the other.


Compare 1975: today’s Russian state broadcasters (Channel One, Rossiya-1, NTV) still dominate the domestic audience, but the monopoly is gone in practice even where it survives in law — VPNs, Telegram, and diaspora media mean everyone who wants an alternative account can usually get one. The regime’s problem has shifted from blocking information to outcompeting it.


Currency check: confirm this framing still holds for MT2026 delivery — Russian media control has tightened steadily since 2022 (foreign-agent law, wartime censorship statutes); check whether “not exclusive” undersells how much the information space has closed.


Don’t let “not exclusive” go unchallenged — flag as a live question, not settled fact.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Same country, fifty years apart — what changed?
text:
Same country, fifty years apart — what changed?
Same underlying job: manage what citizens believe about the regime. What changed between 1975 and 2026 wasn’t the goal. What was it?

Let a couple of students propose an answer before naming Guriev & Treisman next slide.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Fear dictators vs. spin dictators
Guriev & Treisman’s central contrast (Spin Dictators, required):

Fear dictators (the old model) — rule by mass violence and overt terror
Spin dictators (the new model) — rule by manipulating information and pretending to be democratic


The 20th century’s tyrants jailed and killed. Today’s prefer to spin — and to look modern while doing it.

IMAGE — Guriev & Treisman’s own chart tracking the shift from violence-heavy to spin-heavy autocracies over the 20th–21st century (the book’s signature figure; also in their 2019 JEP “Informational Autocrats” piece, fig. 1 or similar). Reproduce or closely redraw it; don’t screenshot the book. This is the single image most worth building properly.


Pressure it: real trend, or survivorship (fear dictators are the ones who got overthrown)? Invite pushback — next slide takes it up.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How do we know the shift is real?
text:
How do we know the shift is real?
Guriev & Treisman’s evidence isn’t a chart alone — it’s a coding exercise: they classify autocrats’ rule by tactics used (violence, censorship, faked elections, propaganda) across decades and track the mix over time.

Pressure it: is this a genuine trend, or survivorship — the fear dictators are disproportionately the ones who got overthrown, so they’re under-represented in a late-period sample?

This is the module’s recurring methodological question, applied to a new case: what would count as evidence for a claim like “dictatorship has changed”? Guriev and Treisman’s own answer is a systematic coding of leader tactics across a large sample of autocracies since 1946, not an impressionistic before/after story — worth naming that as a design choice, because “count things across many cases and code them the same way” is the method that recurs across nearly every reading this term (Geddes/Wright/ Frantz’s regime typology, King/Pan/Roberts’ post classification later this lecture, V-Dem’s whole enterprise).


Use the survivorship pushback as a genuine open question — it’s unresolved in the literature.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Callback: Svolik’s two problems
Week 1’s spine, back again:

Power-sharing — controlling your allies, who could depose you
Control — controlling the masses, who could rise against you


Propaganda and censorship look like mass-control tools by default. The next slide argues they’re doing power-sharing work too.

Say the callback out loud. Sets up the elite twist — don’t give it away, let the next slide land it.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
For the masses: manufacturing popularity
Guriev & Treisman’s whole “informational autocrat” story: propaganda’s mass-facing job is to manufacture the appearance of popularity and competence — not necessarily genuine belief.

This is the mass-facing half of the elite/mass split. The audience doesn’t need to believe the regime is popular; it needs to believe other people believe it, which is a different and easier thing to manufacture — a point that will matter again in Week 11’s discussion of preference falsification.


Keep short — restates fear/spin. New content is next slide.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: For elites: airtime as a loyalty signal
text:
For elites: airtime as a loyalty signal
The twist: state TV airtime also does elite-facing work — who gets invited on, who gets cut off, tells the elite who’s currently in favour.


“Rulers in selectorate theory bribe elites to prevent coups. Our rulers bribe them — or censor them — to stay silent, so as to avoid mass unrest.”
— Guriev & Treisman, “Informational Autocrats” (2019)


Propaganda is easy to read as purely mass-facing (winning over the public), but Guriev and Treisman’s own framing is that informational autocrats have to simultaneously manage a mass audience (via manufactured popularity) and an elite audience (via co-opting or silencing the people who actually know the regime’s flaws). Same tool, two jobs at once — exactly like Week 5’s parties and Week 6’s elections.


Say explicitly: same tool, doing two jobs at once.


The quote and the elite-management framing come from Noah’s own MSc class-1 discussion notes (8056 class 1 notes.txt, POP88264) — his gloss on Guriev & Treisman 2019 was “info autocrat strategy involves shifting threat from public to elites… prevent elite members from revealing the regime’s flaws to the general public.” That’s sharper than anything in the required book chapter alone; worth deciding whether to assign the 2019 JEP article alongside the book chapter, or keep it as a lecture-only addition.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Propaganda nobody believes
The puzzle: much state propaganda is transparently absurd. So why produce it?

Signalling strength — only a powerful regime can flood the zone unopposed
Demonstrating loyalty — repeating the absurd is a costly loyalty test
Demoralisation — convince people resistance is hopeless, not that the lie is true


Cold call: “is propaganda aimed at believers, or at doubters?”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How do we know it’s signalling, not persuasion?
text:
How do we know it’s signalling, not persuasion?
Huang’s design: if propaganda were meant to persuade, more of it should make people believe the regime is more popular. If it’s meant to signal capacity, more of it should make people more certain the regime is strong — whether or not they like it.

His survey evidence backs the second story: heavier propaganda exposure tracks perceived regime strength, not warmer feelings toward it.

Huang, Haifeng. 2015. “Propaganda as Signaling.” Comparative Politics 47(4). The design logic worth naming on-slide: a persuasion account and a signalling account make different predictions about what changes when propaganda exposure goes up — liking, or perceived strength. Huang’s survey data supports the signalling account. This is the third “how do we know?” moment of the lecture — three different research designs (coding leader tactics, classifying censored posts, surveying propaganda exposure) all converging on the same strategic-logic story.


cc: unverified — the specific survey numbers (sample, country, effect size) in Huang 2015 are not independently confirmed in this pass; the finding as stated is the paper’s headline claim per its own abstract/framing, but check the exact figures before quoting a number on-slide.


Third of three “how do we know?” moments — coding tactics, classifying posts, surveying beliefs. Name the set by the end.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The costly-signal trick
Why would a regime want its slogans to be implausible?

Because anyone who repeats an obvious absurdity has publicly burned their own credibility. That’s the point — the lie is the loyalty test.

Cold call, don’t just read the answer. Slow down — most portable idea in the week, returns in Week 11.


Noah: meme placeholder here — the “this is fine” dog, or any current meme about visibly implausible official messaging, would land perfectly on this slide’s argument.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The limiting case: North Korea
If the theory is right, the most absurd propaganda should come from the most secure regimes — not the most fragile ones.


State media reports the Leader shot a record-breaking round of golf, or that the birth of the dynasty was marked by a double rainbow
Nobody inside or outside the country believes it literally
The absurdity is the flex: only total control of the information space lets you say something this ridiculous and pay no price for it


IMAGE — a KCNA (North Korean state media) broadcast still or front page, current to 2026 if possible. Source: KCNA Watch archive or Wikimedia Commons (“Korean Central Television”).


Currency check before delivery: pick a current (2026) North Korean state-media claim rather than reusing an old one — KCNA produces fresh material constantly, no need to rely on a dated example.


Ask first: “which regime should have the most outlandish propaganda — strong or weak?” North Korea is the ceiling case, not an exception.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Havel’s greengrocer
The lived version of the same logic — Václav Havel’s essay “The Power of the Powerless” (1978), on a shopkeeper who puts a sign in his window:


“Workers of the world, unite!”



He doesn’t believe it. His customers don’t believe it. Everyone knows nobody believes it. He puts it up anyway — because not putting it up is the dangerous act.

IMAGE — a communist-era shop-window propaganda sign or storefront, Prague or another Eastern Bloc city, mid-20th century. Source: Wikimedia Commons (search “communist propaganda shop window” / “Prague 1970s storefront”).


Václav Havel, “The Power of the Powerless” (1978). Havel’s point is that the sign isn’t communication, it’s compliance made visible — a small, costless (to the regime) ritual that every citizen performs, and the performing is what holds the system together.


Same logic as the costly-signal slide, from the citizen’s side. Bridges to Week 11’s preference falsification.


Havel isn’t one of the module’s five core-text authors, so this breaks the “scholar’s spiciest line” framing slightly — flagging since the brief specifically nominated this as a big-quote candidate. If you’d rather keep the big quote strictly to a core-text author, the Guriev & Treisman “bribe them — or censor them” line earlier could carry that role instead and this slide could shrink to a supporting example.
PRIOR-EXPOSURE FLAG (verified against the Comparative A dumps): the greengrocer — along with Kuran and preference falsification — appears in Comparative A’s Week 11 (protest), which much of this cohort took. Doesn’t kill the slide (it’s doing propaganda-logic work here, not protest work), but deliver it as “you may remember this fellow” rather than a reveal, and coordinate with Week 11 of THIS module, which also touches Kuran-adjacent material and carries the same flag.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: If nobody’s fooled, why does the sign matter?
text:
If nobody’s fooled, why does the sign matter?
The regime doesn’t need the greengrocer to believe the slogan. It needs him to perform believing it, in public, where his neighbours can see.

Let it sit a beat. Pivot from “why produce unbelievable propaganda” to “why does the audience play along.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Find the lie that’s not meant to be believed
text:
Find the lie that’s not meant to be believed
Pair up, two minutes. Think of a piece of propaganda, current or historical, that nobody involved actually believes.

What is it actually doing, if not persuading anyone?

Noah: bring a real, current propaganda artefact to project — a state-TV clip, a poster, a headline. Doesn’t need to be Russian or Chinese; anything current works as long as the “nobody’s fooled, and that’s the point” logic is visible in it. Your call on which one.


Genuine 2-min pair discussion. Walk the room, pull 2–3 answers before your own artefact. “Hold onto that thought” gestures forward to Week 11.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Two different jobs, one goal

Propaganda manufactures belief (or the performance of it) — what the regime wants said
Censorship manages the absence of belief — what the regime stops others from saying


Both are about controlling the information the regime is judged on. Now the same question, from the other direction: what actually gets censored?

Fast landing slide before King/Pan/Roberts.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
What survives: individual complaint
King, Pan & Roberts on China (they also appeared in Week 4): complaints about local officials, corruption, even the regime itself — mostly survive censorship.

Complaints are useful to the regime — they’re free intelligence on local officials (tie back to Week 5: the party as monitoring device). A ruler who deletes every complaint blinds itself to exactly the information it needs.


Keep short — setup for the contrast next slide, not the punchline.


Prior-exposure flag (brief, “Prior exposure” section). King, Pan & Roberts was very likely on this cohort’s Comparative Politics reading list already (their “Varieties of Authoritarianism” week runs the full KPR study as a standalone case in collective-action theory). Teach it here as “the study you may have met, now placed inside the strategic logic of the week” — i.e. don’t re-derive the empirical design from scratch, do connect it explicitly to the fear→spin and signalling arguments above, which Comparative’s version doesn’t build. Worth a one-line acknowledgement on the slide itself: “you may know this paper from second year — here’s where it fits in this course’s argument.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
What doesn’t: coordination
Censor coordination, not complaint.

Let people grumble about the potholes. Stop them from organising about the potholes.

IMAGE — a “what gets censored vs. what’s allowed” contrast graphic: two mocked-up posts, one complaining about a local official (survives), one calling for a protest gathering (deleted within minutes). KPR’s own coding scheme is a good template if grounding it in the actual paper.


Pair the two slides (“survives” / “doesn’t”) as one beat — no gap between them.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How do we know? The numbers behind “coordination, not complaint”
text:
How do we know? The numbers behind “coordination, not complaint”
King, Pan & Roberts hand-collected and automatically classified millions of Chinese social media posts by topic, then tracked which were censored.

Their finding: posts criticising the state were about as likely to survive as any other post. Posts with collective-action potential — regardless of whether they were pro- or anti-government — were far more likely to be deleted.

King, Gary, Jennifer Pan, and Molly Roberts. 2013. “How Censorship in China Allows Government Criticism but Silences Collective Expression.” American Political Science Review 107(2). Their central finding, in their own phrase, is that individual criticism of the government is tolerated while collective action — organising, mobilising, gathering — is what triggers deletion, whatever its political valence. The design point worth stressing: they didn’t just read posts and guess, they built a system to classify censored versus surviving content at scale and test which feature of a post (criticism vs. organisational potential) predicted removal.


“Individually free but collectively in chains.” Name the method (large-scale automated classification) as a model design.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Censor too much, or too little?
text:
Censor too much, or too little?
Which is the bigger risk for a regime?

No clean answer — that’s the point. Take the vote before the reveal.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
What censorship costs the censor
Recall Week 4: repression destroys the information the ruler needs.

Censor too well → you can’t hear the warning signs either
Officials learn to report what the centre wants to hear
The regime’s own picture of the country degrades


Every information tool cuts both ways. Nobody is more deceived than the successful deceiver.


IMG truth-funnel.png — hand-built conceptual diagram (no external data), copied from the Intro module’s Dictatorships II deck (w08-lec12-img/), full credit in w08img/CREDITS.md. Illustrates truth narrowing as it moves up four reporting layers (local official → agency → inner circle → autocrat) — exactly this slide’s argument, reused rather than rebuilt.


Through-line: control creates blindness. Sets up Week 11 — the regime is often last to know how much opposition exists.


Noah: a Soviet-era anekdot about local officials falsifying harvest reports upward (there are several well-known ones) would land perfectly here — this is exactly the “nobody is more deceived than the successful deceiver” joke in its classic form.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Cases compared: three regimes, one goal
text:
Cases compared: three regimes, one goal
Same underlying goal across all three — control the information the regime is judged on. What differs is how much effort it takes, and when.

IMAGE — a Soviet-era propaganda poster (e.g. a well-known “glory to labour” or harvest-quota poster), for visual contrast with the Russia-today and China entries on the next slide. Source: Wikimedia Commons (“Soviet propaganda poster”).


Let this land as a claim before the table backs it up case by case.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: USSR and Russia: one country, two eras
text:
USSR and Russia: one country, two eras

USSR — the classic model: total control, mandatory belief, gigantic apparatus, fear-dictator era
Russia today — narrative dominance via TV, not total control of speech; Rozenas & Stukal show state TV slants economic news hardest precisely when the real economy is doing worst — management, not blanket lying


The strongest “before/after” case you have all term — same country, same underlying goal, a fifty-year gap in method.

USSR→Russia contrast makes the fear→spin shift concrete before China.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: China: the bridge to next week
text:
China: the bridge to next week
China — vast, selective, and increasingly automated; censors coordination (KPR), leaves grumbling alone.

Three different amounts of effort, three different eras of the fear→spin shift — same underlying job. China is the bridge to next week: the machinery goes digital.

Currency check: China’s censorship apparatus is the one that dates fastest here — note that the automation/AI-moderation side of it belongs properly to Week 9 (Digital Authoritarianism); keep this slide to the analog/organisational picture (censors, directives, the Great Firewall as an institution, not its current technical implementation).


IMAGE — a simple diagram of the Great Firewall as an institutional apparatus (agencies, directives, the licensing system), not a technical/network diagram — that belongs to Week 9. Source: an explainer figure from a source like the China Media Project or a V-Dem/Freedom House report.


Say the bridge to Week 9 out loud — don’t describe the Firewall’s mechanics, that’s next week’s job.


Noah: currency check on the China apparatus specifics before this delivery — personnel/agency names shift; confirm whatever specific detail you want to cite is still accurate for MT2026.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Propaganda and censorship: one strategic logic
text:
Propaganda and censorship: one strategic logic
Both manage what a regime is judged on — belief and behaviour, not truth. Neither tool is really aimed at persuasion; both are aimed at making the right things visible and the wrong things costly.

Propaganda manufactures compliance (Havel) and signals capacity (Huang)
Censorship protects the picture by removing what threatens coordination (King/Pan/Roberts), at the cost of the regime’s own information (Week 4)


Next week: what happens to both when the tools go digital, and whether a machine can do this work more cheaply than a censor or a state broadcaster ever could.

Say the throughline out loud: information control is never about truth, always about behaviour and belief.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Key readings this week

Guriev & Treisman, Spin Dictators — selected chapter
Huang, “Propaganda as Signaling,” Comparative Politics (2015)


Recommended: King, Pan & Roberts, “How Censorship in China Allows Government Criticism but Silences Collective Expression,” APSR (2013)


Candidates for the recommended list, not committed — propose only: Guriev & Treisman, “Informational Autocrats,” JEP (2019) (the article version of tonight’s core argument, and the source of the elite-signalling quote used earlier — citation verified 2026-09-16); Rozenas & Stukal, “How Autocrats Manipulate Economic News,” J. of Politics (2019) (Russia-specific empirical grounding, from Noah’s own MSc reading bank — POP88264 “Hybrid Regimes” week, not yet on any undergrad list; citation verified 2026-09-16).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
For next week
Week 9 — Digital Authoritarianism

Hellmeier, “The Dictator’s Digital Toolkit: Explaining Variation in Internet Filtering in Authoritarian Regimes,” Politics & Policy 44(6) (2016): 1158–1191
Xu, “To Repress or to Co-opt? Authoritarian Control in the Age of Digital Surveillance,” AJPS 65(2) (2021): 309–325

Think about — and this is your response-paper prompt seed: if propaganda is mostly signalling rather than persuasion, does it still “work” once everyone knows that’s what it’s doing? Or does the signal collapse once the audience is in on the game?

One line only — don’t start Week 9’s material. Ask them to write down a guess before they leave.

See you next Friday

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Buying Loyalty
Parties, Parliaments & Patronage
Why build a parliament you control? Because it’s useful — not decorative.


Puzzle: why build institutions you could just not have — and then pay the people inside them?
Answer: tools, not theatre.



MERGED WEEK (former Week 5, parties & legislatures + former Week 8, co-optation & distributive politics — decided 2026-07-29, see PLAN-MT2026.md §2). One argument runs through the whole 50 minutes: autocrats institutionalise in order to make co-optation credible, and the currency that flows through the machine is offices, rents and spoils. This is now the longest week in the module. If it won’t fit: cut “When does the bargain break?” first and fold a compressed version into Week 11 — flagged again at that slide below. Don’t cut the Mexico/China/Gulf cases; they’re doing the load-bearing comparative work.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Today

Why do dictatorships bother with parties and parliaments?
Institutions as tools of co-optation and credible power-sharing
Cases: Mexico’s PRI, China’s NPC, Russia’s United Russia
Patronage, clientelism, spoils — and who’s worth buying, elites or masses?
Case: the Gulf bargain vs. Jordan’s no-oil version
Rents and the authoritarian bargain — and when it breaks


Signpost: machinery first, then the currency flowing through it — one system.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
This week in autocracy


Noah: two or three stories from this week. One line each — headline, country, and the concept it illustrates (elite problem or mass problem?). This slide is the same shape every week, same slot, right after the plan.


Five minutes, no more. Ask the room first: “what happened this week that belongs in this module?” — then show yours. The point is the habit: by teaching week 12 they should be bringing the stories, not you.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Why would a dictator ever share power?
text:
Why would a dictator ever share power?
If the dictator makes all the decisions, why have a legislature at all? Why tolerate a “ruling party” with its own bureaucracy, its own factions, its own appetite?

Cold call: ask someone to defend “it’s all fake, window-dressing” — let the room dismantle it before the quote on the next slide.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
“Not mistakes, not window-dressing”

Authoritarian institutions are not mistakes, and they are not window-dressing. They do work for the regime.


But what work, exactly — and work for whom?

Political scientists used to treat authoritarian parties and legislatures as props — evidence of a dictator’s vanity, or a fig leaf for the outside world. The newer institutionalist literature (Gandhi, Magaloni, Svolik) argues the opposite: these bodies cost the regime real money and real risk to build and maintain, and regimes don’t spend real resources on pure theatre for decades at a time. If institutions survive, they must be doing work.


If “it’s all fake” is already on the table, this quote is the rebuttal — let it land.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Two functions

Co-optation — give rivals and constituencies a seat at the table, a stake in the system’s survival, not just the leader’s
Credible power-sharing — make the leader’s commitments to the elite observable and enforceable, so a promise isn’t just a promise


Recall Week 3: institutions can substitute for trust that can’t otherwise exist between people who each have the means to destroy the other.

Co-optation means bringing potential rivals — individuals, factions, groups — inside the regime with a formal stake in its survival, rather than leaving them outside as opposition. Credible power-sharing means the leader’s promises to elites are backed by something more than the leader’s word: a rule, a body, a procedure the leader would pay a real cost to override. Institutions do both jobs at once.


Diagram: “ruling party / legislature” branching to → co-optation (outsiders brought in) and → power-sharing (insiders bound). Two arrows off one box. Build in Keynote or a simple SVG, drop in w05img/.


Payoff of Week 3’s commitment-problem setup. Gandhi & Przeworski = co-optation; Magaloni = credible commitment — complementary, not competing (common misreading to pre-empt).


Prior exposure flag (brief §“prior exposure,” applies to Weeks 2/6/8/11/12 generally, and lands here too): Comparative Politics A’s authoritarianism week already told students that “institutionalised regimes seem to last longer,” gave Mexico under the PRI as the headline example, and cited Magaloni by name as the reference for why. So this is not students’ first contact with “institutions solve commitment problems” — it’s their first contact with the mechanics. Say so explicitly in the room: “you met this idea in Comparative; today we open the machine up.” Don’t reintroduce it as news.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Parties as the autocrat’s best friend
text:
Parties as the autocrat’s best friend
If you take one piece of advice from this module into your career as a dictator: get a party.

Distribute spoils and careers → bind the ambitious to the regime, not just to the leader personally
Mobilise voters, monitor local loyalty, gather information the leader can’t get any other way
Outlast any single leader → solve the succession problem that personalist regimes (Week 2) struggle with


Single-party regimes are the most durable authoritarian type on record (recall Week 2). This is why — not because one party is more popular, but because it is a machine for manufacturing loyalty at scale.

A single-party regime, in this sense, is not “one popular party” — it is a career structure. Everyone ambitious inside the country has a reason to join the party rather than oppose it, because the party is where careers, salaries and protection actually come from. Personalist regimes (Week 2) lack this: loyalty runs to one man, and when he goes, the machine has no rails to run on.


Bridge to Week 2: they’ve seen single-party regimes outlast others — this supplies the mechanism.


Source: Waller, Statecraft 10 Sep 2026 — “If you’re trying to build an authoritarian regime, you really, really, really want a party,” on parties as the single best-value institution a would-be autocrat can build.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
No re-election, ever
How did a single party actually run this for seven decades? First moving part, per Magaloni:

Every office — municipal, state, federal — turned over on a fixed clock. That sounds like accountability.
It’s actually a career escalator: everyone in the party is always queuing for the next rung, which means everyone has a stake in staying inside the machine, not in winning votes against it.


The camarilla ladder. Careers ran through patron–client networks (camarillas) — a rising politician attaches to a senior patron, rises with them, and is expected to bring loyal juniors of their own up behind. Climb by loyalty to your camarilla, not by winning votes.

IMAGE — the camarilla ladder as a diagram: patron → juniors → juniors’ own juniors, three tiers, arrows down. Build in Keynote or a simple SVG, drop in w05img/.


Term limits usually read as a democratic safeguard. Here the same rule does authoritarian work instead: because no one can entrench in one office, every ambitious politician stays inside the party’s internal competition for the next rung rather than breaking away to build an independent power base.


Go slower here than anywhere else — most counter-intuitive slide in the deck.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Why generalise the PRI rule?
The camarilla ladder isn’t a Mexican quirk — it’s one version of a general fix every durable regime needs.

Rotation of cadres: move people through posts on a fixed clock, so no one entrenches a personal power base and everyone ambitious keeps climbing toward the next rung
Same logic runs modern militaries — commands rotate every 2–3 years even in peacetime, precisely so no officer builds their own fiefdom
Fail to rotate, and careers block: officials age in place, juniors stop rising, and the regime loses both fresh blood and a loyal reason to stay


Elite circulation and blockage: a durable regime needs elites to believe their careers are still moving. Classical elite theory (Michels, Mosca, Pareto) noticed that the people at the top of any organisation persist across upheavals even when institutions change completely around them — which is exactly why regimes manage circulation deliberately rather than leaving it to chance. Rotation of cadres is the tool: fixed terms, planned promotions, posts that don’t become permanent fiefdoms. When rotation stops — when the same person holds the same post for a decade or more — juniors stop rising, ambition curdles into resentment, and the regime has manufactured its own discontented elite.


Currency check — live Russian illustration, flag speculation as speculation. Alexei Dyumin (53): Putin’s bodyguard → provincial governor → head of the State Council — the rotation model working as designed, and speculatively discussed as a possible successor (unconfirmed; Putin has not named an heir). Against him: Alexander Bortnikov, FSB director since the early 2010s, still in post — the blockage pathology, with his deputies aging in place beneath him. Putin himself is “almost 74.” Source: Waller, Statecraft 10 Sep 2026.



Say it: this is the failure mode Mexico’s rule guards against.
Dyumin/Bortnikov = clean before/after pair.
Keep succession as speculation — don’t let “next president” sound settled.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: The peasant with a stake in the PRI staying in office
text:
The peasant with a stake in the PRI staying in office
Second moving part: corporatist incorporation. The PRI didn’t just co-opt elites.

It formally absorbed labour (CTM), the peasantry (CNC), and the urban “popular” sector (CNOP) as official party sectors
Land reform (ejidos) ran through the peasant sector: access to land was administratively tied to party loyalty


An entire agrarian class had a direct, personal stake in the PRI staying in office — this is co-optation reaching the masses, not just the elite.

Ejido point: co-optation of the masses, not just elites — mass-side mirror of the camarilla ladder. Pause here.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Elections as an internal instrument
Here’s the sharpest reframe in the literature: PRI elections were mostly not for the voters.

Elections were a sorting device inside the party — they showed which local bosses could still deliver turnout, which is exactly the information the centre needed to allocate the next round of promotions
They legalised intra-party competition — factions duking it out at the ballot box instead of at gunpoint


First half: elections as party management, not public contest. Riskier claim (only holds while mass support lasts) is next slide.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: When do internal elections stop being safe?
text:
When do internal elections stop being safe?
They only became genuinely risky once mass support for the regime itself started to erode.

Elite unity depends on mass support — not the other way around.

It is tempting to think elites hold power and decide, one by one, whether to share it with the public. Magaloni’s argument runs backwards: elite loyalty is downstream of mass opinion. Elites stay loyal only as long as they believe defecting would fail — and that belief tracks how much public support the regime still commands.


This is Magaloni’s real argument — plant it, don’t resolve fully; the big-quote slide later closes it.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
China’s National People’s Congress

The world’s favourite “rubber-stamp legislature.” Nearly 3,000 delegates. Approval rates north of 99%. So why does the Party keep it running?


Delegates channel local grievances upward and act as an early-warning system for problems the central leadership would otherwise only learn about from unrest
The NPC — and its provincial-level equivalents — genuinely monitor implementation: are local officials delivering on directives, skimming funds, mishandling a scandal?
None of this constrains the Party’s decisions. All of it improves the Party’s information.


“Rubber-stamp” is the standard shorthand and it isn’t wrong about votes — the NPC has never rejected a leadership bill. It is wrong about function. Nearly 3,000 delegates, drawn from every province and sector, are a cheap way to gather information a closed leadership cannot get any other way: which local officials are underperforming, where a policy is landing badly, where unrest risk is building. Not decorative. Not democratic either. A monitoring institution wearing a legislature’s clothes.


IMG party-congress.jpg (18th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, 2012 — full hall, tiered seating) — technically the Party Congress rather than the NPC itself, used here as a visual stand-in for “the machinery of mass institutionalised representation”; swap for an actual NPC chamber shot if you find one on Commons. Credit in w05img/CREDITS.md. Delete the image line to drop it.


Point: break the lazy “rubber stamp = meaningless” equivalence.


Truex, Making Autocracy Work (2016) is the strongest single source for this slide’s claim and isn’t currently in _course.yml’s recommended list for this week — propose adding it there rather than assuming it’s already covered. Worth pairing with King/Pan/Roberts (already recommended, Week 4) as two halves of the same “authoritarian institutions as information technology” family.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How would we know a legislature is doing real work?
text:
How would we know a legislature is doing real work?
Approval rate north of 99% either means total control, or total irrelevance — which is it, and what evidence would tell them apart?

Answer: look at what changes between bill-in and bill-out, not the final vote. Same move as Week 4’s propaganda-effects problem.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: What is a Duma seat actually for?
text:
What is a Duma seat actually for?

United Russia was assembled in December 2001 — not to win arguments. To organise loyalty.

2021: 324 of 450 seats — a constitutional supermajority
A seat buys a salary, immunity from prosecution, and a place near whoever hands out contracts
Lose the party’s favour and you lose all three at once


The difference from Mexico and China: this party was built after the leader already had power, to lock it in — not the other way round.

Adapted from the POU11011 Dictatorships I deck’s “What is a Duma seat actually for?” slide (../POU11011 Intro to Political Science MT2026/slides/w08-lec11.qmd) — same cohort could take both modules, so this is deliberately shorter and folded into the comparative frame rather than reused verbatim. Sources there: Prensa Latina, 22 Sep 2021; Wikipedia, United Russia (founding congress 1 Dec 2001).


IMG duma.jpg (State Duma plenary session, 10 March 2020 — full chamber, tiered seating). Credit in w05img/CREDITS.md. Delete the image line to drop it.


Quick — third case, not third argument. One beat: same loyalty-machine logic works even when the party comes after the strongman. Sets up “Cases compared.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Cases compared

Mexico (PRI) — the textbook single-party machine: careers, camarillas, corporatist sectors
China (NPC) — a “rubber-stamp” legislature that does real monitoring work
Russia (United Russia) — a party built after Putin already had power, to lock it in rather than to win it


Different origins, same underlying logic: bind elites, manage rivals, distribute the spoils, and manufacture the information the centre needs.
One more distinction worth holding onto (Week 2): Mexico and Russia are dominant-party regimes — a party that organises power alongside other, weaker parties. China is a party-state — the party doesn’t sit alongside the state, it shadows and runs it. Different machines, not different sizes of the same machine.

Source: Waller, Statecraft 10 Sep 2026 — the party-state (Leninist, party parallel to every state institution) vs. the dominant-party regime (Mexico’s PRI, Russia’s United Russia) as genuinely different organisational forms, not points on one spectrum.


Three regimes, three different starting points — a hegemonic party that predates any one leader (Mexico), a Leninist party-state (China), a party built to lock in power a leader already held (Russia) — converging on the same design problem: elites need a reason to stay in, and the centre needs information it cannot get by decree alone.


IMAGE — a PRI-era rally or campaign photo (Wikimedia Commons; search “PRI Mexico rally” or the party’s historical archive) to complete the three-case visual set alongside duma.jpg and party-congress.jpg already placed on their own slides above. Drop in w05img/.


Mined from Noah’s own material (per brief): Russian Politics HT2027 week06/week08 (AY2026-27/POU44172 .../slides/week06.qmd, week08.qmd) carry his own Russia patronage examples in detail — political machines and clientelism (Frye/Reuter/Szakonyi), “patrimonial capitalism” (Robinson), crony capitalism (Sharafutdinova), the “grabbing hand” (Frye & Shleifer). The next two slides pull from that material. Flagging per the brief: this is the same cohort that could plausibly take Russian Politics too, so don’t lean on identical examples in both modules the same term — pick a different Russia anecdote here than whatever ends up in POU44172’s live delivery, or make the overlap explicit and treat it as reinforcement rather than repetition.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The toolkit of co-optation

Patronage — jobs, contracts, offices for the loyal
Clientelism — targeted goods exchanged for support, one relationship at a time
Spoils — let your coalition skim the rents, and make sure everyone knows the tap can be turned off


Repression makes people afraid to oppose you. Co-optation makes them want not to.

Three overlapping terms, worth keeping distinct. Patronage is the broadest: distributing state jobs, contracts or offices as rewards for loyalty. Clientelism is patronage’s retail form — a targeted exchange between a specific patron and a specific client, good for good. Spoils is patronage at the top: letting a ruling coalition profit from office, with the implicit threat that the tap can be turned off if loyalty lapses.


A patronage-flow diagram — ruler → broker → client → vote/loyalty — or an oil-rents bar chart for a Gulf state. Drop in w05img/.


Say it: the party is the distribution machinery from before — institutions and co-optation are one coin.


Optional Russia beat here, mined from POU44172 week08: Frye & Shleifer’s “grabbing hand” vs. “helping hand” vs. “invisible hand” framing (state as predator vs. developmental partner vs. neutral referee) is a clean, portable one-liner if you want a fourth region represented on this slide without a full case study. Robinson’s “patrimonial capitalism” — political leadership outside democratic constraint, using formal rules to punish disloyalty while informal practice consolidates elite control of rents — is the denser version if you have the two minutes.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Which lever does each case pull?
text:
Which lever does each case pull?

Mexico — patronage (careers) + clientelism (ejido land)
China — patronage (party rank) + information, not spoils
Russia — patronage (Duma seats as salary and immunity)
Gulf — spoils, distributed as universal rents


No case uses only one tool. The mix is the diagnosis.

Rhetorical mapping — don’t let it become a taxonomy slide. One toolkit, different mixes.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Two minutes, in pairs
Pick a regime you know something about — doesn’t have to be one we’ve covered. In pairs: is it buying loyalty mostly from elites, mostly from the masses, or genuinely both? What’s the evidence you’d point to?

Pair discuss, actually two minutes — set a timer. Pull 2–3 pairs before the next slide resolves elite/mass.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Who do you buy: elites or masses?
text:
Who do you buy: elites or masses?
Limited resources. You can’t pay everyone. So whom?

Buy the elites to prevent coups (Week 3’s problem, and Week 10’s). Buy the masses to prevent revolts (Week 11’s problem). Most regimes do some of both — but rarely in equal measure, and the mix tells you a lot about a regime’s actual vulnerability.


Spine callback: Svolik’s elite control vs. mass control (Week 1).
Chalkboard both threads, keep up — weeks 6/10/11 return to this.
Cold call: which lever did Mexico lean on? The Gulf?

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: The spiciest line in the reading
text:
The spiciest line in the reading

“In electoral dictatorships, elite unity requires mass support, whereas the absence of mass support boosts potential opponents’ chances to attain power by forming a rival political organization and mobilizing citizens against the dictator.”
— Magaloni, Comparative Political Studies (2008), p.729


Read that twice. Elite loyalty isn’t independent of mass opinion — it’s downstream of it. Elites defect when they think the public would let them get away with it.

Let it sit without narrating. Resolves the elite-vs-mass binary: buying mass quiescence keeps elite loyalty cheap.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
What we parked in week 1
“Are dictatorships good at anything? Growth? Order? Getting things done?”

You banked answers about China. Time to test them.

Callback to week 1’s straw poll — remind them what they said before the next slide complicates it.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: The case for: get things done fast
text:
The case for: get things done fast
No opposition to negotiate with, no election to lose, no court to overrule you.

Singapore — decades of high growth under one-party dominance (PAP)
South Korea under Park Chung-hee (1961–79) — military rule, state-led industrialisation, the “Miracle on the Han”
China since 1978 — the fastest sustained growth in human history, no multiparty competition at any point


The intuition: a dictator can just decide, and build the dam.

The naive case for dictatorship rests on decisiveness: a leader unconstrained by opposition parties, courts or elections can commit to a long infrastructure project or an unpopular reform and see it through, where a democratic government facing re-election every few years might not. Singapore, Park-era South Korea and post-1978 China are the examples this argument reaches for almost every time it’s made.


Let this case land before complicating it — it’s the prior from week 1’s poll.


IMAGE — a Park Chung-hee-era industrial photo or Singapore skyline (Wikimedia Commons) as a .img-right beside the bullets.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: For every Singapore, there’s a Zaire
text:
For every Singapore, there’s a Zaire

Przeworski & Limongi, “Political Regimes and Economic Growth,” Journal of Economic Perspectives 7(3), 1993
Across the full historical record, regime type doesn’t reliably predict average growth — democracies and dictatorships grow at similar rates on average
What dictatorship predicts is variance: autocracies produce both the best growth performances on record and the worst


Singapore and Zaire under Mobutu are both dictatorships. Only one built anything.

Przeworski and Limongi’s finding is a selection problem, not a growth recipe. If you only look at the successful autocracies — Singapore, South Korea, China — dictatorship looks like a growth strategy. Widen the sample to every autocracy that ever existed and the average disappears into noise, because dictatorship also produced Mobutu’s Zaire, Idi Amin’s Uganda and North Korea’s famine. The lesson isn’t “autocracy helps or hurts growth” — it’s that autocracy removes the guardrails in both directions at once.


Mobutu’s Zaire is the standard illustrative contrast case in this literature (a kleptocratic personalist dictatorship with severe, sustained economic decline); it is not necessarily the specific comparator country used in Przeworski & Limongi’s own regression sample — treat it as illustrative, not as a citation to their data.


Go slower here — the real work of the block. Selection-effect point is a survivorship-bias argument; name that parallel.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Why would a self-interested dictator ever build anything?
text:
Why would a self-interested dictator ever build anything?
If he answers to no one, what stops him from just taking everything now?

Cold call: let someone try “fear of a coup” or “wants to be loved” — Olson’s answer is colder than either.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: The bandit who decides to stay
text:
The bandit who decides to stay
Olson, “Dictatorship, Democracy, and Development,” American Political Science Review 87(3), 1993.

A roving bandit grabs what it can and moves on — no reason to leave anything behind
A stationary bandit who plans to rule this territory forever has an encompassing interest: tax the same economy for decades, and it pays to let it grow first


Even a purely self-interested autocrat becomes, in effect, a long-term investor in his own tax base.

Olson’s insight reframes the autocrat’s self-interest rather than assuming he has any public-spirited motive at all. A roving bandit maximises this year’s plunder because there is no next year with this population. A stationary bandit who expects to rule the same territory for decades maximises his share of a growing pie over time — which means investing in roads, courts and property rights that a purely predatory ruler would never bother with. The same self-interest that makes a bandit dangerous also, under the right time horizon, makes him a developer.


Payoff to the cold call: not benevolence — self-interest over a long horizon does the job of a growth strategy.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Where the logic breaks
Encompassing interest assumes the dictator expects to still be there to collect the second half of the pie.

Succession uncertainty shortens the time horizon — a ruler unsure he’ll survive to next year discounts the future hard, and starts behaving like a roving bandit again
Same logic explains looting sprees at the end of personalist regimes, not just at the start


Week 10’s succession problem is this same logic, one level up: coup-proofing also costs growth.

Forward link only — flag Week 10’s succession connection, don’t teach it yet.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Back to this week’s frame
The whole machine you’ve spent the lecture on — parties, patronage, rents — runs on money.

Development is where the money comes from. A dictatorship that can’t grow the pie has less to buy loyalty with, elite or mass.

Tie-back: this answers “where does the co-optation budget come from.” Say it before the Gulf case — the purest version, rents without growing anything.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Why does every defence of dictatorship cite Singapore?
text:
Why does every defence of dictatorship cite Singapore?
One small, unusual city-state. Never Zaire. Never North Korea. Why?

Pair discuss, 2 min. Honest answer: survivorship bias + Singapore’s unusual starting conditions — steer back to the variance point.


Boundary, said out loud in the room, per PLAN-MT2026.md §3: this block stays on what autocracy does to growth performance — selection, variance, time horizons. Modernisation theory and the democratisation-and-development question (does growth cause democratisation?) belong to Democracy & Development A (D’Arcy) — credit her module by name if a student asks about that direction of the arrow.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The authoritarian bargain
The implicit deal in many resource-rich states:


We give you welfare, jobs, subsidies, and security. You give up political voice.



“No taxation, so no representation.” Rents let rulers skip the bargain that historically built democracies — the state doesn’t need your money, so it doesn’t need your consent either.

One line only. Boundary: D’Arcy’s module does taxation-and-state-building — credit it, don’t teach Tilly here.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Case: the Gulf monarchies
Vast hydrocarbon rents → generous subsidies, public jobs, no income tax → a durable bargain.

But what happens when the oil money gets tight?

IMG gulf-skyline.jpg (Dubai skyline at dusk). Credit in w05img/CREDITS.md. Delete background-image= and background-opacity= from the heading to drop it · raise/lower background-opacity to taste (0.35 now, tuned so the yellow subtitle stays legible).


This is the “masses” half of the elite/masses spine, made concrete — cleanest version of mass-side co-optation in the module.


Currency check: any specific fiscal figures used live (oil price, subsidy-spending-as-share-of-GDP, sovereign wealth fund size) need refreshing against 2026 sources before delivery — this is exactly the kind of number that goes stale fast.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Contrast case: Jordan, without the oil
text:
Contrast case: Jordan, without the oil
No comparable oil wealth. So how does a monarchy without a rentier bargain survive?

Patronage still runs through land, public-sector jobs, and tribal networks — East Bank Jordanian tribes in particular — rather than through a sovereign wealth fund
Foreign rents substitute for oil rents: aid flows from the US and Gulf states do real distributive work


The rentier bargain (welfare and jobs in exchange for political silence) is one route to mass co-optation, but it needs oil or a comparably large, unearned income stream. Jordan shows the same goal — buy quiescence — pursued with a much thinner resource base: patronage through land and public employment, topped up by foreign aid rather than a sovereign wealth fund.


Same monarchy type (Week 2), same goal, no oil. Sharper half (elections as management) is next slide — give it its own beat.


Jordan material here is built from general literature (Lust-Okar, “Elections under Authoritarianism,” Democratization 2006, the recommended reading) rather than from Noah’s own notes. Worth a fact-check pass on the East Bank tribal detail before delivery; flagging rather than asserting with full confidence.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Why does Jordan hold elections at all?
text:
Why does Jordan hold elections at all?
Elections are held — and manipulated — to manage and divide the opposition, not to select the ruler.

Lust-Okar’s argument: districting and electoral rules are engineered so competition happens among co-opted candidates, keeping any unified opposition from ever forming.


Same goal as the Gulf case — buy quiescence — achieved with a much thinner resource base and a much busier electoral toolkit.

Sharper half of the Gulf/Jordan contrast. Bridges to Week 6’s “elections as management” thread.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Which bargain is more fragile — the Gulf’s or Jordan’s?
text:
Which bargain is more fragile — the Gulf’s or Jordan’s?
Show of hands.

Straw poll — don’t resolve. Depends what shocks: oil-price crash hits the Gulf, aid cut/succession crisis hits Jordan.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
When does the bargain break?

Resource shocks — the money runs out
Demographic pressure — too many mouths, too few spoils
Rising expectations — yesterday’s gift is today’s entitlement
Or you change the deal. Everyone’s hand has been in the till; the moment prosecution becomes selective, every loyalist does the same arithmetic at the same time


Co-optation is durable — but it’s not free, and it’s not forever.

Source: Waller, Statecraft 10 Sep 2026 — on Russia’s elite contract: small-scale graft was tolerated as part of the loyalty deal; the FSB now arresting governors and businesspeople “more or less at will” reneges on that deal, and “you don’t want nervous elites.”


A stat on subsidy-cut protests (bread/fuel riots) as the hinge into the breakdown weeks. Currency-check whatever figure you use.


Noah / CC — cut this section first if the week is overrunning. Per the merge decision (PLAN-MT2026.md §2), a compressed version of “when the bargain breaks” can fold into Week 11 instead. This is the one slide-pair in the deck explicitly designed to be droppable without damaging the argument — the “why do institutions fail” question-slide immediately after can absorb its job in a single line if you do cut it.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
And why do institutions fail?
If parties and parliaments are so useful, why don’t they save every regime?

When institutions stop being credible — when the leader can override them at will — they revert to theatre. And the deal unravels.

Greene: what sustains vs. erodes single-party dominance (usually loss of resource advantage). Foreshadows weeks 10–12 — one beat only.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Three ways to buy loyalty

Careers — parties (Mexico, Russia) turn loyalty into a life-long ladder
Information — legislatures (China) turn loyalty into surveillance the centre couldn’t otherwise afford
Rents — patronage and subsidies (Gulf, Jordan) turn loyalty into a standing transfer payment


Different currencies, same trade: voice, given up, for a stake in the system that governs you.

Recap — don’t re-explain each bullet, this is the zoom-out moment.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Key readings this week

Gandhi & Przeworski, “Authoritarian Institutions and the Survival of Autocrats,” Comparative Political Studies (2007)
Magaloni, “Credible Power-Sharing and the Longevity of Authoritarian Rule,” Comparative Political Studies (2008)


Recommended: Lust-Okar on Jordan · Greene on single-party dominance · Blaydes on Mubarak’s Egypt


Propose adding Truex, Making Autocracy Work (2016) to the recommended list — it’s the strongest single source for the China NPC slide and isn’t currently in _course.yml. Flagging as a candidate only, per the brief’s “propose in cc notes, don’t add to required” instruction.


Flag mid-term essay deadline, point to the sheet. Build-a-Regime option: check they picked a case in Week 3.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
For next week
Week 6 — Elections Without Democracy

Schedler, “Elections Without Democracy: The Menu of Manipulation,” J. of Democracy (2002)
Magaloni, Voting for Autocracy — selected chapter

Think about — and this is your response-paper prompt seed: if you already control the parliament, why hold elections at all — especially ones you might have to rig, and might, in theory, lose?
See you next Friday

Continues the PRI elections-as-internal-instrument thread — say the connection out loud.


Response-paper spec is still unwritten (PLAN-MT2026.md §6.4, 10% of the mark with no guidance document anywhere yet). The “think about” question above is written to double as that prompt, per the brief, but there’s no confirmed format (length, due date relative to lecture, submission mechanism) to give students yet — don’t publish this as a formal prompt until the spec exists.

text:
See you next Friday

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How Autocrats Take and Hold Power
text:
How Autocrats Take and Hold Power
The problem isn’t seizing power. It’s keeping your friends from taking it back.

IMG parade-alt.jpg (2018 Moscow Victory Day Parade) · delete background-image= and background-opacity= from the heading to drop it · reused from the POU11011 pool, credits in w03img/CREDITS.md.


Cold open, no admin. The reframe: the deadliest threat to a dictator is usually not the masses — it’s the inner circle. Set this up immediately, don’t rush past it.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The plan for today

Where dictators come from — in five minutes, on purpose (that’s D’Arcy’s course, not ours)
The real puzzle: why can’t a dictator just trust the people who put him there?
Svolik’s answer: the commitment problem, and what regimes do about it
Cases: Stalin’s USSR, Putin’s Russia, Saddam’s Iraq — three roads to the same dilemma


Today’s readings (Svolik chs. 2–3; Boix & Svolik 2013) both turn on one idea: an authoritarian leader cannot rely on courts or constitutions to enforce deals with the people who keep him in power, so power-sharing has to be solved some other way. Everything on today’s slides is a different regime’s answer to that same problem.
