title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
This week in autocracy


Noah: two or three stories from this week. One line each — headline, country, and the concept it illustrates (elite problem or mass problem?). This slide is the same shape every week, same slot, right after the plan.


Five minutes, no more. Ask the room first: “what happened this week that belongs in this module?” — then show yours. The point is the habit: by teaching week 12 they should be bringing the stories, not you.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Origins, compressed
How a regime seized power shapes how it holds it — revolution, coup, colonial inheritance, resource wealth. A real question, with a real literature.

Revolution — strong party, ideological glue (USSR)
Coup — the military at the core from day one (much of the Middle East, Latin America)
Colonial legacy / state formation — inherited borders, inherited weakness
Economic structure — who controls the wealth, and how mobile is it? (Acemoglu & Robinson)


These four origin stories are each the subject of an entire literature — we name them and move on, because Democracy & Development A (POU33051) owns this question in depth this same semester. If any of the four is unfamiliar by name, that reading list is the place to go, not this deck.


Fast — twenty seconds, no lingering. Next slide’s the point.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: We are not doing this module
text:
We are not doing this module
State formation, colonial legacies, and the economic origins of regimes are the subject of an entire module running this semester, to this same cohort: Democracy & Development A (POU33051, Dr Michelle D’Arcy). Go there for the deep version.

Per PLAN-MT2026.md §3, this is a binding boundary, not a soft suggestion — literally name D’Arcy’s module on the slide, out loud, in class. The risk on this slide isn’t under-teaching origins, it’s over-teaching them out of completeness-reflex; if this section grows past two slides, that’s the tell to cut it back. Acemoglu & Robinson is only recommended reading for exactly this reason — flag it, don’t build it out.


Two minutes, no more. Then pivot hard: “Fine — a dictator has seized power. Now what?”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
A dictator needs a coalition
Nobody rules alone. Even the most absolute-looking autocrat needs a ruling coalition — generals, party bosses, ministers, oligarchs, clan elders — people whose cooperation makes the regime run.

But the same people who put you in power can remove you.



The greatest threat to a dictator’s power comes not from the masses he rules, but from the inner circle of the regime — the people with whom he shares power. (Svolik, paraphrased)


The big-quote slide for this deck — one scholar’s spiciest line, set large. Pull the exact wording from Svolik ch. 2 rather than my paraphrase before this goes live; the paraphrase captures the claim but isn’t a citable quote yet.


Commitment problem, defined: a situation where two parties could both be better off cooperating, but neither can credibly promise to hold up their end once the other has already acted — because nothing outside the relationship can force them to. It is the single idea underneath everything in this lecture.


Should surprise the room: most deposed dictators fall to coups/palace plots, not popular revolutions (Svolik: roughly two-thirds elite-driven). Get this on the board.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Game of Thrones, but it’s political science
text:
Game of Thrones, but it’s political science
Rule by fear of your subjects is the Hollywood image. Rule by fear of your friends is the real story.

Every person close enough to the dictator to help him rule is also close enough to have him killed, arrested, or quietly retired.

Noah: your own line or example here if you have a better one than the GoT comparison — a Moscow anecdote, a recent headline, whatever lands live.


“This is basically every Small Council scene in Game of Thrones: nobody trusts anybody, everybody could end everybody else.” If they haven’t seen it: “any palace-intrigue story you’ve watched” works too.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Callback: this is Svolik’s spine
Week 1: every autocrat faces two problems — power-sharing with allies, and control of the masses.

Today is entirely about the first one. Repression (Week 4) is mostly about the second. Keep asking, all term: is this tool solving the elite problem, or the mass problem?

This is the deck’s required visible spine-callback moment (BUILD-BRIEF.md — “every later deck has a visible callback moment”). Consider literally putting the Week 1 two-problems slide back on screen for ten seconds before this one, rather than just re-describing it in prose — a true repeat, not a paraphrase, lands the “toolkit” idea harder.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The problem of authoritarian power-sharing
The leader and the ruling coalition need each other — and neither can fully trust the other.

The leader wants to concentrate power (and skim more of the rewards)
The allies want guarantees they won’t be purged once they’re no longer needed
Neither side can credibly commit to holding up their end


Why not? Because there’s no referee.

Set up next slide: what’s missing that makes this harder than an ordinary contract dispute?

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Why can’t they just trust each other?
text:
Why can’t they just trust each other?
Commitment problems: promises are cheap when no one can enforce them.

There’s no independent court, no constitution that actually binds the dictator, no third party who can punish either side for reneging. So how do elites protect themselves from a leader who might turn on them tomorrow?

Cold-call — don’t answer it yourself. Let the room generate options (loyalty oaths? mutual implication? own military?) before Svolik’s answer next slide.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Svolik’s answer: the essence of dictatorship
text:
Svolik’s answer: the essence of dictatorship

The absence of an independent authority that can enforce agreements among the dictator and his allies is the essence of dictatorship. Promises made at one point may be broken later, when they become inconvenient. (Svolik, The Politics of Authoritarian Rule, paraphrased)


This single fact — no enforcer — is doing almost all the analytical work in this week’s readings. Everything else is a workaround for it.

Same flag as the earlier quote slide: pull Svolik’s exact sentence (ch. 2, around the “essence of dictatorship” passage in the class-1 MSc notes) before delivery — currently a close paraphrase, not a verbatim citation.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Two ways the dilemma resolves

Contested autocracy — the balance of power between leader and allies stays genuinely uncertain; elites retain enough independent strength to credibly threaten a coup, so the leader can’t safely grab everything
Established autocracy — the leader wins that contest decisively, and personal power consolidates; the “allies” become subordinates who serve at his pleasure, not partners who constrain him


Svolik’s chs. 2–3: most authoritarian regimes start contested and some slide toward established. That slide is not automatic — and it’s the story of the next two slides.

Contested vs. established autocracy, defined for reference: contested means the elite coalition could still credibly remove the leader if pushed too far; established means it can’t anymore. Nothing about the label is permanent — a regime can move from one to the other, in either direction, which is exactly what today’s cases show.


The USSR case (coming up) is the canonical illustration of contested → established, not just a scary history example.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Institutions as monitoring devices
If elites can’t trust the leader’s word, what can they trust instead?

Boix & Svolik: institutions — a Politburo, a ruling party congress, a council of elders — that make the leader’s behaviour observable.

Regular meetings mean regular chances to notice if the leader is freezing someone out
Formal roles mean it’s visible who is losing influence, and when



IMG party-congress.jpg (18th National Congress of the CPC) — used as a generic image of a ruling party congress, not a Russia-specific reference; .img-right reserves a column so the list can’t be covered. Reused from the POU11011 pool.


Institutions don’t need to bind the dictator by force. They just need to make cheating legible — visible enough that the coalition can catch it and punish it together. This is the direct bridge to Week 5 (“Buying Loyalty: Parties, Parliaments and Patronage”) — we see the why today, Week 5 is the how. Gandhi & Przeworski’s version of the same argument: institutionalisation is what lets a ruler make policy concessions and share spoils credibly — a party or legislature is the commitment device, not window-dressing.


Say out loud: “we’re seeing the why today; week 5 is the how.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: So when does it break down?
text:
So when does it break down?
Boix & Svolik: constrained, “limited” authoritarianism is the equilibrium of a leader and elites who are roughly balanced in power — elites strong enough to credibly threaten a coup, weak enough that outright grabbing power is too costly.


If the balance tips toward the leader — a security service he alone controls, a personal power base, a weakened or purged coalition — the constraint erodes
Personalism is what’s left once it’s gone: an established autocracy where the “allies” are subordinates, not partners


IMAGE/CHART — a small trend chart showing the global share of personalist regimes over time (V-Dem or the GWF/Geddes-Frantz-Wright dataset via Our World in Data), to make “some regimes slide toward established” visually concrete rather than just asserted. scripts/make_chart.py in the teaching repo can build this from OWID if a fitting series exists; otherwise cite the dataset’s own figure.


Portable concept worth stating explicitly on-screen if time allows: personalism isn’t a starting category of regime (contra some Week 2 typology talk) — it’s often an outcome, the endpoint of a contested-to-established slide. Flag this as a genuine tension with Week 2’s Geddes/Frantz/Wright typology (which does treat personalism as one type among several) — both framings are defensible, worth naming the tension rather than picking a winner in front of the room.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Contested or established: where’s Russia now?
text:
Contested or established: where’s Russia now?
Ask the room: in 2026, is Russia’s regime closer to contested (Putin still needs to balance real rival power centres) or established (the coalition is fully subordinate, no credible internal threat left)?

Show of hands — get commitment before the Russia case complicates it. Revisit after: did anyone move?

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: From collective rule to one man
text:
From collective rule to one man
1920s: the Politburo is a genuinely contested body. Lenin’s death leaves no agreed successor; power is distributed among several rivals who need each other and watch each other.

By the late 1930s: Stalin has purged the coalition that put him there — the Great Terror reaches into the Party’s own top ranks, the military officer corps, the security services themselves. Established autocracy, textbook case.

Pause here — next slide is the harder question, don’t rush into it.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Why purge your own useful allies?
text:
Why purge your own useful allies?
The twist Svolik stresses: purging your own elite is costly and irrational if the point of elites is to help you rule. Stalin did it anyway.

Two readings, both defensible: (1) repeated purges are how an established autocrat keeps re-proving dominance once trust has fully collapsed — terror as a maintenance cost, not a one-off; (2) Stalin’s information environment was so degraded by the mid-1930s that he could no longer tell loyal allies from threats, so he purged indiscriminately rather than strategically. Neither requires the other to be false.


Invite the room to argue both readings before moving on.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The inner circle’s dilemma
Put yourself inside Stalin’s Politburo in 1936. You have two options, and both are bad.

Stay loyal, keep serving him — and risk being purged later anyway, once you’re no longer useful or once he simply feels less secure
Move against him now — and risk everything immediately: discovery means death, and coordinating a plot under total surveillance is close to impossible


This is the trap of an established autocracy: by the time personal power is fully consolidated, the coalition that could have stopped it usually can’t anymore.

Pair discussion (2 min): one argues “stay loyal,” one argues “move now” — using only what they’d know in real time, not hindsight. Debrief with a show of hands.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Same country, a very different power-sharing arrangement
text:
Same country, a very different power-sharing arrangement
Yeltsin’s 1990s: genuinely dispersed power, oligarchs, regional governors, a weak centre — closer to Svolik’s “contested” pole than anything since.

Putin’s 2000s: the “power vertical” — co-optation of the Duma, recentralisation from the regions, taming of the oligarchs, control of the media. A deliberate, sustained move toward the established pole.

Reused with adaptation from Noah’s own POU44172 Russian Politics HT2027 deck, slides/week04.qmd (“Formal and Informal Power in Russia”) — the “power vertical” framing and the Yeltsin→Putin arc are his existing material. Flagging per BUILD-BRIEF.md so Noah can decide whether the same example appearing in two modules the same cohort could take is a problem — POU44172 is a final-year Russian Politics seminar, so there’s real overlap risk if students take both.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Factions: how Putin manages his own commitment problem
text:
Factions: how Putin manages his own commitment problem
Kremlinology’s favourite question: are these categories real, or are we just pattern-matching on gossip?

Liberals / technocrats — economic managers, more market-oriented
The St Petersburg clan — Putin’s original circle from the 1990s
Siloviki — security-service and military veterans (Kryshtanovskaya & White’s “Putin’s Militocracy”)



IMG awards-ceremony.jpg (Putin with award recipients, 2022) — used to illustrate patronage/loyalist-rewarding, not a specific faction. Reused from the POU11011 pool. Also adapted from POU44172 week04 (same reuse flag as above). Note the framing shift for this course: POU44172 treats factions descriptively (who’s who in Russian politics); here they’re recast explicitly as a worked example of elite-balancing as commitment-problem management — that reframe is new, not lifted.


Siloviki, defined: Russian officials with security-service or military backgrounds (FSB, military intelligence, the armed forces) who form one of several informal power blocs around Putin. The term comes from sila, “force” — literally “the force people.”


Function is Svolik’s: balancing rival power centres so no single faction gets strong enough to move against him. Good live puzzle: is Putin in one of these factions, or the arbiter above them?

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: United Russia: a party as a credibility device
text:
United Russia: a party as a credibility device
Why build a dominant party at all, if you’re already personally strong?

Because a party is a commitment device that runs in both directions — it lets Putin coordinate and reward loyalists at scale, and it gives the coalition something more durable than one man’s personal word.


IMG duma.jpg (Putin addressing the State Duma, 2020) — reused from the POU11011 pool.


Currency check: is this still an accurate read on United Russia’s role as of 2026? The Ukraine war has visibly personalised power further — worth updating this slide with the most current assessment before delivery, not the 2024-era framing this is drafted from.


Say so: “we’ll spend an entire week on exactly this mechanism soon” (week 5).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The Ba’ath Party purge
July 1979: Saddam Hussein becomes president. Within days, he stages a televised Party congress — names “conspirators,” has them dragged out one by one, and has the remaining members personally participate in the firing squads that execute their former colleagues.

This is established autocracy arriving in days, not decades — and it is designed to be watched.

Noah: a personal framing line or content-warning judgment call here — this is the most graphic case in the deck; you may want a heads-up before delivering it, or a note on how explicit to go live.


Vivid, don’t sanitise — but don’t dwell for shock value. The point: forcing survivors to participate makes loyalty self-enforcing, not merely stated. Everyone implicated — that’s the design.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Why force the survivors to pull the trigger?
text:
Why force the survivors to pull the trigger?
If Svolik is right that autocrats can’t credibly monitor loyalty, what does forcing your own inner circle to participate in a purge actually solve?

Cold-call. Let the room work toward it: participation is irreversible — you can’t claim you were a secret dissenter after firing the gun yourself. Dark mirror of the institutional-monitoring solution a few slides back.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: The information problem underneath it all
text:
The information problem underneath it all
Blaydes’ State of Repression on Iraq: even a regime that terrifying was still constrained by what it actually knew. Financial capacity, weak “legibility” of the population, miscalculated foreign reactions — the Ba’athist state was never as omniscient as it wanted to look.

Which loops back to today’s core problem: repression and purges are partly a response to an information deficit, not a sign of a leader who has already solved his commitment problem. He hasn’t. He’s still guessing.

Lighter touch than Week 4 deserves — Blaydes is the anchor reading for Week 4’s repression theme (Kneafsey overlap boundary), so keep this to the one information-problem beat that motivates this week’s argument, not a full repression treatment. Save the deep Blaydes engagement for Week 4.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Contrast: pacted exits, not just violent consolidation
text:
Contrast: pacted exits, not just violent consolidation
Power-sharing problems don’t only resolve toward personalism. Some ruling coalitions negotiate their way out instead.

Southern Cone military juntas (Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, 1980s) — officers who could see the regime’s coalition fraying negotiated exit guarantees (amnesties, retained privileges) rather than risk being purged or overthrown from within


Same underlying commitment problem — “can I trust the deal that gets me out safely?” — just answered by transition instead of terror.

IMAGE — a Southern Cone transition moment (e.g. Chile’s 1988 plebiscite, or a Pinochet-era junta portrait) from Wikimedia Commons, to give the “exit” case the same visual weight as the “consolidation” cases above it.


Deliberately thin — this is the pointer, not the full case; a genuine pacted-transition case study (with named sources) belongs either as a standalone slide if the deck runs short, or gets cut first if running long. Noah’s call on whether to build this out or keep it as the one-slide contrast.


Pacted transition, defined: a negotiated exit from authoritarian rule in which outgoing elites bargain for guarantees (amnesty from prosecution, retained wealth or status, sometimes a continuing political role) in exchange for relinquishing power, rather than being removed by force or losing it through elections.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Elite-control or mass-control?
The spine question, asked out loud, as required every week:

Everything today — power-sharing institutions, faction-balancing, purges, pacted exits — is elite-control machinery. None of it is aimed at the public. That’s next week.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Most of the world is not free
text:
Most of the world is not free
74% of the world’s population lives under some form of autocracy — and 46% under an electoral autocracy, now the most common regime type.

That share has been rising for about fifteen years — the “third wave of autocratization” you’ll meet properly in week 12.


So: three of your five guesses were “authoritarian” by most measures.

Verified 2026-09-16 (by the week 2 pass, web search): V-Dem, Democracy Report 2026: Unraveling the Democratic Era? (10th ed.) — 74% of world population under autocracy, 46% (~3.8bn) under electoral autocracy, the single most populous regime type; democracy for the average person back to roughly 1978 levels. Ask the room to guess first; they guess low.


Two things to hold apart: the share of countries that are autocracies (the chart, which counts states) and the share of people who live in them (the number on the slide, which is dominated by China and India). The trend on both has run the same way since about 2010. V-Dem’s “Regimes of the World” uses four categories — closed autocracy, electoral autocracy, electoral democracy, liberal democracy — and the fastest-growing category is electoral autocracy: regimes that hold multiparty elections and are not democracies. That is the type this module spends most of its time on.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Goals of this module

How do dictatorships actually work? Who really holds power?
Why are so many of them so durable?
What tools do autocrats use — and what do the tools cost them?
How do dictatorships end — and what comes next?


And underneath: get better at political science by taking non-democracies seriously as political systems, not as pathologies.

Frame these four as the through-questions of the whole course — you’ll say them out loud most weeks.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Why study dictatorship?

It’s where most people live — and where the century’s biggest stories are
It’s a puzzle: ruling without consent should be hard. Why isn’t it?
It sharpens our theory of politics everywhere — including democracies
Democracies can slide toward it. Hold that thought until week 12


The puzzle deserves stating plainly. A democratic government has an obvious answer to “why do people obey you?” — they chose you, and can un-choose you. An authoritarian government has no such answer, yet many of them last for decades, tax, conscript, build, and are obeyed by millions who were never asked. The comparative politics of authoritarianism is the attempt to explain that without resorting to “fear” (which turns out to be expensive and unreliable) or “culture” (which explains nothing that varies over time).


China and covid

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How people used to sort regimes
text:
How people used to sort regimes
For two thousand years the question was who rules, and for whom:




For the common good
For themselves




One
monarchy
tyranny


Few
aristocracy
oligarchy


Many
“polity” / mixed regime
democracy (the mob)




We threw out the second axis. Not because it’s unimportant — because nobody can code “rules for the common good” without picking a side.

Plato, Aristotle and Polybius sorted regimes by two questions — how many rule (one, few, many) and whether they rule in the common interest or their own — and the medieval and early-modern writers (Aquinas, Bodin, Machiavelli) kept the scheme. Modern political science dropped the normative axis, because “does this regime serve the common good?” cannot be answered by a neutral coder, and kept only structure: how the people at the top are chosen and whether they can be removed. That is why “authoritarian” ended up as a residual category — everything that is not an electoral democracy — rather than a positive description. The residual is a choice with a history, not a definitional accident.


Payoff: “residual category” isn’t laziness — it’s what’s left once you refuse to grade regimes on virtue. Cut if running long.


Added 2026-09-16 from the Waller Statecraft episode (his opening rabbit-hole on the classical lexicon and why social science dropped the normative axis). Cheap, and it gives “residual category” a history.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Democracy vs. non-democracy — where’s the line?
text:
Democracy vs. non-democracy — where’s the line?
What’s the minimum a regime needs to count as a democracy?

Free and fair elections?
More than one party that could actually win?
Rights — speech, press, assembly?
The losers actually hand over power?


Authoritarianism is, in part, a residual category: whatever fails the test.


Draw the Dahl space on the board (b): contestation vs. participation. Polyarchy = top-right corner
Week 2 is the fight over where the line falls



Robert Dahl’s two dimensions are the standard way of thinking about this. Contestation asks whether the government can actually be opposed and replaced through elections; participation asks how much of the adult population is allowed to take part. A regime can be high on one and low on the other (the nineteenth-century British parliament was highly contested among a tiny electorate; the Soviet Union had universal suffrage and no contestation). “Polyarchy”, Dahl’s word for real-world democracy, is high on both.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
One working definition

An authoritarian regime is one in which rulers acquire and hold power by means other than free and fair multiparty competition — and are not reliably constrained by it.


Nothing here about how brutal, how popular, or how stable the regime is. Those are things to explain, not assume.

This is close to the “minimalist” definition used by Przeworski and colleagues and adopted by Svolik: a country is a dictatorship if it fails at least one of two tests — the legislature is chosen in free, competitive, multiparty elections, and the chief executive is either chosen that way or by a legislature chosen that way. The definition is deliberately thin. It says nothing about rights, repression, ideology or popularity, which is exactly what lets us treat those as variables to be explained rather than as part of the label.


Resolve cold-call: Russia/Singapore/Mexico pre-2000 fail cleanly; Hungary contested (wk2, wk12); US is uncomfortable — park it out loud for wk12.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Linz brings the definition

“…political systems with limited, not responsible, political pluralism; without elaborate and guiding ideology (but with distinctive mentalities); without intensive nor extensive political mobilization (except some points in their development); and in which a leader (or occasionally a small group) exercises power within formally ill-defined limits but actually quite predictable ones.”

— Juan Linz, Totalitarian and Authoritarian Regimes

Big-quote slide (one per deck). This is Linz’s canonical 1964/2000 definition as widely reproduced; confirm the exact wording against the assigned pages before Friday — the assigned Linz extract is [TBD: selected pages] in _course.yml, and this quote should be in the pages you set.


Read it slowly, dense on purpose. Ask what it adds vs. the working definition: pluralism, mentalities not ideology, low mobilisation, and the last clause (“formally ill-defined but actually quite predictable” — Putin’s Russia).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Thick or thin?
Two ways to define things – thick and thin:

Thin (Przeworski, Svolik): fails the election test → dictatorship. Clean, codable, says nothing about how it rules.
Thick (Linz): a whole style of rule — limited pluralism, mentality not ideology, demobilised society.


We’ll generally use the thin one to count and the thick one to describe. Both are choices, and the choice has consequences — that’s week 2.

Why does the choice matter? A thin definition puts North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Singapore and 1990s Mexico in the same box, which is useful for counting and for statistical work but hides everything interesting about how they differ. A thick definition captures the texture of rule but is hard to apply consistently — two coders will disagree about “distinctive mentalities”. Most of the field now uses a thin definition to draw the boundary and a typology (week 2) to sort what falls inside it.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Totalitarian, authoritarian — or neither?

Linz’s other distinction. According to his definition, totalitarian regimes have:

a single, official, all-explaining ideology
a mass party that mobilises everyone, all the time
no tolerated pluralism — not even in a chess club


Is North Korea totalitarian? Is China? Was the USSR in 1985?

IMG kim-succession.jpg — Kim Jong-un, 2019 (CC BY 4.0). North Korea is the one case most rooms will call totalitarian without hesitation; the argument starts with China.


Cold-call the three questions. Point: “totalitarian” is a small box; most of what we study is the untidy “authoritarian” middle. Cut first if running long; week 2 revisits.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: What’s the one thing keeping your dictator in power?
text:
What’s the one thing keeping your dictator in power?
Think of a country you’d call authoritarian. Fear, money, ideology — or something else?

Two-minute pair discussion, then pull three answers. Expect “fear” and “money” — bank both, they’re about to become Svolik’s whole architecture.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: The whole course in one idea
text:
The whole course in one idea
Every autocrat faces two problems (Svolik):

Power-sharing — controlling your allies, who could replace you
Control — controlling the masses, who could rise against you


Almost everything we study — parties, elections, repression, propaganda, coups — is a tool for managing one of these two problems.

Svolik’s framing is the spine of the module. The “problem of authoritarian power-sharing” is the dictator’s relationship with the people who put and keep him in power — generals, party bosses, oligarchs, a royal family — who could remove him and whom he cannot credibly promise to reward, because nobody can enforce a promise against a dictator. The “problem of authoritarian control” is his relationship with everybody else, who vastly outnumber him. Historically the first problem has been the more dangerous: far more dictators have been removed by insiders than by uprisings.


THE most important slide of the term. Slow down, put it on the board. Say: “every week I’ll ask — elite-control tool or mass-control tool? Sometimes both.” Map the pair-discussion answers onto it: fear = control, money = mostly power-sharing.

text:
Most of the world is not free

74% of the world’s population lives under some form of autocracy — and 46% under an electoral autocracy, now the most common regime type.
That share has been rising for about fifteen years — the “third wave of autocratization” you’ll meet properly in week 12.
So: three of your five guesses were “authoritarian” by most measures.


Two things to hold apart: the share of countries that are autocracies (the chart, which counts states) and the share of people who live in them (the number on the slide, which is dominated by China and India). The trend on both has run the same way since about 2010. V-Dem’s “Regimes of the World” uses four categories — closed autocracy, electoral autocracy, electoral democracy, liberal democracy — and the fastest-growing category is electoral autocracy: regimes that hold multiparty elections and are not democracies. That is the type this module spends most of its time on.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
section: What people think they know about dictators
text:
What people think they know about dictators


“It’s all about one evil guy at the top.”


“Dictators rule purely through fear.”


“Elections in dictatorships are meaningless theatre.”


“They’re irrational — or just crazy.”


“They’re always one push from falling over.”

We’ll spend twelve weeks complicating each of these.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
text:
Goals of this module


How do dictatorships actually work? Who really holds power?
Why are so many of them so durable?
What tools do autocrats use — and what do the tools cost them?
How do dictatorships end — and what comes next?

And underneath: get better at political science by taking non-democracies seriously as political systems, not as pathologies.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
text:
Why study dictatorship?


It’s where most people live — and where the century’s biggest stories are
It’s a puzzle: ruling without consent should be hard. Why isn’t it?
It sharpens our theory of politics everywhere — including democracies
Democracies can slide toward it. Hold that thought until week 12



The puzzle deserves stating plainly. A democratic government has an obvious answer to “why do people obey you?” — they chose you, and can un-choose you. An authoritarian government has no such answer, yet many of them last for decades, tax, conscript, build, and are obeyed by millions who were never asked. The comparative politics of authoritarianism is the attempt to explain that without resorting to “fear” (which turns out to be expensive and unreliable) or “culture” (which explains nothing that varies over time).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
text:
Authoritarianism and political science

This module touches most of political science:

Regimes — what is a democracy, and who decides?
Institutions — parties, parliaments, elections, courts (yes, in dictatorships)
Political economy — rents, patronage, oil, corruption
Coercion and information — repression, propaganda, censorship, surveillance
Collective action — protest, revolution, why nobody saw 1989 coming

Growth? Order? Getting things done?

Where’s the line — and who gets to draw it?

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
section: How people used to sort regimes
text:
How people used to sort regimes

For two thousand years the question was who rules, and for whom:




For the common good
For themselves




One
monarchy
tyranny


Few
aristocracy
oligarchy


Many
“polity” / mixed regime
democracy (the mob)



We threw out the second axis. Not because it’s unimportant — because nobody can code “rules for the common good” without picking a side.


Plato, Aristotle and Polybius sorted regimes by two questions — how many rule (one, few, many) and whether they rule in the common interest or their own — and the medieval and early-modern writers (Aquinas, Bodin, Machiavelli) kept the scheme. Modern political science dropped the normative axis, because “does this regime serve the common good?” cannot be answered by a neutral coder, and kept only structure: how the people at the top are chosen and whether they can be removed. That is why “authoritarian” ended up as a residual category — everything that is not an electoral democracy — rather than a positive description. The residual is a choice with a history, not a definitional accident.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
section: Democracy vs. non-democracy — where’s the line?
text:
Democracy vs. non-democracy — where’s the line?

What’s the minimum a regime needs to count as a democracy?

Free and fair elections?
More than one party that could actually win?
Rights — speech, press, assembly?
The losers actually hand over power?

Authoritarianism is, in part, a residual category: whatever fails the test.


Robert Dahl’s two dimensions are the standard way of thinking about this. Contestation asks whether the government can actually be opposed and replaced through elections; participation asks how much of the adult population is allowed to take part. A regime can be high on one and low on the other (the nineteenth-century British parliament was highly contested among a tiny electorate; the Soviet Union had universal suffrage and no contestation). “Polyarchy”, Dahl’s word for real-world democracy, is high on both.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
text:
One working definition


An authoritarian regime is one in which rulers acquire and hold power by means other than free and fair multiparty competition — and are not reliably constrained by it.

Nothing here about how brutal, how popular, or how stable the regime is. Those are things to explain, not assume.


This is close to the “minimalist” definition used by Przeworski and colleagues and adopted by Svolik: a country is a dictatorship if it fails at least one of two tests — the legislature is chosen in free, competitive, multiparty elections, and the chief executive is either chosen that way or by a legislature chosen that way. The definition is deliberately thin. It says nothing about rights, repression, ideology or popularity, which is exactly what lets us treat those as variables to be explained rather than as part of the label.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
text:
Linz brings the definition


“…political systems with limited, not responsible, political pluralism; without elaborate and guiding ideology (but with distinctive mentalities); without intensive nor extensive political mobilization (except some points in their development); and in which a leader (or occasionally a small group) exercises power within formally ill-defined limits but actually quite predictable ones.”

— Juan Linz, Totalitarian and Authoritarian Regimes

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
text:
Thick or thin?

Two ways to define things – thick and thin:

Thin (Przeworski, Svolik): fails the election test → dictatorship. Clean, codable, says nothing about how it rules.
Thick (Linz): a whole style of rule — limited pluralism, mentality not ideology, demobilised society.

We’ll generally use the thin one to count and the thick one to describe. Both are choices, and the choice has consequences — that’s week 2.


Why does the choice matter? A thin definition puts North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Singapore and 1990s Mexico in the same box, which is useful for counting and for statistical work but hides everything interesting about how they differ. A thick definition captures the texture of rule but is hard to apply consistently — two coders will disagree about “distinctive mentalities”. Most of the field now uses a thin definition to draw the boundary and a typology (week 2) to sort what falls inside it.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
text:
Totalitarian, authoritarian — or neither?


Linz’s other distinction. According to his definition, totalitarian regimes have:

a single, official, all-explaining ideology
a mass party that mobilises everyone, all the time
no tolerated pluralism — not even in a chess club

Is North Korea totalitarian? Is China? Was the USSR in 1985?

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
section: What’s the one thing keeping your dictator in power?
text:
What’s the one thing keeping your dictator in power?

Think of a country you’d call authoritarian. Fear, money, ideology — or something else?

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
section: The whole course in one idea
text:
The whole course in one idea

Every autocrat faces two problems (Svolik):

Power-sharing — controlling your allies, who could replace you
Control — controlling the masses, who could rise against you

Almost everything we study — parties, elections, repression, propaganda, coups — is a tool for managing one of these two problems.


Svolik’s framing is the spine of the module. The “problem of authoritarian power-sharing” is the dictator’s relationship with the people who put and keep him in power — generals, party bosses, oligarchs, a royal family — who could remove him and whom he cannot credibly promise to reward, because nobody can enforce a promise against a dictator. The “problem of authoritarian control” is his relationship with everybody else, who vastly outnumber him. Historically the first problem has been the more dangerous: far more dictators have been removed by insiders than by uprisings.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism — lecture notes
section: How would you measure support for a dictator?
text:
How would you measure support for a dictator?


Send in a pollster and ask? If honesty is risky, people say what’s safe.
The list experiment: half the sample counts four harmless items; the other half counts the same four plus “the president”. Compare the averages.
No individual ever admits anything. The truth shows up only in the aggregate.


The problem with asking directly in a repressive setting is not that people lie randomly but that they lie in a predictable direction — toward whatever is safe to say to a stranger. A list experiment gets round this by never asking about the sensitive item on its own: respondents report only how many items on a list apply to them, and the difference in average counts between a group that saw the sensitive item and a group that didn’t estimates how common it really is. This method returns in week 6 (elections), week 8 (propaganda) and week 11 (protest).

Module Description
This module introduces the comparative politics of authoritarian regimes: how dictatorships are organised, how they survive, and how they fall. We pair classic and cutting-edge research with contemporary cases from Russia, China, the Middle East, Latin America, and Africa.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Module description
Why do some rulers govern without meaningful elections, free media, or the rule of law — and why are so many of them so durable? This module introduces the comparative politics of authoritarian regimes: how dictatorships are organised, how they survive, and how they fall.
We examine the major varieties of authoritarian rule — personalist, single-party, military, monarchical, and hybrid or “electoral authoritarian” — and the core strategies autocrats use to stay in power: co-optation, repression, propaganda, elections without democracy, and managing rival elites. Cases are drawn from Russia, China, the Middle East, Latin America, and Africa.
The organising idea runs through every week: a dictator has two problems, not one — controlling the people who put him in power, and controlling everybody else. Nearly everything authoritarian regimes do (parties, parliaments, elections, propaganda, the secret police) is an answer to one of those two problems, and by the end of term you should be able to look at an unfamiliar regime and work out which one it is currently losing.

Learning outcomes
On successful completion of this module, you should be able to:

Distinguish between the major types of authoritarian regime and explain how they differ in their institutions and survival strategies.
Explain the central dilemmas autocrats face — the problems of power-sharing and of control — and the tools they use to manage them.
Evaluate competing theories of authoritarian durability, repression, co-optation, and regime breakdown.
Assess how elections, parties, propaganda, and information operate under authoritarian conditions.
Apply concepts and research from comparative politics to analyse contemporary authoritarian regimes and the global state of democracy.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
How the module works

Lectures
There are eleven lectures, one a week, Fridays 14:00–16:00, across teaching weeks 1–6 and 8–12. Reading week (teaching week 7) has no lecture.
Discussion happens inside the two-hour block: each session mixes presentation with argument, cases, and questions. Come having done the reading.
Attendance is not taken, but material is covered in the room that is not in the readings, and the slides are a prompt for what I say, not a transcript of it.
Slides are posted on the course website after each lecture.


Readings
There is no set textbook. Readings are journal articles and book chapters. Journal articles you find yourself, through the Library or Google Scholar — part of the training. Book chapters and anything else you cannot easily find are provided via Blackboard. Five books recur often enough that you will get to know them:

Milan Svolik, The Politics of Authoritarian Rule (Cambridge, 2012)
Barbara Geddes, Joseph Wright & Erica Frantz, How Dictatorships Work (Cambridge, 2018)
Steven Levitsky & Lucan Way, Competitive Authoritarianism (Cambridge, 2010)
Jennifer Gandhi, Political Institutions under Dictatorship (Cambridge, 2008)
Sergei Guriev & Daniel Treisman, Spin Dictators (Princeton, 2022)

Each week has required readings to complete before the lecture, plus recommended readings for going deeper. Some weeks also carry a short Bonus list — a blog post, an essay, a podcast episode, a film. Bonus items are not course material: not required, not examinable, and not sources for your written work. The list in the schedule below is indicative; Blackboard and the course website carry the current version.

Full instructions, prompts and essay questions are released in lecture and on Blackboard.

Response papers (10%)
Short pieces of thinking, not summary: take the week’s required readings and do something with them — challenge an argument, apply it to a case the author didn’t use, put two readings into conflict, or connect the reading to something happening now.

Length: 400–500 words, 10% either way.
How many: two across the term — one in teaching weeks 1–6, one in teaching weeks 8–12. You choose the weeks.
Due: Wednesday 23:59 in the week you choose, via Blackboard.
Marking: each paper receives a mark; the two together make up the 10%.
The test: could someone who has already done the reading learn something from your response? Restating the argument fails that test; arguing with it passes.

Full mechanics: response papers sheet.


Mid-term essay (30%)
An analytical essay of 2,000 words, 10% either way (excluding bibliography), answering one of several set questions, building an argument out of the academic literature rather than summarising it. Questions are released in lecture and on Blackboard in due course.

Due: Sunday 1 November 2026, 23:59.
Submission: Word or PDF via Blackboard, which submits to Turnitin.

Full instructions and the topic options are in the separate essay sheet.


Examination (60%)
An in-person examination at the end of term, covering the whole module. It rewards the same thing the response papers do: applying a concept from the literature to a case, in your own words, under pressure.
The date is set centrally — check the College examination timetable. Format details will be given later in term.


Written work: formatting requirements
In line with department guidelines, written work for this module must:

observe the stated word limit and state the final word count — limits carry a 10% tolerance either way, and going outside that range costs up to 5 marks;
be submitted to Blackboard, in Word or PDF format;
use proper citation and referencing — any consistent style is acceptable (the TCD Library style guide will help);
include an alphabetised bibliography;
be spellchecked;
have the School of Social Sciences and Philosophy Assignment Submission Form attached as its first page, completed in full (see Academic integrity below).

Back your work up, and submit early enough to survive a technical problem. Keep your submission receipt. Computer crashes, corrupted files, and internet problems are not grounds for late submission.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Policies

Late work
All late work, unless excused in advance by me, is penalised at 5 marks per day or part thereof, up to a maximum of 20 marks. There are many good reasons a student cannot submit on time and I am happy to make reasonable accommodations, but not for requests made after the deadline or a few hours before it.
Requests go through your College Tutor, who contacts me. Extensions are not granted retrospectively except in exceptional medical circumstances, which require a medical certificate. Work is not accepted after it has been marked and returned to other students, or after the end of teaching term — in both cases the mark is 0. It is your responsibility to make sure your College Tutor knows the correct procedure.


Contacting me
Email me at noah.buckley@tcd.ie. Read this document first.
I will do my best to reply within two business days. Email is for logistics: extensions, difficulties, things only I can settle. For substantive questions about the material, come to office hours (by appointment) or raise it in lecture. I will not be able to fill you in on a lecture you missed.


Disability
Students with a disability liable to affect their ability to participate fully in this — or any — module are encouraged to register with the University’s Disability Service, which exists to make sure appropriate accommodations are in place.


Discussion in the room
The lecture is where the arguing happens. People in the room have different backgrounds and personal stakes in these questions — several of the regimes we study are somebody’s home country. Engage seriously with the arguments and generously with the people making them.


Keeping up with current events
Read the news! Any serious source you like, national or international. This is a module about the present tense as much as the past one. Half the value of it is having something concrete in your head when a concept turns up, and the other half is noticing that a concept explains something you read last week.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Academic integrity
Do not plagiarise. Academic dishonesty is a serious matter with serious consequences, up to and including no credit for the assignment, failure of the module, and expulsion. It is never permissible to submit work containing other people’s ideas without acknowledgment, and careless note-taking is not an excuse: put direct quotations in quotation marks, and reference paraphrases too. Trinity’s guidance is at libguides.tcd.ie/plagiarism, and if you have not already completed the Library’s Ready, Steady, Write tutorial, do that before your first submission. You must also submit only new work — not work submitted previously for another module.

Generative AI
These tools exist, you probably use them, and you will almost certainly use them in whatever you do after you get your college degree. But this module is not assessing whether you can obtain a competent paragraph about authoritarian politics from an LLM. It is assessing whether you can read an argument, find its weak point, and put your own case in your own words. So, in general: use these tools to help guide you and to help you fix your prose; do not use them to do your thinking or produce the prose.
What is permitted for each assessment is in that assessment’s sheet, in the vocabulary of the School of Social Sciences and Philosophy Assignment Submission Form — the same words you tick on the form. “Permitted” means you may do it and must tick the box. “Not permitted” means doing it is an academic integrity matter, whether or not you disclose it. The examination is in person and is not covered: nothing to declare, no form.
Trinity offers further resources in the Statement on Generative AI, the Library’s GenAI guide, and the College GenAI hub.


The Assignment Submission Form
Every piece of written work — response papers and the mid-term essay — must have the Assignment Submission Form as its first page. This is a department-wide rule. The form is on Blackboard in Word and PDF. Complete it in full, including the plagiarism declaration and the GenAI disclosure, ticking every category that applies to what you actually did. A submission without a completed form is not accepted — it is returned unmarked and treated as not submitted, accruing late penalties until you resubmit with one. The form does not count toward your word limit, and ticking a permitted box carries no penalty.
I reserve the right to modify this outline as necessary during term. The current version is always the one on the course website and Blackboard.

Schedule

Part I — Foundations

Teaching week 1 · Fri 18 September
What is authoritarianism? How much of the world is unfree, and the two questions the module returns to: how autocracies work, and why they last.
Required:

Part II — The dictator’s dilemmas

Teaching week 3 · Fri 2 October
How autocrats take and hold power. Ruling coalitions, elites, and why autocrats can’t simply trust one another.
Required:

Barbara Geddes, Joseph Wright and Erica Frantz. 2018. How Dictatorships Work. Cambridge University Press. Chs. 1–2.

Teaching week 4 · Fri 9 October
The control problem: repression. Too much repression and too little are both dangerous — does it work, and when does it backfire?
Required:

Teaching week 6 · Fri 23 October
Elections without democracy. Why hold elections you might lose or have to rig, and what elections actually do for autocrats.
Required:

Coups & the military. The coup trap — the people who keep you in power can remove you — and the cost of coup-proofing.

title: Asides bank — POU33201
text:
How to use this bank
This deck is never taught as-is. Copy one ## Title {.aside} slide at a time into a real lecture at a natural pause point. One aside per lecture, maximum. Sessions are Friday 2-4pm — a two-hour slot has more natural pause points than a single-hour lecture, but that’s still not licence for more than one. Asides are never on the exam.

Delete this slide if it ever accidentally ends up in a real deck. This bank has fewer entries than POU11011’s — trim further rather than padding; a third-year room doesn’t need the university-101 material a first-year room does.

title: Asides bank — POU33201
section: What AI is actually good at, for you
text:
What AI is actually good at, for you
At this level: summarising a dense article before you commit to reading it properly, checking whether your citation format is consistent, or stress-testing an argument you’ve already built. What it can’t do: decide whether your argument about, say, Hungary’s democratic backsliding is any good. That’s still you.

Third-years have usually already formed AI habits by now — this lands better as “here’s how to use it well” than as an intro-101 explainer. Use early in the term, before the mid-term essay brief goes out.


Noah: swap the example for something from the actual reading list that week — Hungary is a placeholder.

title: Asides bank — POU33201
section: The essay isn’t the deliverable, the argument is
text:
The essay isn’t the deliverable, the argument is
A polished 2,500 words that doesn’t commit to a claim is worth less than a rough 2,000 that does. AI is very good at the polish. It cannot decide what you think about whether Orbán’s Hungary is still a democracy — and that decision is the entire assignment.

Best right before or just after the mid-term essay brief lands. This is the framing slide — put it ahead of the “where the line is” slide below.

title: Asides bank — POU33201
text:
Where the line actually is
Check the brief for this specific assessment, not your instinct and not what worked in another module. Different assessments in this department allow different things. When in doubt, ask.

Deliberately generic so it doesn’t need updating as policy shifts. Use once, near the mid-term essay brief.


Noah: point this at wherever the department’s live AI-policy-by-assessment guidance ends up once it’s settled.

title: Asides bank — POU33201
text:
How to email a professor
Bad: “hi wondering if you could go over my essay plan asap.” Good: a subject line that says what it’s about, your name and module code, one clear question, and a sign-off. By third year this should be automatic — it usually isn’t yet.

Even third-years get this wrong more often than you’d expect, especially before the mid-term essay. Use early, ideally before the essay-planning period.


Noah: a real (anonymised) bad example lands harder than an invented one — swap in if you have one you’re comfortable using.

title: Asides bank — POU33201
section: What office hours are for, at this stage
text:
What office hours are for, at this stage
Not “I don’t understand the reading” — by now, come with a claim you’re not sure holds up, or a source you think undercuts your own argument. Office hours get more useful the more formed your thinking already is, not less.

Different pitch than a first-year version of this slide — third-years should be using office hours to pressure-test arguments, not to catch up. Use around essay-planning time.

title: Asides bank — POU33201
section: How marks work at Trinity, the reminder
text:
How marks work at Trinity, the reminder
You’ve had two years of this scale by now, but the reminder is cheap: 70 is a First, the top of the scale is deliberately hard to reach, and the number on its own tells you less than the feedback next to it.

Shorter than the first-year version — this is a reminder, not an explainer. Use once, after the mid-term essay marks come back.


Noah: check the marking-scale description is current before using.

title: Asides bank — POU33201
text:
This week in authoritarianism
A reusable frame: what happened, which of this module’s concepts explains it best, and what a rival concept from a different week would say instead. Same three moves, new headline.

This is the template — duplicate and fill in a live case before each use, roughly every 2-3 sessions. The “rival concept” move is what makes this module-specific rather than generic current-events filler — use it to force students to choose between, say, personalism and institutionalism explanations of the same event.


Noah: fill in a real case close to delivery date.

title: Asides bank — POU33201
text:
Read past the headline
The headline tells you a leader did something authoritarian. It rarely tells you whether the institutions around them let it happen, resisted it, or don’t matter. That’s the question this module actually trains you to ask.

Works any time, but especially useful once the elite/mass or institutions material is a few weeks in and students have a framework to apply. Keep it short.

title: POU33201 — Mid-term essay
text:
Essay Topics
Choose one. Each asks you to build an argument using the academic literature — not to summarise it.


Topic 1: The Dictator’s Toolkit
An autocrat can stay in power by co-opting rivals or by repressing them. Drawing on the literature on authoritarian survival, when and why do dictators rely on one strategy over the other? Illustrate your argument with at least one contemporary case.


Topic 2: Why Institutions?
Dictatorships routinely hold elections, run parliaments, and tolerate ruling parties — institutions that appear democratic but operate under authoritarian conditions. Why? Evaluate competing explanations (co-optation, credible power-sharing, information-gathering, signalling) and say which you find most persuasive, and why.


Topic 3: Durability vs. Fragility
Some autocracies endure for decades; others collapse with little warning. What does political science tell us makes an authoritarian regime durable — and what makes it fragile? Use the literature on breakdown, repression, and power-sharing, and apply it to one regime of your choice.


Topic 4: Build a Regime [TBD — pending Noah’s go/no-go, see _drafting/DECISIONS-FOR-NOAH.md]
A different kind of essay. Read the guidance below carefully before choosing it.
Pick a real country at a real moment in time — anywhere in the world, any point from 1900 to the near future — and write the counterfactual: how would an authoritarian regime be built here, and how would it survive?
The country may currently be a democracy (in which case you are describing an autocratisation episode) or an existing autocracy (in which case you are describing a transition from one kind of authoritarian rule to another). Your essay must answer:

Where and when, and what regime type you are moving from and to.
How power is seized — coup, self-coup, civil war, an authoritarian party, backsliding from within, or something else — and the pretext used.
How the regime survives its first years — the ruling coalition, the coercive apparatus, the basis of popular support, the international environment.
How it survives decades — which institutions, ideologies, economic structures and personalities do the work.
Succession — what happens when the leader dies or goes; this is where most regimes fail.
How it might eventually end.

This is not fiction writing, and it is not a morality tale. It’s an exercise in using the module’s toolkit — regime types, power-sharing, co-optation, repression, information control, coup-proofing — on a case concrete enough to resist hand-waving. Write as an analyst, from inside the regime’s own strategic logic; command of the theory is what earns marks.
Ground rules:

Your regime may not end in democratisation — you are explaining how authoritarian rule is built and sustained.
Pick a real leader or real party to head the regime wherever you can, rather than inventing someone.
Include one diagram — a faction map, institutional schema, timeline, or party-system chart.
No “nothing went wrong” essays (“what if the USSR never collapsed”) — clear it with me first if you want to attempt one.
It has to pass the smell test: if you can’t explain the premise to a friend and have them nod, it won’t work on paper.

Two warnings, from experience with this assignment elsewhere:

The default answer is boring. A Western European country, a far-right election win, capture the media and courts, stop there — it’s the Hungarian playbook, but the interesting questions (how was the election won? what do the factions want?) get skipped.
The more alien regimes score better. A closed party-state or military junta forces you to specify the whole apparatus — coercion, mobilisation, ideology, succession — and that’s what shows command of the material.
Counterfactual civil wars (“what if the losing side had won”) work for the same reason.
No credit for a regime you think I would approve of, or for democratising early. A neutral, analytic tone throughout is what impresses.

Say explicitly: “you did this in second year — not re-teaching GFW from scratch.” What’s new: the USE of the typology (prediction), what the boxes hide (personalism is continuous), monarchy, and who draws the lines.


Prior-exposure calibration (brief §“Prior exposure”). This cohort took POU22031/32 Comparative A, Week 5 (Monday + Thursday), which already covers: Przeworski et al.’s minimal definition, V-Dem/Freedom House measurement, Svolik’s elites/public framing, the four-type taxonomy (single-party/military/ personalist/monarchy) with the same example countries used below (China, Egypt, Belarus, Saudi Arabia), Brownlee on hereditary succession, and Schedler’s “menu of manipulation” for electoral authoritarianism.
