title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
This week in autocracy


Noah: two or three stories from this week. One line each — headline, country, and the concept it illustrates (elite problem or mass problem?). This slide is the same shape every week, same slot, right after the plan.


Five minutes, no more. Ask the room first: “what happened this week that belongs in this module?” — then show yours. The point is the habit: by teaching week 12 they should be bringing the stories, not you.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The reminder, fast
You already have this from Comparative. One slide, then we move past it:

Personalist — power concentrated in one leader, thin institutions
Single-party — a ruling party controls succession and access to office
Military — the officer corps rules, directly or from behind a front
Monarchy — hereditary, dynastic succession
Hybrid / electoral — real-looking elections, an unfair playing field


Five regime types, for anyone who didn’t take Comparative Politics in second year. Personalist: power concentrated in one leader; formal institutions (party, army, parliament) exist but don’t constrain them. Single-party: a ruling party, not an individual, controls access to office and manages succession. Military: the officer corps rules, whether directly (juntas) or from behind a civilian front. Monarchy: succession runs through bloodline, not election or appointment. Hybrid/electoral: elections are held and opposition is legal, but the contest is rigged well before polling day — through media access, gerrymandering, vote-buying, or selective repression, not ballot-stuffing alone. The coding scheme is Geddes, Wright & Frantz (GFW), How Dictatorships Work (2018).



Under 90 seconds — say “you know this,” don’t re-derive GFW
Optional check: cold-call someone to define “personalist” from memory



This slide is deliberately thin — a reminder card, not a taxonomy lecture. Comparative Week 5 Monday already ran the full “types of authoritarian regimes” walkthrough with these same five categories and largely the same named examples (Belarus, Franco’s Spain, Mugabe’s Zimbabwe for personalist; China/USSR for single-party; Saudi/Brunei/UAE for monarchy). If this slide starts growing sub-bullets, that’s the tell you’re re-teaching Comparative — cut back to the reminder card.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Why has nobody built a new party-state since 1989?
text:
Why has nobody built a new party-state since 1989?
Two things hide inside “single-party”:

A party-state — a parallel party organ shadowing every state institution; the party decides, the state implements. Lenin’s design, Stalin’s perfection, exported 1945–70.
A dominant-party regime — one party wins every election, but the state is still the state. The PRI’s seventy years; Singapore’s PAP; United Russia.


Every party-state still running is a legacy — China, Vietnam, Cuba, Laos, North Korea’s shell. The design works. The recipe is lost.

The distinction matters because the two machines fail differently. A party-state has a Leninist answer to almost every survival problem — cells in every barracks, ministry and classroom, so the party can watch the army and the police watch each other (week 4), and a Politburo that manages succession (week 3). Nobody has built one from scratch since the Cold War: the ideological fuel, the wartime origins and the Soviet patron are all gone. Dominant-party regimes are the buildable modern version — a party that wins every election and distributes the spoils (week 5) but does not fuse with the state — and they are very successful, but they lose when the vote-share machine breaks (Mexico 2000). Whether Xi’s personalisation means China’s party-state still works the way it used to is an open question, and a good response paper.


Ask the room to name a party-state founded after 1989 — there isn’t one (Eritrea is the closest offer, but it’s personalist with a party badge).


Source: Waller, Statecraft podcast, 10 Sep 2026 — his party-state vs dominant-party distinction and “we don’t know how to build them anymore”; see _drafting/WALLER-EPISODE-CHECK-2026-09-16.md §A 20–23. Week 5’s “Cases compared” gets the callback (Mexico/Russia dominant-party, China party-state). The “no new party-state since the Cold War” claim is his; treat as a strong generalisation, not a coded fact.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
So what’s actually NEW here?
You know the four boxes. So why is this a whole lecture and not five minutes?

Because the box tells you almost nothing about what happens next.

Let the room feel baited (“wait, that’s it?”), then reveal: the content was never the boxes, it’s what they predict.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: The GWF payoff: type predicts survival
text:
The GWF payoff: type predicts survival
Geddes, Wright & Frantz didn’t just classify regimes — they tracked how they end.

Personalist regimes — the most erratic. More war-prone, more likely to end in violence, and the leader’s death or exit is often the regime’s death too
Military regimes — often short-lived on purpose: the officers have a barracks to go back to, and a corporate interest in not running the country badly
Single-party regimes — the most durable of all four types, by a wide margin — survive leader turnover because the party, not the person, holds the machinery


Same box, very different actuarial tables. That’s the analytical payoff — the type is a leading indicator.

Spend real time here — the one genuinely new empirical claim. Cold-call: “which type still standing in 20 years, which ends in a coup or a funeral?” Callback to week 1’s teaser — say it out loud.


Currency/data check: cite GFW’s actual base rates (median duration by type, % ending in violence) if you have the table handy — this claim is much stronger with real numbers on screen than as a verbal assertion. GFW How Dictatorships Work Ch. 1-2 has the summary stats.


cc: unverified. The three claims above (personalist regimes most erratic/ war-prone, military regimes short-lived on purpose, single-party regimes most durable) are GFW’s well-established headline findings and almost certainly right in direction — but I did not pull the actual base-rate numbers (median years in power, % ending in coup/collapse/violence by type) to put on screen, which is what the placeholder above is asking for. Don’t present a specific number that isn’t in the table in front of you.


GFW’s contribution wasn’t just a typology — it was tracking outcomes by type across a large cross-national dataset (Geddes, Wright & Frantz, How Dictatorships Work, 2018, building on Geddes’s original 1999/2003 coding). The finding that regime type predicts how a regime ends, not just what it looks like while in power, is the empirical backbone of the “type as predictive tool” argument this lecture makes.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Which type would you bet on — and which would you bet against?
text:
Which type would you bet on — and which would you bet against?
Twenty years from now: which of the four is still standing, and which ends in a coup or a funeral?

Cold-call. Take 2–3 answers, no wrong answer. If someone lands on single-party=durable/personalist=erratic, that’s the GFW finding in their own words — say so.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Same tool, new lens: which problem does “type” solve?
text:
Same tool, new lens: which problem does “type” solve?
Every week this module asks: is this an elite-control tool or a mass-control tool?

Regime type is really a bundle of default answers to that question, set at the moment of formation.

Personalist — elite control is weak (that’s the definition); everything rests on the leader personally
Single-party — elite control is institutionalised (the party disciplines everyone, including the leader)
Military — elite control runs through the officer corps’s collective interest
Monarchy — elite control runs through kinship and dynastic hierarchy


Week 1 callback, explicit: “today’s whole typology is four factory settings for solving the elite-control half of Svolik’s problem.” Mass control comes later — flag forward, don’t build it out.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The problem with the boxes
GFW’s own coding puts every regime into exactly one category. But regimes drift.

A single-party regime can personalise around its leader without ever changing its formal label. The party stays; the substance of power concentrates in one office, or one man.

The one thing to land if they remember nothing else: the boxes are a snapshot — the interesting political science is in the trajectory.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Case: Russia’s drift

Formally: dominant-party-adjacent system, with United Russia, a parliament, a constitution.

Substantively: since roughly the mid-2000s, decision-making has concentrated overwhelmingly in one office. Most serious observers now code Russia as personalist, not single-party — even though the party trappings never went away.

The party exists to co-opt and channel elites, not to constrain the leader
Succession planning is opaque and personalised — the single clearest personalist signature
Compare early Putin (more collective, more oligarch bargaining) to Putin now



Some students also take Russian Politics: vary the examples



Cross-module overlap flag (brief’s “borrowing his own Russia examples” guidance): POU44172 Russian Politics doesn’t currently run a dedicated “personalization of the Putin system over time” slide by that name, so this is probably safe as written — but Noah should sanity-check against whatever HT2027 ends up covering, since that deck’s content/schedule mismatch is still being resolved (see CLAUDE.md session log). Low risk, worth one look.


Currency check: this is a 2026-live claim about the current state of Russian elite politics. Confirm the framing still holds (succession speculation, elite composition) close to delivery — this is exactly the kind of thing that can shift meaningfully between drafting and term.


cc: unverified. Did not web-verify the specific 2026-live claim above beyond what’s already flagged in the placeholder — the general “Russia has drifted personalist since the mid-2000s” scholarly consensus is solid (Frantz/ Kendall-Taylor/Wright’s personalization research, cited two slides on), but any specific current-elite-composition detail Noah adds live should be checked close to delivery, not sourced from this deck.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Why the spectrum matters more than the box
text:
Why the spectrum matters more than the box

The GFW survival stats (two slides ago) are actually claims about degree of personalism, not the label
A “single-party” regime that’s 80% personalised behaves like a personalist regime — erratic succession, leader-dependent stability
Measuring where on the dial a regime sits is harder than sorting it into a box — and it’s where the live research frontier actually is (Frantz/Kendall-Taylor/Wright on personalization)


Close the loop: a mislabelled regime behaves like its substance, not its label — useful warning for the essay and exam.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Why monarchy gets skipped

Most intro treatments spend 90% of their time on personalist/single-party/military and wave at monarchy in one bullet.

That’s backwards. Gulf and MENA monarchies are among the most durable authoritarian regimes on Earth — and the mechanism is genuinely different from the other three types.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Which monarchy?
“Monarchy” is three different things:

Democratic monarchy — the crown reigns, an elected government rules. Britain, Spain, Japan. Not our subject.
Absolute monarchy — the crown rules, no parliament worth the name. Saudi Arabia, pre-1789 France.
Authoritarian constitutional monarchy — a parliament exists, elections happen, and the king picks the prime minister. Morocco, Jordan, Kuwait.


The third one was invented in nineteenth-century Europe — Austria-Hungary, Imperial Germany — once parliaments could no longer be avoided and rigging was still hard. The Habsburgs kept closing parliament. It didn’t matter: the crown chose the cabinet.

The type that matters for this module is the authoritarian constitutional monarchy, because it shows how the apex of power can be chosen top-down while everything below it looks electoral. The nineteenth-century European monarchies built the template when suffrage was widening and elections could not yet be reliably rigged: let the parliament sit, let it be elected, and keep the appointment of ministers with the crown. Morocco, Jordan and Kuwait run the same design today — real parliaments, real (if managed) elections, and a prime minister who answers to the palace. Week 5 returns to Jordan for what those parliaments are actually for.


Cold-call: “Is Morocco a democracy? It has elections and a parliament.” Let them work out it turns on who picks the PM. Habsburg line gets a laugh.


Source: Waller, Statecraft podcast, 10 Sep 2026 (§A 30–31 of the check file). Splits the old single “monarchy” box; the durability puzzle on the next slides is unchanged.


Name the gap explicitly: most syllabi under-invest in monarchy relative to how interesting and durable it is.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Two puzzles, one type

Why does hereditary succession work at all in the modern world, when it looks so fragile on paper — one bad heir away from collapse?
Why are Gulf monarchies so stable, when they have almost none of the institutional apparatus (parties, elections, ideology) the other types rely on?


Same answer to both: succession as a focal point, and rents that make co-optation cheap.

Sets up next two slides: Brownlee answers puzzle 1, Menaldo (+ rents preview) answers puzzle 2.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Brownlee: succession as a focal point
text:
Brownlee: succession as a focal point

Why does hereditary succession actually work as a stabilising device?

Elites fear a leadership vacuum more than they fear a mediocre heir — a clear rule beats no rule
Hereditary succession works best when the ruler predates the party (or there’s no party at all) — nothing else is available as a focal point
Compare: Mexico’s PRI used a different focal point (the dedazo, the outgoing president’s chosen successor) — same function, no bloodline required


A focal point (Schelling 1960) is a solution to a coordination problem that stands out to everyone as the obvious answer, with no need for explicit negotiation — not necessarily the best solution, just the one everyone independently expects everyone else to pick. Applied to succession: elites would often prefer almost any predictable rule to none, because the alternative — an open contest with no agreed rule — risks a fight that damages everyone, including the eventual winner. Bloodline succession and the PRI’s dedazo both work by the same logic: whoever is designated becomes the obvious focal point, which itself becomes a reason to accept them.



Mexico comparison: elites need SOME predictable succession rule, blood is just one option — ties to week 5
Image is Kim Jong-un, not a monarch, deliberately: North Korea’s dynastic succession without a formal monarchy. Say so if anyone raises an eyebrow

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Menaldo: how MENA monarchs stayed put
text:
Menaldo: how MENA monarchs stayed put
Victor Menaldo’s puzzle: MENA monarchies survived the same 20th-century pressures (decolonisation, Arab nationalism, oil shocks) that toppled monarchies almost everywhere else.

His answer: a political culture — invented, not inherited — of constitutions, Islamic legitimating principles, and informal norms that gave regime insiders a durable stake in the system.

Contrast with the credible-commitment story (institutions solve monitoring problems) — Menaldo’s argument leans more on legitimacy than mechanism
Worth pressing on: is “political culture” doing real explanatory work here, or is it a label for “things we can’t otherwise explain”? Ask the room


Culture-vs-institutions tension is genuinely contested — let students push back rather than present as settled.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Rents make the whole thing cheap
text:
Rents make the whole thing cheap
Gulf monarchies layer one more advantage on top of the succession focal point: oil.

When the state’s money comes from the ground, not from your paycheck, the state doesn’t need your consent the way a tax-dependent state does.

Public-sector jobs, subsidies, no income tax — co-optation at a scale poor autocracies simply can’t afford
This is rentier-state theory (Beblawi & Luciani, Ross) — namecheck only, not a full unit
Preview: this is exactly the mechanism Week 5 builds out properly (“Buying Loyalty”)


Rentier-state theory (Beblawi & Luciani 1987; Ross 2001, 2012) argues that a state funded by resource rents (oil, gas, minerals) rather than taxation faces weaker pressure to democratise or bargain with citizens — “no taxation, no representation demanded.” The mechanism: rents let the state buy loyalty (subsidies, public jobs, no income tax) without needing citizens’ consent to raise revenue, which is precisely backwards from the tax-bargaining story of European state formation. Week 5 covers this in full; here it’s one line of the monarchy answer.


Keep to one line — week 5 teaches it in full. Flag forward so the argument feels cumulative.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Is Saudi Arabia just a monarchy?
text:
Is Saudi Arabia just a monarchy?
Monarchy, obviously. But is that the whole story?

Pair discussion, 2 minutes: Saudi Arabia has a legislature (the Majlis al-Shura, unelected), state media, an enormous security apparatus, and a crown prince who has personalised power well beyond what “monarchy” usually implies. Does the label still fit — or is this a monarchy drifting personalist, the way Russia drifted the other direction?

Full two minutes, then 2–3 answers cold. No clean right answer — sets up the measurement-fight section. Cut if short on time.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Pin these to the board

  


IMAGE — Egypt panel: a military-parade or Sisi-podium image to complete the four-case grid (China/Saudi/Russia are filled from the reuse pool above, credited in w02img/CREDITS.md). Wikimedia Commons search “Sisi military parade” or “Egyptian Armed Forces parade” — nothing suitable was on hand in the Intro pool (its one parade photo is Moscow’s Victory Day parade, wrong country).


China — single-party, though watch how personalised it’s become since 2012 (same drift logic as Russia, opposite starting point)
Saudi Arabia — monarchy, with an active personalisation subplot (previous slide)
Egypt — military-origin regime, now heavily presidentialised under Sisi
Russia — nominally hybrid/electoral, substantively personalist


Notice the pattern: every single one of these is more personalist than its formal label suggests. That’s not a coincidence — it’s the era.

The “aha” moment: name it explicitly as a live global trend, not a coincidence of case selection.


Could reorganise this deck to lead with the four-case grid (cases-first per the voice guide) rather than close on it — I chose to close on it because the personalisation pattern only lands once students have seen the spectrum argument. Flagging as a real structural option, not a settled call — try it the other way if the cold open needs more punch.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Throw me a country
Name one. I’ll tell you what it is — and where it gets hard.

Lightning round, 5 min. Room throws countries, you classify live — hedging IS the lesson.

If silent, pocket four: Iran (theocratic-personalist, IRGC), North Korea (party-state structure, personalist function, monarchical succession), Morocco (king picks the PM), Singapore (dominant-party)
Say once: “whenever someone says autocracies always do X — run away”



Source: Waller’s own move on the Statecraft episode (10 Sep 2026) — “let’s do a lightning round”. Zero prep; it’s the analytical habit the whole module is selling. Nothing on the slide but the invitation, by design.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The slippery middle
What about regimes that hold real-looking elections — but rig the playing field, not just the count?

Electoral authoritarianism — elections happen, opposition exists, but the terrain is tilted so far the outcome is never seriously in doubt
Competitive authoritarianism (Levitsky & Way) — the opposition can compete, and occasionally even win something — but the deck is stacked
Their key move: these aren’t “diminished democracies” or “not-quite-there-yet” — they’re a stable regime type of their own, not a transition stage


Competitive authoritarianism (Levitsky & Way, Journal of Democracy, 2002; book-length treatment 2010): regimes where formal democratic institutions (multiparty elections, a legislature, courts) exist and are the main arena of political contestation, but incumbents abuse the state to tilt that contest heavily in their favour — control of media access, selective enforcement of law against the opposition, uneven access to state resources. Distinct from a straightforwardly closed autocracy (no real contest at all) and from a flawed democracy (contest is real, just imperfect). Their argument, worth remembering for the essay: this is a stable equilibrium some regimes settle into, not a way-station en route to democracy.


Cohort already met Schedler’s “menu of manipulation” (Comparative). New here: L&W’s claim that competitive authoritarianism is an equilibrium, not a way-station to democracy — dwell on it.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Why hybrid is the modal type now
text:
Why hybrid is the modal type now
Since the end of the Cold War, closed autocracy (no elections at all) has become the minority case.

Almost every surviving autocracy today performs some version of electoral ritual — Russia, Hungary, Turkey, Venezuela, Cambodia, and dozens more.

Elections generate information the regime actually wants (who’s disloyal, who’s popular)
Elections co-opt the opposition into playing a game the regime controls
Elections buy international legitimacy more cheaply than any alternative


The “so what”: this is now the default mode of authoritarianism worldwide — most of weeks 6 and 8 are really about THIS type.


Verified, 2026-09-16: V-Dem’s Democracy Report 2026 (10th edition) puts electoral autocracy as the single most populous regime type in 2025 — 46% of the world’s population (~3.8 billion people) — and 74% of the world’s population now lives under some form of autocracy overall, more than in closed and liberal democracies combined. Democracy for the average person is back to roughly 1978 levels. Source: V-Dem Institute, Democracy Report 2026: Unraveling the Democratic Era?, v-dem.net. Good concrete number to put on screen in place of the old placeholder below.


Optional: the exact chart (Regimes of the World, closed/electoral autocracy vs. electoral/liberal democracy shares over time) is in the V-Dem 2026 report PDF if you want a visual rather than just the number above.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How do we even measure this?
text:
How do we even measure this?
V-Dem? Freedom House? Polity? GFW’s own coding rules?

Every index encodes a theory of what democracy is. The disagreements are real, and they’re not just noise.

Ask if anyone can name a country the indices disagree on — Hungary is the classic case. Disagreement isn’t sloppiness, it reflects what each index counts.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Why classification is contested

Concept stretching — call too many regimes “democracy” (or “authoritarian”) and the word stops doing analytical work (Collier & Levitsky, “democracy with adjectives”)
Borderline cases — where’s the actual cut-point between “flawed democracy” and “competitive autocracy”? Nobody agrees, and the cut-point changes what gets counted where
Regimes drift within a type — the whole personalism-spectrum argument from earlier is itself a measurement problem: Russia 2000 ≠ Russia 2026, same formal label


Three measurement projects come up repeatedly in this module and in the essay literature. V-Dem (Varieties of Democracy, University of Gothenburg) uses several thousand country experts per country-year and a Bayesian model to aggregate their judgements into indices, including the “Regimes of the World” four-way classification used above. Freedom House scores political rights and civil liberties on its own analyst panels, producing the familiar “Free / Partly Free / Not Free” bands. Polity (now Polity5) codes executive constraint and competitiveness from historical case records, going back further in time than the other two. Concept stretching (Collier & Levitsky, “Democracy with Adjectives,” World Politics, 1997) is the worry that piling on qualifiers — “illiberal democracy,” “competitive authoritarianism,” “hybrid regime” — to cover awkward cases eventually empties the core concept of analytical content.


Say out loud: “we already saw this twice today, with Russia and Saudi Arabia — same problem, not a bolted-on topic.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Hungary: a live case study


Who decides? V-Dem uses expert coders and a Bayesian aggregation model. Freedom House uses its own analyst panel. GFW uses hand-coded historical case files. None of them is wrong — they’re answering slightly different questions.

Verified, 2026-09-16: V-Dem has coded Hungary an electoral autocracy since the late 2010s (sources disagree on the exact year quoted publicly — 2018 in V-Dem’s own commentary, 2022 in some secondary reporting — check the current report before stating a year on-slide) — the first EU member state ever classified as a hybrid regime/electoral autocracy by V-Dem. Freedom House’s Freedom in the World 2026 scores Hungary “partly free,” 24/40 on political rights and 41/60 on civil liberties — also a first for an EU member. Both classifications hold as of this pass; the chart above (V-Dem electoral/liberal democracy indices, generated via OWID/V-Dem data) shows the trend rather than a single year, which sidesteps the exact-year dispute. Sources: V-Dem Institute Democracy Report; Freedom House, Freedom in the World 2026.


Push on WHY the disagreement exists, not just describe it. Worth saying explicitly: measurement is never theory-free (they’ll cite these indices in essays).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Is Hungary a democracy?

Discussion device (this lecture’s #3 of three) — ask the room, show of hands: “hands up if you’d call Hungary a democracy.” Then reveal the V-Dem/Freedom House split and ask who wants to switch their vote once they see the indices disagree.


Room will split — that’s the point. Don’t resolve it: “depends which theory of democracy you’re using” IS the lecture’s argument.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The big quote

“The very fact that no consensus exists on how to measure something as basic as regime type tells you something important: classification is never a neutral, purely empirical exercise. It’s a theoretical claim in disguise.”


Flag: this reads as Noah’s synthesis rather than a scholar’s actual sentence. If you’d rather the “one big quote” slot be a literal spicy line from a named scholar (Collier & Levitsky’s “democracy with adjectives” title itself is almost quote-worthy, or a sharper Munck & Verkuilen line on measurement validity), swap it in — flagging rather than deciding per the brief.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Key readings this week

Geddes, Wright & Frantz, How Dictatorships Work — Chs. 1–2
Levitsky & Way, “The Rise of Competitive Authoritarianism,” J. of Democracy (2002)


Recommended: Magaloni & Kricheli, “Political Order and One-Party Rule,” Annual Review of Political Science (2010)


Recommended candidates, not yet added to _course.yml (propose only, per the brief — mining sources aren’t for adding to required lists): Brownlee 2007 “Hereditary Succession in Modern Autocracies” and Menaldo 2012 “The MENA’s Resilient Monarchs” both did real work in this deck’s monarchy section and arguably deserve a place in the recommended list, not just the slides — Noah’s call. Frantz/Kendall-Taylor/Wright on personalization would also strengthen the spectrum-argument slides if a recommended-reading slot opens up.

Svolik, The Politics of Authoritarian Rule — power-sharing chapters (2–3)

See you next Friday

Two-part hook: closes the “classify X, defend it” device (response-paper angle), then primes week 3’s power-sharing problem. Say both explicitly.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The Control Problem: Repression


Boundary, said once so it doesn’t need repeating on every slide (PLAN-MT2026.md §3 / _course.yml wk4 notes): Political Violence A (Kneafsey, same JS cohort, same semester) owns civil-conflict logic — Kalyvas, Weinstein, the causes and dynamics of political violence itself. This deck stays entirely on the RULER’S side of the transaction: repression as a management problem the dictator is solving, not as a form of conflict to be explained. No Kalyvas, no civil-war microfoundations. If a slide starts asking “why do people join violence,” that’s the tell it’s drifted into his territory.

The bluntest tool in the kit — and the one most likely to blow up in your hand

Last week: allies (power-sharing). This week: masses (control). Set the tension up front — not a horror-show tour, a management problem from the dictator’s desk.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Today

The dictator’s dilemma — why repression can blind the very ruler who orders it
Who guards the guards — the secret police as a threat in its own right
Informers and the economics of surveillance — the Stasi, in vivid numbers
Targeted vs. indiscriminate — and why blunt repression backfires
Hard, soft, and where this is all heading (bridge to Weeks 8–9)


Move fast through this slide — content earns the time, not the agenda.

Nothing deleted. Density: 52.4 → 53.4 w/slide; slides 22 → 32

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
This week in autocracy


Noah: two or three stories from this week. One line each — headline, country, and the concept it illustrates (elite problem or mass problem?). This slide is the same shape every week, same slot, right after the plan.


Five minutes, no more. Ask the room first: “what happened this week that belongs in this module?” — then show yours. The point is the habit: by teaching week 12 they should be bringing the stories, not you.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Callback: Svolik’s two problems
Week 1’s spine, back again:

Power-sharing — controlling your allies (Week 3: commitment problems, coups-in-waiting)
Control — controlling the masses, who could rise against you


Repression is the headline mass-control tool. But — plot twist for today — managing the security services who do the repressing is itself a power-sharing problem. The two boxes bleed into each other the moment you look closely.

Say the callback out loud. Double duty: re-anchors the spine AND previews today’s argument — don’t rush past the second bullet.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
You’re the security minister
You’ve just been appointed head of the secret police. Your boss is a dictator who has ruled for twenty years. Name the thing that keeps you up at night.

Run it live. 60 sec with a neighbour, then 2–3 answers before revealing the framing next slide. Listen for: leader turning on me / agents lying to me / not knowing the provinces / being blamed — all map onto later slides.


This is the deck’s built-in discussion device #1 (the brief wants 2–3 per week; this deck now has 3). It also front-loads the whole lecture’s argument as a puzzle before any theory appears — cases/puzzle-first, concept named after, per the voice guide.


Noah: any personal story from fieldwork or interviews about how officials talk about “what keeps them up at night”? A real anecdote here would land better than the hypothetical framing alone.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The dictator’s dilemma
Ronald Wintrobe’s core insight — required reading this week:

Repress too little → opposition organises in the open, you fall
Repress too much → nobody dares tell you the truth, and fear looks identical to loyalty from the outside
The more you terrorise, the less you actually know about what people think


A feared ruler is, in a specific and dangerous sense, an uninformed ruler.

A simple curve: “repression” on the x-axis, “information the ruler receives” (or “regime security”) as an inverted-U, peaking somewhere in the middle. The dilemma made visual — drop in w04img/. Currency-neutral, doesn’t date.


The dictator’s dilemma (Wintrobe): repression is meant to buy security, but it also destroys the information a ruler needs to know how much repression is actually necessary. Loyalty that is compelled looks identical, from the outside, to loyalty that is real — so the more a ruler represses, the less they can trust any signal of support they receive.


THE big idea of the lecture — everything else is elaboration. Loyalty is unverifiable; repression makes it MORE unverifiable, not less. Connects forward to week 8 (propaganda) and week 11 (preference falsification).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Why can’t the ruler just ask?
text:
Why can’t the ruler just ask?
The dilemma isn’t only about citizens. It runs through everyone who works for the ruler too.

Every layer between the dictator and the street is an agent reporting up to a principal — and agents have their own incentives
A police chief who reports bad news may get blamed for it; a governor who reports unrest may look incompetent; both have reason to say what the boss wants to hear
This is a general problem in organisations (the principal-agent problem) — dictatorships just have an unusually severe version, because the normal fixes (free press, independent courts, elections) are the things they’ve removed


Principal-agent problem / agency loss: a principal (here, the dictator) depends on an agent (an official, a police chief, an informer) to act on their behalf and report back honestly. When the agent’s incentives diverge from the principal’s — for instance, an incentive to report good news rather than true news — the principal loses reliable information about what’s actually happening. Democracies manage this with a free press, courts, and elections that create independent information channels; autocracies, having dismantled those channels, are unusually exposed to it.


Bridge into “who guards the guards”: the same agency-loss logic that hides citizens’ true preferences also makes the security services hard to monitor. Land it explicitly.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Big quote

“The general point is that repression, by silencing all opposition, makes it impossible for the dictator to know what people really think — and therefore impossible to know how much repression is actually needed.”


— paraphrasing Wintrobe’s dictator’s dilemma


Currency/accuracy flag: paraphrase, not a verified direct quotation — pull the actual line from The Political Economy of Dictatorship before this goes in front of students, or replace with the closest sourced sentence. The brief asks for one big-quote slide per deck; alternative candidate below if you’d rather go literary instead of social-scientific.


Alternative if you want to vary the register: Havel’s “greengrocer” passage, or Arendt on total terror making plurality impossible.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: The secret police: a tool that can turn on you
text:
The secret police: a tool that can turn on you
The institution built to manage the control problem is itself a control problem.

It needs real intelligence capacity — which means real autonomy
Autonomy plus a monopoly on coercion is exactly the profile of a coup threat
So the dictator faces a nested version of Week 3’s dilemma, one layer down: how do you keep the people with the guns loyal to you, specifically?


Coup-proofing: the set of strategies a ruler uses to stop their own armed forces or security services from being able to overthrow them — splitting agencies against each other, staffing them with loyalists, duplicating capabilities across rival organisations. It trades off against effectiveness: the more you coup-proof, the harder it is for the same forces to actually do their job well.


Greitens’ core move: the design of the coercive apparatus is itself a strategic choice, trading off two different threats.


Greitens is recommended-candidate, not currently on _course.yml’s reading list for this week (Davenport + Wintrobe are required; King/Pan/Roberts is the one recommended item currently listed). Strong case for adding her as a second recommended reading — she’s the clearest “organisation of coercion” argument in the literature and this slide leans on her directly. Noah’s call.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Who watches the watchers, themselves?
The agency-loss problem doesn’t stop at the top of the secret police — it runs all the way down through it.

A secret police that watches society still needs someone to watch it
Internal monitors, rival agencies, and parallel reporting lines exist to catch the security services lying to the ruler — but each of those checks is itself run by agents with their own incentives
There is no clean stopping point: at some layer, the ruler simply has to trust someone


This is why coup-proofing and information quality trade off against each other — you’re about to see the trade-off made explicit.


Unless you have a party. Then you don’t need a layer that watches — you have a member in every room.

The party as the answer to “who guards the guards”: coup-proofing (next slides) manages the problem by splitting and duplicating agencies against each other. A party manages it differently — cells inside the military, the intelligence services and even the schools, so there is always a loyal informant embedded in every institution, reporting up through a parallel channel the security services don’t control. It doesn’t solve the agency problem so much as blanket it: total coverage instead of a clean hierarchy of checks.


Source: Waller, Statecraft 10 Sep 2026 — “the party solves so many things… there’s a member of the party elite that is informing on everyone in every classroom,” on party cells inside China’s military, intelligence apparatus and schools as the alternative to coup-proofing.


Point: adding another layer of monitoring doesn’t solve it, just relocates the problem. Gesture back to cold-call: “my own agents lying to me” is exactly this. A party is a genuinely different answer — worth week 5.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Greitens’ trade-off: fragmented vs. unitary

Fragmented, socially exclusive security services (multiple competing agencies, drawn from a narrow loyal group) → harder to coup-proof against elites, but worse intelligence and more violent, indiscriminate repression
Unitary, socially inclusive services → better intelligence, more targeted and less violent repression — but a bigger coup risk, because you’ve just built one well-organised armed institution


You cannot optimise the secret police against both threats at once. Every autocrat is choosing a point on this trade-off, whether they say so or not.

IMAGE/diagram — a simple two-axis chart: x-axis “fragmented ↔︎ unitary,” y-axis “coup risk ↔︎ intelligence quality,” with a diagonal trade-off line. Drop in w04img/. Could be built the same way as POU11011’s list-experiment-diagram.png (matplotlib, no photographic source needed).


Loop back to the cold-call slide: whichever fear the room named, ask which side of this trade-off it sits on.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: The trade-off, worked: two real points on the map
text:
The trade-off, worked: two real points on the map

East Germany / Stasi — comparatively unitary, socially embedded service → the best intelligence coverage of any surveillance state on record (next slide’s numbers), and correspondingly less need for indiscriminate mass violence
Gulf monarchies (e.g. Saudi Arabia’s multiple, overlapping intelligence and security bodies) — deliberately fragmented and rivalrous by design → stronger insurance against a coup, weaker single-source intelligence picture


Same underlying trade-off, two different answers — neither is “correct,” each is a bet about which threat the ruler fears more.

IMAGE — could reuse a Gulf-monarchy visual from the POU11011 image pool (w08-lec11-img/gulf-skyline.jpg or -alt.jpg) as a contrast image beside the Stasi archive photo two slides on. Check its CREDITS.md entry before reuse; if the licence doesn’t fit a contrast use, source a fresh one.


Makes Greitens’ trade-off concrete before the deck commits to the Stasi as its detailed case study.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Informers and the economics of surveillance
text:
Informers and the economics of surveillance
Mass repression isn’t just violence — it’s an information-gathering operation, and information is expensive.

Every regime that tries total surveillance runs into the same constraint: watching everyone requires an army of watchers
Who watches them? The informant network needs its own loyalty problem solved
The ratio of watchers to watched is a number you can actually put on a slide


Informer networks: unofficial, often part-time collaborators (not uniformed officers) who report on neighbours, colleagues, and family in exchange for money, favours, or protection from punishment themselves. They are cheaper than professional police but create their own monitoring problem — an informer can fabricate reports, settle personal scores, or simply lie about what they’ve seen, and the regime usually has no independent way to check.


The Stasi ratio, vivid numbers: East Germany’s Ministry for State Security had roughly 91,000 full-time employees and (by most estimates) 170,000–190,000 unofficial informants (Inoffizielle Mitarbeiter) among a population of ~16 million — something like one informer for every 60–90 citizens, the highest surveillance density ever documented for a state. Verify the exact figures (estimates vary by source and by era of the GDR) before this goes in front of students; currency-check not needed (historical, won’t drift), but accuracy does. Consider a simple stat-card visual rather than a wall of numbers.


Land the ratio hard — the single most memorable fact in the lecture.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Total control, total collapse
One of the most pervasive surveillance states ever built — and it still collapsed, almost overnight, in 1989.

Total information, total control… until it wasn’t. Why?

Make “repression hides true preferences” land physically: files on nearly everyone, and the regime STILL didn’t see 1989 coming. Foreshadow week 11 (Kuran’s cascades) — say the callback out loud.


Image: a Stasi file room / archive photo (the paper-record scale is its own argument — floor-to-ceiling shelving, the “if laid end to end” stat for the files). Drop in w04img/.


Noah: a joke about East German bureaucratic thoroughness usually lands here — your call on tone, but there’s room for one before the pivot to “and it still collapsed.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Two ways to repress: the vocabulary
text:
Two ways to repress: the vocabulary
Before the mechanism — the two basic shapes repression comes in.

Targeted / selective repression: punishment aimed at specific named individuals — leaders, organisers, people who committed a specific act. Everyone else is left alone.
Indiscriminate / collective repression: punishment applied to a whole group, region, or identity category, regardless of who among them actually did anything — a substitute for identifying the specific people responsible.


Quick vocabulary slide — the distinction does real work in the next few slides.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Targeted vs. indiscriminate
Not all repression is the same shape.

Targeted / selective — go after named leaders, organisers, specific acts; leave everyone else alone
Indiscriminate / collective — punish whole groups, regions, or identities for the acts of a few (or of no one identifiable)


Lisa Blaydes’ finding on Saddam’s Iraq: regimes reach for collective punishment specifically when their information is weakest — it’s a substitute for precision, not a strategy of strength.

Collective punishment: punishing an entire group for the actions attributed to some unidentified members of it. Blaydes’ argument is that regimes reach for this specifically when they lack the fine-grained information to identify who is actually responsible — it is what a government does instead of precision, not a sign of strength.


Blaydes’ State of Repression is recommended-candidate (from the MSc bank, not yet on _course.yml), and does real conceptual work here — she inverts the intuition that indiscriminate repression signals a strong state; for her it signals an information-poor one. Strong case for adding as a second recommended reading alongside/instead of Greitens if only one slot is wanted.


Pivot into “why repression backfires.” Broad punishment teaches everyone that organising is safer in numbers — collective punishment manufactures the solidarity it’s trying to prevent.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Why indiscriminate repression backfires

It punishes people who did nothing — removing their incentive to stay uninvolved
It teaches dense, high-cohesion networks to form, because shared punishment creates shared fate
Visible brutality can create martyrs and international attention rather than deterring anyone


Davenport (required): the empirical record on repression’s effects is genuinely mixed — sometimes it deters, sometimes it radicalises. The backfire risk rises specifically with indiscriminate, highly visible violence.

States do respond to threats with repression fairly reliably, but whether it works is genuinely contested — don’t oversell a clean finding.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How would we even know if repression “works”?
text:
How would we even know if repression “works”?
A honest methods pause, since the deck has just made an empirical claim.

Repression events are undercounted by design — autocracies that repress well tend to also control what gets reported about it
Most cross-national repression data comes from event coding of news reports and NGO monitoring — which means the least transparent regimes are systematically the most undercounted
“No repression detected” in a dataset can mean “no repression happened” or “no one was able to report it” — the two look identical in the data


IMAGE — a simple illustration of the measurement problem: a redacted or blacked-out newspaper clipping / a “missing data” heatmap by country, next to a V-Dem or Political Terror Scale coverage map. Source: V-Dem codebook’s own discussion of measurement limitations, or Political Terror Scale documentation.


Worth a genuine minute — students remember this longer than the substantive finding. Ties back to the dictator’s own information problem: researchers face a milder version of the same blindness.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Discussion moment: pair up
Two minutes, with your neighbour. Name one historical or contemporary case where a crackdown triggered the very uprising it was meant to prevent.

Full two minutes, then cold-call 2–3 pairs. Likely answers: Ceaușescu’s Timișoara crackdown, Amritsar, Tunisia’s self-immolation. Don’t correct a good example — the exercise is the point.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Russia today: what does targeted repression cost?
text:
Russia today: what does targeted repression cost?
A modern, targeted (not indiscriminate) example — legalistic rather than violent.

Since February 2022, Russia has prosecuted “discrediting the army” as an administrative offence — criticism of the war, reframed as a specific, named legal violation
Between 24 Feb 2022 and 17 Feb 2025: 10,778 first-instance administrative cases under this one article
Each one needs a police report, a prosecutor, a court hearing — targeted repression is not free, it just spends a different kind of resource than indiscriminate repression does


Source: OVD-Info, “Three Years into the Full-Scale War” (https://ovd.info/en/antiwar_3_years), figure verified 2026-09-03 and already used in POU11011’s dictatorships lecture (w08-lec11.qmd) — reused here rather than re-derived, cited to both. OVD-Info is a Russian human-rights monitoring project, itself designated a “foreign agent” by the Russian state; the fact that this count exists at all, and who had to leave the country to keep counting, is itself part of the lecture’s point about information and repression.


Chart — a simple bar or line showing the case count over the three-year window (monthly or yearly), in the deck palette, styled like POU11011’s regimes-over-time.png. Not essential; the number alone works if time is short.


Same cohort could be taking POU44172 Russian Politics — cited explicitly so Noah can decide whether to vary the example if there’s overlap in the room. This keeps to targeted repression (fits this week’s frame) rather than pulling in civil-conflict material, so it stays on the right side of the Kneafsey boundary.


Pairs with Blaydes two slides back: targeted repression in practice — bureaucratic, expensive in a different currency (court time, not violence).


Noah: your own framing here — a Meduza or OVD-Info story from the last few weeks would update this past the 2025 cut-off and make it feel current rather than archival.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Selective control without violence at all
text:
Selective control without violence at all
You don’t have to censor or punish everything — just the dangerous things.

King, Pan & Roberts on China (recommended): the censorship apparatus lets criticism of the government through, but crushes anything that could enable collective action — organised protest, real-world gatherings.

Modern repression isn’t about volume — it’s precisely targeting coordination while tolerating everything else. Pause before the punchline.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Target coordination, not complaint
Target coordination, not complaint.

Selective/informational control: rather than repressing broadly, a regime allows most expression — including criticism — and concentrates its enforcement narrowly on the one thing that actually threatens it: coordination. King, Pan & Roberts’ China finding is the clearest example — individual complaints stay online; calls to gather at a specific time and place are removed within minutes.


The King/Pan/Roberts finding as a simple before/after: “criticism of local officials — stays up” vs. “call to gather at 3pm Saturday — deleted within minutes.” The counterintuitive punchline (complaint is safer to allow than organising) students consistently find sticky. Drop the concrete example pair in w04img/ or as text on the slide.


Sets up weeks 8/9 directly — say so.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Which would you rather run?
You’re advising a new autocrat with a limited budget. One option: heavy, visible, indiscriminate repression. The other: light, selective, mostly invisible control. Which do you recommend, and why?

Show of hands for the two options. No clean textbook answer — use the split to set up the hard/soft slide that follows.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Hard vs. soft — and where this is going
text:
Hard vs. soft — and where this is going

Hard repression — violence, imprisonment, killing, the visible secret police
Soft / “sharp” repression — harassment, surveillance, legal pressure, a tax audit, a deplatforming, a visa that doesn’t renew


Why fill prisons when a quieter tool does the same job with less blowback? The shift toward low-visibility control is one of the biggest stories in authoritarian politics right now — and it’s most of what Weeks 8 and 9 are about.

Hard vs. soft (“sharp”) repression: hard repression is visible and physical — arrest, imprisonment, violence. Soft or “sharp” repression works through ordinary-looking bureaucratic and legal tools — tax audits, licensing rules, defamation suits, denial of a visa or a permit — that produce the same chilling effect with far less international attention and far less risk of creating a visible martyr.


Deliberate one-line teaser only, per the boundary brief: keep the digital/high-tech surveillance specifics (China’s architecture, facial recognition, the social-credit story, transnational repression) OUT of this week — that’s all Week 9 (Digital Authoritarianism). This slide should whet the appetite, not spend it. If it starts growing bullet points about specific technologies, that’s the tell to cut it back.
Image note: stick.jpg (reused from POU11011 w08-lec11-img/, credited in w04img/CREDITS.md) used as the divider background here — “the stick” literally, and it’s the one slide in the deck where a blunt visual fits without overclaiming a specific case.


Land as a genuine cliffhanger — say explicitly “we’ll spend an entire week on exactly this soon.”


Noah: a meme about “soft repression” (the tax-audit-as-punishment genre) would land well here if you have one in mind — the concept is a little dry without a vivid modern example on-slide.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Case: a Latin American junta
A different point on the same map — indiscriminate terror as doctrine, not accident.

Argentina’s “Dirty War” (1976–83): the desaparecidos — forced disappearance as a deliberate strategy of deniability, not just brutality as a side effect
No files, no trials, no confirmed fate — repression designed to defeat even the information that a crime occurred


Compare to the Stasi: paper-heavy, bureaucratic, everything documented, versus a junta strategy built on the absence of a record. Two very different answers to “how much does the ruler want to know, and how much does the ruler want others to know.”

IMAGE — Plaza de Mayo, the Madres/Abuelas white-headscarf protest (a strong, well-known, Commons-licensed image of the response to forced disappearance rather than a graphic image of the violence itself — check Wikimedia Commons). Drop in w04img/. Alternative: a simple map/timeline of the 1976–83 period.


LatAm beat required by the brief. Argentina is the canonical case (Chile/Pinochet’s DINA works equally well and is arguably more tightly-coupled to a single coercive institution — swap in if you’d rather pair it more cleanly with the “secret police as institution” thread earlier in the deck). Deliberately not building out mechanisms/numbers here to avoid drifting toward Kalyvas/civil-conflict territory — Kneafsey’s boundary.


Loop back to the Stasi comparison: same problem, opposite toolkits — total documentation vs. total deniability.


Noah: swap to Pinochet/DINA if you’d rather keep the running “secret police as institution” thread tighter — see the cc above; your call, both work.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Cases compared

East Germany / Stasi — analog totalitarian surveillance, total documentation, huge informer ratio
Latin American junta (Argentina) — indiscriminate terror by design, built on deniability rather than records
Russia (targeted, legalistic) — narrow, bureaucratic, modern
China (teaser only — full case in Week 9) — selective, informational, increasingly digital


Same underlying goal — control the masses — four very different answers to “how much information do I want, and how visible does the punishment need to be?”

IMAGE — a simple 2x2 or spectrum graphic plotting the four cases by “documentation ↔︎ deniability” and “targeted ↔︎ indiscriminate.” Could reuse the same matplotlib approach as POU11011’s diagram assets.


Say the comparison out loud rather than reading the bullets — recap before the elite/mass callback.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Elite-control or mass-control?
The spine question, asked directly:

Repression aimed at citizens is obviously mass control. But today’s biggest twist — managing the secret police itself — is a power-sharing problem wearing a mass-control costume.


The tools bleed into each other. That’s normal — most real institutions do more than one job at once.

Don’t let it be a throwaway — sets up next week, where the co-optation toolkit shows the same bleed-through the other direction.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: In one line: what’s the dictator’s dilemma, again?
text:
In one line: what’s the dictator’s dilemma, again?
No notes, no neighbour — from memory. Finish the sentence: “The more a dictator represses, the less they actually know, because…”

Not graded — just forces reconstruction of the day’s big idea. Take one or two answers, don’t linger.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Key readings this week
Required:

Davenport, “State Repression and Political Order,” Annual Review of Political Science (2007)
Wintrobe, The Political Economy of Dictatorship — the dictator’s dilemma


Recommended:

King, Pan & Roberts, “How Censorship in China Allows Government Criticism but Silences Collective Expression,” APSR (2013)

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Elections Without Democracy

Why would a dictator hold an election they could lose — and then rig it anyway?

IMG ballot-box.jpg (ballot box, Astana polling station, Aug 2026 — Wikimedia Commons, reused from POU11011 w08-lec12-img/; credit in w06img/CREDITS.md) · full-bleed on the title slide · delete background-image= / background-opacity= from the heading to drop it.


Cold open, no admin. Puzzle: most autocracies now hold elections — risky, expensive, seem to invite contestation. Why? Then: how much cheating is the right amount?

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Today

Three cases, no fraud in common: Russia, Zimbabwe, Singapore
What elections actually do for an autocrat (it’s not “fake democracy”)
The menu of manipulation — you know this one, we go fast
The hard part: how much rigging is too much? What a stolen election reveals vs. conceals — and the bridge to Week 11


Flag up front: “you already have Schedler’s menu and Levitsky & Way from Comparative — today is the sequel, not the intro.”


Prior-exposure assumption, flagged per BUILD-BRIEF §“Prior exposure”: this cohort’s Comparative A “Varieties of Authoritarianism” week (mined from compA/POU22031 ... W5 Thursday.txt and Week 6 Monday.txt) already covers Schedler’s menu, Levitsky & Way’s competitive authoritarianism, and even a first pass at Magaloni’s four functions of hegemonic-party elections almost verbatim (force/invincibility/information/trap-the-opposition). So this deck treats all of that as known vocabulary and spends its time one level up: the strategic-logic questions Comparative didn’t ask (margin calibration, reveal-vs-conceal, fraud as a focal point). If Noah judges the cohort’s Comparative recall is patchier than assumed, the menu slide (below) has a one-slide compressed version ready to expand back out.
