title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
This week in autocracy


Noah: two or three stories from this week. One line each — headline, country, and the concept it illustrates (elite problem or mass problem?). This slide is the same shape every week, same slot, right after the plan.


Five minutes, no more. Ask the room first: “what happened this week that belongs in this module?” — then show yours. The point is the habit: by teaching week 12 they should be bringing the stories, not you.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
What makes an election “unfree,” exactly?
An electoral authoritarian regime holds elections that are regular, multi-party, and formally contested — but not free and fair: the incumbent controls the conditions of the contest, not just the count.

This is the vocabulary you already have from Comparative’s varieties week (Schedler; Levitsky & Way’s “competitive authoritarianism” is the harder variant, where the opposition’s odds are genuinely non-zero). Today’s job isn’t to re-teach the definition — it’s to ask why a regime bothers with this arrangement at all, and how much manipulation it takes before an election stops doing what elections normally do.


Fast — say it’s recall, not new, so nobody notes a definition they have.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Russia: the managed election

Regular presidential and parliamentary elections. A constitution. Opposition names on the ballot.

And: no serious challenger has had a realistic path to victory since 2000. The menu is worked hardest before anyone votes — media control, candidate exclusion, “administrative resources” — with some blunter instruments (ballot stuffing, inflated turnout) layered on top.

“Competitive authoritarianism” (Levitsky & Way) names this pattern: formal democratic institutions — elections, a constitution, an opposition — exist and are genuinely contested at the margins, but incumbents use their control of the state to tilt the playing field so far that the ruling party’s victory is never seriously in doubt. Russia since 2000 is the paradigm case.


Image/data: the Kobak–Shpilkin–Pshenichnikov “Putin’s peaks” turnout/vote-share scatterplot (statistical fingerprint of fraud) — vivid, and a nice bridge into “what a stolen election reveals.” Currency-check: use the most recent available Russian election result at time of delivery.


Keep efficient — POU44172 Week 5 has the deep dive if a student takes both.


Reuse flag (BUILD-BRIEF “Mining sources”): this case draws on your own AY2026-27/POU44172 Russian Politics HT2027/slides/week05.qmd (“Elections and Electoral Authoritarianism”) — same term, same JS-adjacent cohort could plausibly take both modules. Deliberately kept thin here (managed-election headline only, no mayoral-elections/political-machines detail, no Frye-Reuter-Szakonyi clientelism material) so the two decks don’t duplicate. If you’d rather swap in a different lead case for variety, Belarus or Azerbaijan cover similar ground — your call.


IMG duma.jpg (State Duma plenary session, 10 March 2020 — reused from POU11011 w08-lec11-img/; credit in w06img/CREDITS.md) · reserved right column (.img-right) so it can’t collide with the text.


Noah: your own line/anecdote here — you’ve watched several of these elections up close in ways a textbook can’t. Also a natural spot for a dry aside about “administrative resources” as a euphemism.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Russia 2026: the live case

Currency slot — fill before delivery. Russia’s State Duma election is scheduled for 18–20 September 2026 — five weeks before this lecture (see the same currency flag on POU11011’s w08-lec11.qmd, which teaches the same fact six weeks before its own delivery date). By 23 October the result will be known: swap in the official turnout and United Russia’s reported seat share as the live version of “no serious challenger since 2000,” and note whether independent observers (Golos, OSCE if present) flagged irregularities. cc: unverified — the schedule is the fixed Russian electoral calendar (elections to the Duma are held on the second Sunday of September under the 2020 law); confirm the exact date and result nearer delivery.


Pull the actual numbers in before presenting. If nothing newsworthy happened, say so — “the least interesting result is also data.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Zimbabwe: the crude end
Elections since independence. Regular, contested, internationally observed.

And also: violence against opposition supporters, military and “war veteran” intimidation, contested vote counts, occasional outright annulment or delay of results. The menu’s during/after columns doing the heavy lifting, not the before.

Where the “before” columns of the menu (media control, candidate disqualification, gerrymandering) are weakly built, a regime that still wants to win falls back on cruder, more visible tools deployed during and after the vote itself: intimidation at polling stations, contested counts, outright annulment. These are the tools most likely to be caught on camera and condemned internationally — which is exactly why they are Schedler’s “last resort,” not his default.


IMAGE — a Zimbabwean election scene (a queue at a polling station, a ZANU-PF rally, or post-election unrest), Wikimedia Commons; search “Zimbabwe election” + year. Place .absolute bottom-right, ~28% width, to match the Russia/Singapore treatment either side of it.


Contrast with Russia: Russia wins the game before it starts; Zimbabwe needs cruder coercion because the “before” tools were never built out.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Cheaper up front, costlier over time
text:
Cheaper up front, costlier over time
Zimbabwe’s ruling ZANU-PF has paid a real price for relying on visible coercion — sanctions, diplomatic isolation, a “pariah state” reputation — that Russia’s subtler, earlier-stage manipulation has mostly avoided. Crude tools are cheap on election day and expensive for years afterward.

Land it: crude tools are cheap on the day, expensive to have used — why Schedler ranks fraud as the last resort, not the default.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Singapore: no fraud needed

Free, competently administered, minimally-disputed elections. Nobody credibly alleges ballot stuffing.

And yet the PAP has never lost power since 1959, opposition MPs are a small minority, and the playing field is tilted so far — gerrymandered Group Representation Constituencies, defamation suits, media control, a long track record of delivering growth — that the outcome has never seriously been in doubt.

Group Representation Constituencies (GRCs) bundle several seats into one multi-member district that a single party slate contests as a block — officially to guarantee minority representation, but their boundaries and size have also been used to make it harder for a small opposition to field a full slate and win. Combined with defamation suits against critics and a media landscape the PAP effectively controls, the “before” column of the menu can do the entire job without a single contested ballot.


IMG singapore.jpg (Marina Bay Dusk, 2018 — reused from POU11011 w03-lec04-img/; credit in w06img/CREDITS.md) · reserved right column.


IMAGE/DATA — a diagram of a Singapore GRC boundary or a PAP-vs-opposition seat-share chart since 1959 (Singapore Elections Department / Wikipedia “Elections in Singapore”) would make the gerrymandering point visually, next to or instead of the skyline photo above.


Important case: breaks “authoritarian elections = fraud.” Zero cheating on election day, “before” column does 100% of the work. Cold call: “is Singapore even authoritarian?”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Is Singapore even authoritarian?
If nobody stuffs a single ballot — no fraud, no violence, competent and correct vote-counting, real opposition candidates on real ballots — is it still fair to call the outcome rigged?

Cold call. There’s a real “no” answer — take it seriously. Depends how you define “free and fair”: formal process vs. contestable outcome.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Three cases, one spectrum
Russia manages the field and tops it up with some fraud. Zimbabwe leans on coercion because the field-tilting was never fully built. Singapore never needs to cheat at all.
Which of these is “most authoritarian” — and does that question even make sense?

Fraud intensity and regime durability are not the same axis, and this slide’s cold-call is designed to expose that: Singapore, the case with the least visible cheating, has also been in power the longest of the three by a wide margin. Cruder tools (Zimbabwe) are often a sign that the subtler ones were never available, not that the regime is stronger for using them.


IMAGE/DATA — a world map or scatterplot of electoral-autocracy scores (V-Dem Electoral Democracy Index, or the V-Dem Regimes of the World typology) would let students place Russia, Zimbabwe and Singapore against the full global spread rather than just against each other.


Cold call, push for disagreement — no clean answer. Singapore, the “cleanest” case, is probably the most durable of the three.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Two jobs, aimed at elites
Magaloni’s account of hegemonic-party elections, generalised — starting with the elite-facing half:

Information harvesting — which regions, which local brokers, actually deliver? Elections are a census of who can turn out a vote and who can’t.
Elite management — a controlled test of who can mobilise support, without anyone needing to declare their ambitions out loud


Beatriz Magaloni’s Voting for Autocracy (2006) develops this account from Mexico’s PRI, which held power from 1929 to 2000 through elections it rarely needed to steal outright. The PRI used local vote totals as a performance review for its own regional bosses — deliver the vote, keep your position; fall short, and you’ve revealed yourself as a weak link, whether or not you intended to defect.


Testing loyalty among people who already have power — Svolik’s harder problem than controlling the mass public.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Three jobs, aimed outward
The other half of Magaloni’s account — aimed at the mass public and the outside world:

Deterrence through overwhelming victory — the margin itself is a warning, not a courtesy (next slide)
International cover — the “democratic” props for donors, trade partners, and diplomatic recognition
Controlled blame release — a scheduled, bounded outlet for public grievance, on the regime’s calendar rather than the street’s


Generalised beyond the PRI case, the claim is that hegemonic-party elections are not a democratic veneer over “real” authoritarian rule — they are a genuinely functional piece of the regime’s machinery, doing work that no other institution could do as cheaply: manufacturing deterrence, buying international legitimacy, and channelling discontent into a scheduled, survivable outlet.


Spine of the week — spend real time. Callback: which of these five are elite-control tools, which are mass-control? Svolik framing, next slide.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Elite tool or mass tool?
Svolik’s two problems, back again:

Power-sharing (elites) — info-harvesting and elite-management: who delivers, who’s testing the water, who might defect
Control (masses) — deterrence and blame-release: convince ordinary people that resistance is pointless, and give them somewhere to vent
International cover doesn’t fit either bucket cleanly — a third audience (donors, markets, foreign publics) that most weeks don’t need, but this week does


Same toolkit, doing double (or triple) duty. That’s most of why elections are worth the trouble.

Spine callback — point back to Week 1’s framing slide: “here it is again, split five ways.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The signalling logic
Why win with 90% when 55% would do the job of “winning”?

Because the margin itself is the message: “resistance is futile, don’t bother defecting.” Magaloni: hegemonic-party landslides are built to look invincible, not merely victorious.

Pause here. Sets up next section: rigging is a calibration problem, not a yes/no one.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: The menu of manipulation — the recap slide
text:
The menu of manipulation — the recap slide
You have this from Comparative’s varieties week. One slide, not a march:

Before — exclude candidates, gerrymander, control media, buy votes
During — stuff ballots, miscount, intimidate at the polling station
After — annul, ignore, jail the winners


Schedler’s point, restated fast: fraud is the last-resort tool, cruder, more visible, and more expensive to your legitimacy than anything upstream of it. Zimbabwe leans on it; Singapore never touches it.

IMAGE — a simple before/during/after menu infographic (three columns, the sub-bullets above as icons or short labels) would make this recap slide scannable at a glance rather than text-only. A quick original diagram, not a Commons find.


Deliberately compressed to one slide per the prior-exposure assumption above — Comparative’s version of this exact slide (see compA/... W5 Thursday.txt) spends three slides building the menu up from scratch. If a straw poll or cold-call reveals the room doesn’t actually remember it, this is the easiest slide to expand back out live — the sub-bullets are already there to unpack.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: What is the “chain of democratic choice”?
text:
What is the “chain of democratic choice”?
Schedler’s real contribution isn’t the menu — it’s naming everything an election depends on, upstream and downstream of the vote itself.

Empowerment, freedom of choice, freedom of supply, equality, inclusion, ballot secrecy, integrity of counting, honest tabulation
Break any one link, and the whole chain fails — a “free” vote in a media environment with no independent information isn’t actually free


This is the strategic-logic reading Noah is pointing you back to. The menu of manipulation (before/during/after) is really a menu of which link in the chain to break — and Schedler’s argument is that a regime only needs to break one link, at the point of its choosing, to control the outcome without ever touching a ballot on election day itself.


The piece Comparative’s version skips — worth the extra minute.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Two-minute pair discussion
With the person next to you: pick one case (Russia / Zimbabwe / Singapore). Where on the menu — before, during, or after — does most of the work happen? And what would it cost the regime to move one column to the left?

Pair discuss, ~2 min, then cold-call 2–3 pairs. “Move a column left” bridges into the calibration question next.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The calibration problem
If the margin is the message, the autocrat has a genuine optimisation problem, not a binary “rig or don’t rig.”

Too honest — a close or lost election signals real vulnerability; elites read it as a defection opportunity
Too crude — an implausible landslide (99.9% turnout, 97% for the incumbent) signals desperation, not strength, and invites ridicule and scrutiny it can’t survive


“Too crude” is not a moral judgement, it’s a signalling failure: a regime that has to fake a landslide is telling elites and the public exactly what it’s most trying to hide — that it does not, in fact, command that much genuine support. The number itself becomes evidence against the claim it was meant to support.


Two failure modes — hold “just right” for the next slide.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The calibration problem, part two

Just right — a win big enough to deter, small enough to be believable — Magaloni’s PRI rarely needed outright fraud to clear this bar


The skill isn’t rigging. It’s knowing where the line is — and it moves, case by case, year by year.

Magaloni’s Mexican PRI data show a regime that could usually clear the “just right” bar without outright fraud — routinely winning 60–70% in presidential elections through the tools upstream of the ballot box, rarely needing the implausible 90%+ landslides more repression-dependent regimes have leaned on. The comparison across cases is itself evidence for the calibration argument: the more upstream control a regime has built, the less crude fraud it needs to hit the same target margin.


Centrepiece — spend real time. Poll on the next slide lands it, don’t pre-empt.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Strength, or desperation?
Ask the room — for each result, hands up for strength, hands down for desperation: (1) 97% turnout, 96% for the incumbent; (2) 68% for the incumbent on a contested but plausible count; (3) 51–49%, genuinely close.

Swap in real recent vote-share numbers if you have a cleaner set at hand (e.g. from the Russia 2026 slide above, once the result is in) rather than the generic figures given.


Straw poll. Trick answer: (1) reads as desperation, not strength — that’s the calibration problem.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
What a stolen election reveals

Forensic statistical signatures (turnout spikes, round-number vote shares, the “Putin’s peaks” pattern) — you can often prove fraud happened, after the fact, from the numbers alone
Which regions/precincts needed heavy intervention — a map of fraud is a map of the regime’s actual weak points, hiding in plain sight


Statistical forensics of elections works because honest vote-counting has predictable mathematical properties (e.g. digits should be roughly uniformly distributed, turnout and vote share shouldn’t cluster at round numbers) that hand-adjusted results violate. Researchers such as Kobak, Shpilkin and Pshenichnikov have used exactly this method on Russian election data — see the placeholder on the Russia slide above. cc: unverified — cite the specific paper/dataset before using the scatterplot on-slide.


Slow down — evidence base for everything claimed about Russia earlier.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
…and what it conceals
Fraud destroys the very signal — true underlying support — that elections exist to collect. The autocrat trades away some of Job #1 (information) to protect Job #3 (deterrence): genuine popularity and a manufactured margin become indistinguishable from the outside.

Make it explicit: info-harvesting and deterrence pull in opposite directions. Rig too hard and you’ve blinded yourself on information.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Downstream risk: fraud as a focal point
text:
Downstream risk: fraud as a focal point
A rigged election isn’t just a signal to elites and voters — it’s a coordination device for the opposition.

A specific, dated, visible act of theft gives people a shared reason to believe everyone else is also angry, right now. That’s the hardest thing for a would-be protest movement to manufacture on its own.

A “focal point” is a solution to a coordination problem that stands out as obviously shared — everyone can guess that everyone else will pick it too, without needing to communicate directly. Under preference falsification (Week 11’s Kuran), nobody knows how many others secretly share their grievance; a stolen election gives a specific date, place and injustice that lets strangers coordinate on “now” without ever having spoken.


Bridge to Week 11 — say the week number. Mechanism: fraud converts private grievance into public, common-knowledge grievance. Don’t resolve it here, just plant the flag.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The big quote

“I consider it completely unimportant who in the party will vote, or how; but what is extraordinarily important is this — who will count the votes, and how.”
— attributed to Stalin (apocryphal, but the field keeps repeating it because it’s structurally exactly right)


Attribution is contested — say so if asked. Cleanest one-line summary: the problem was never “win or lose,” it was “control the count.”


Alternative big-quote candidates if you’d rather commit to something verifiably real: Schedler’s own “electoral authoritarianism is a system in which opposition parties lose elections” (vs. democracy, where they merely can) is sharp and unambiguously his. Your call which lands better live — left both options visible rather than picking for you, per the brief.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Does the whole thing stabilise — or destabilise?
text:
Does the whole thing stabilise — or destabilise?
The open debate, worth leaving genuinely open:

Stabilising — elections entrench the regime, test elites safely, co-opt rivals, deter challengers.


Destabilising — they create the one focal point Kuran-style cascades need, and sometimes, even rigged, the opposition wins anyway.

The “electoral revolutions” of the 2000s (Georgia 2003, Ukraine 2004, Kyrgyzstan 2005) are the clearest cases of the destabilising path: fraud that was too obvious to swallow became the trigger for mass mobilisation that removed the incumbent. They remain the exception rather than the rule — most rigged elections do not end in the ruler’s removal — which is part of why the stabilising/destabilising question stays genuinely open.


Noah: your own call on which side of this debate you actually lean, and whether you have a better worked example than the 2000s “colour revolutions” — your Russia/Moscow material would land well here.


Leave it open — strong essay/exam question, sets up the final third of the module.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Three cases, one logic

Russia — before-heavy, some after; margin calibrated for deterrence
Zimbabwe — before weak, during/after doing the work; costly abroad
Singapore — before does 100% of the job; nothing left to fake


All three are solving the same optimisation problem from different starting endowments. A regime with a well-built “before” machinery (media, courts, gerrymandering) never needs the crude, costly, internationally visible tools; a regime without one has to buy the same outcome at a much higher reputational price. That’s the whole week in one sentence.


Closing recap — gesture back at the opening puzzle and answer it directly.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
This week in autocracy


Noah: two or three stories from this week. One line each — headline, country, and the concept it illustrates (elite problem or mass problem?). This slide is the same shape every week, same slot, right after the plan.


Five minutes, no more. Ask the room first: “what happened this week that belongs in this module?” — then show yours. The point is the habit: by teaching week 12 they should be bringing the stories, not you.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The liberation-technology moment
The early-2010s consensus:

Cheap communication solves the opposition’s coordination problem
Regimes can’t censor what they can’t see coming
The Arab Spring proved it — “the Facebook revolution”


Fifteen years on, that reads as a period piece. What happened?

The “liberation technology” thesis, associated with writers like Larry Diamond in the early 2010s, held that cheap digital communication should systematically favour opposition movements over incumbent regimes: it solves the coordination problem that has always been the hardest part of organising against a government that controls the streets, and it does so faster than a regime can react. The Arab Spring, and especially the role of Facebook and Twitter in Tunisia and Egypt in 2011, was read at the time as confirmation. The coordination logic was not wrong — it is the same logic Kuran’s information-cascade model gives for any collective-action problem under authoritarian rule (see Week 11). What the thesis underestimated is that the same infrastructure that lets ten thousand strangers find each other also tells a regime, automatically and retrospectively, exactly who those ten thousand people are.


Image, w09img/: 2011 Tahrir Square (crowds, phones held up) directly beside a 2020s surveillance-camera wall / facial-recognition dragnet shot. The whole week’s argument in one slide — how completely the 2011 question flipped into the 2026 answer. Currency check: use a genuinely recent surveillance image, not a stock 2018 one. Candidate source: Wikimedia Commons (Tahrir Square 2011 has several CC-licensed options); a facial-recognition/CCTV-wall photo needs sourcing fresh — nothing in the Intro image pool fits.


Cold open: show of hands — does the internet help dictators or dissidents more today? In 2011 nobody hesitated; now watch them hesitate.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
What the regime learned

Surveillance got cheap — no informant network required
Networks are legible — who talks to whom, mapped automatically
Control moved upstream — to platforms, cables, and app stores
And the regime learned to participate rather than only block


The technology didn’t pick a side. It lowered costs — for both sides. The question is who adapted faster.

“Legibility” is doing a lot of work in that first bullet: a regime doesn’t need to read every message to map a network, it only needs metadata — who contacted whom, when, how often — which digital communication generates automatically and which a human informant network never could at that scale. Moving control “upstream,” to the small number of platforms, cables, and app stores a population actually depends on, is cheaper than trying to police every individual message downstream — a handful of compliance requests to a handful of firms does the work that would once have taken thousands of censors.


Resist techno-determinism in either direction — likely exam question.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Key term: digital authoritarianism

Digital authoritarianism: the use of digital information and communication technology to surveil, censor, persuade and repress, in ways that extend a regime’s existing toolkit rather than replace it.


Note what the definition does not say: it doesn’t claim a new set of goals. Same two problems as every other week — power-sharing, mass control. New infrastructure.

This definition is deliberately conservative. A tempting alternative would define digital authoritarianism as a qualitatively new phenomenon — an “algorithmic” or “AI-powered” mode of rule distinct from everything that came before it. The framing this module uses instead, and the one the week’s readings support, treats digital tools as an extension of the repression/ co-optation/legitimation toolkit built in Weeks 4–8: cheaper surveillance, cheaper censorship, cheaper propaganda, aimed at the same two structural problems every autocrat has always faced. The technology is the variable; the underlying strategic logic is the constant.


Say explicitly: if they remember one sentence from this lecture, this is it.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Spine callback: which problem does this solve?
text:
Spine callback: which problem does this solve?
Recall Week 1: every autocrat manages two problems — power-sharing with elites, and control of the masses.

Digital tools are unusual: they serve both, at once, through the same infrastructure.

Mass control — the obvious one: dragnet surveillance, censorship, flooding
Elite control — the less obvious one: the same data that watches citizens also watches ministers, generals, and rivals. Loyalty can be monitored, not just assumed



Most weeks answer “elite tool or mass tool?” with a pick. This week the honest answer is: the same tool, aimed either way.

Elite-facing digital control is easy to under-teach because most of the public case material — China’s Great Firewall, Iranian internet shutdowns — is mass-facing by design and therefore more visible. But the same surveillance and data-analysis capacity that maps a citizen population also maps an inner circle: anti-corruption investigations selectively deployed against a rival, monitored phone and financial records of officials, and loyalty-tracking inside a ruling party are all digital-authoritarian tools aimed at the elite-control problem rather than the mass-control one.


Don’t skip even if short on time — stops the week reading as tech show-and-tell. Name the elite-facing half explicitly: anti-corruption surveillance used selectively, phone monitoring of officials.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: What does watching everyone actually buy you?
text:
What does watching everyone actually buy you?
Recall the dictator’s dilemma (Week 4): repression destroys information.

Surveillance is the attempted escape from that trade-off.

Cold call — make someone propose a mechanism before revealing Xu’s argument next slide.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Xu’s argument: surveillance changes the menu
text:
Xu’s argument: surveillance changes the menu
Week 4’s dilemma: repress too little and threats grow; repress too much and you destroy the information (and the loyalty) you need.

Xu (required, AJPS 2021): better information lets a regime substitute.

Set up the mechanism — next slide gives the payoff and evidence.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Substitution, not just cheaper repression
Better information means a regime can identify who’s actually a threat, and who’s just noisy but harmless, and co-opt the real threats specifically — a promotion, a payoff, a targeted favour — while repressing only the smaller, identified group who won’t be bought.

So digital surveillance doesn’t just make repression cheaper. It makes co-optation more precise — which is arguably the bigger deal.

Xu’s empirical design uses the staggered rollout of digital surveillance systems across Chinese counties (a difference-in-differences design) and finds that counties that gain surveillance capacity see local governments’ public security spending and arrests of political activists rise, while public-goods provision falls. Read against the mass-co-optation logic of Week 5, that looks paradoxical — more surveillance, less redistribution? The resolution is precision: a government that can identify the specific individuals most likely to organise unrest no longer needs to buy off everyone to keep the peace; it can narrow co-optation to the people who matter and repress the smaller, identified residual instead. The prediction that follows is a general rise in targeted repression alongside a decline in universal redistribution as surveillance technology improves.


This is the sharpest and most citable idea in the deck — worth protecting from cuts if the lecture runs long. It’s also the cleanest bridge back to Week 5 (buying loyalty): surveillance is what tells you whom to buy.


Verified 2026-09-16 (this pass), web search: Xu, “To Repress or to Co-opt? Authoritarian Control in the Age of Digital Surveillance,” American Journal of Political Science 65(2), 2021, pp. 309–325 (DOI 10.1111/ajps.12514). Confirms the printnote’s design/findings summary above.


Put Week 4’s inverted-U back on the chalkboard (b). Surveillance doesn’t shift the curve — it lets the regime split the population and apply a different tool to each slice.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: One big idea, one big quote
text:
One big idea, one big quote

Digital surveillance “resolves dictators’ information problem of not knowing individual citizens’ true anti-regime sentiments,” letting a regime “substitute targeted repression for nonexclusive co-optation.”
— paraphrasing Xu (2021), AJPS 65(2), abstract


Not a verbatim quotation — flagged, not invented. This pass could confirm the article’s abstract language (above, lightly requoted from the published abstract text found via web search) but could not access the full PDF to pull a single punchier in-text sentence. If you have library access to the piece, swap in the sharpest actual line you find; otherwise this is safe to use as written, since it draws directly on the author’s own published framing rather than an invented paraphrase.


Don’t paraphrase-as-quote live — find the real line if you want one sharper than the abstract text above.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
China: control by architecture

The Firewall as infrastructure, not a blacklist
Platform-level responsibility — make the companies do the censoring


The Great Firewall is better understood as infrastructure than as a list of banned sites: it operates at the level of network architecture (filtering, throttling, and blocking at the internet-service-provider level) rather than as a simple index a censor updates by hand. A second, distinct mechanism is platform-level responsibility — Chinese law makes domestic platforms legally liable for content their users post, which outsources the actual moderation work to companies with a direct commercial incentive to over-comply rather than under-comply.


Friction and distraction, not outright blocking — “acts as if it sees everything” without claiming it does.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: China: seeing you and shaping you
text:
China: seeing you and shaping you

Facial recognition and predictive policing at scale, in public space
Not a panopticon that sees everything, everywhere — a system that makes people act as if it does


The deterrent effect doesn’t need full coverage to work. Uncertainty about who’s watched does the job cheaper than actually watching everyone.

The result is a system that need not actually monitor every message or every person to have its intended effect: users who cannot be sure what is and isn’t being watched moderate their own behaviour accordingly. This is the same logic Bentham’s original panopticon design relied on — visibility of the possibility of observation, not observation itself, disciplines behaviour — now delivered through cameras and facial-recognition systems rather than architecture.


Currency check, every September: confirm the Firewall/platform-regulation details are still accurate — this apparatus changes fast (new laws, new enforcement targets). Image, w09img/: China’s surveillance-camera density, one recent data point (city count, camera count) from a source you can defend live — Comparitech’s annual “most-surveilled cities” ranking is a plausible source to check.


Panopticon callback is optional — don’t force it if the room hasn’t seen Bentham/Foucault elsewhere.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Social credit: what’s real, what’s mythologised
text:
Social credit: what’s real, what’s mythologised
The Western media version: one unified national score, dystopian and total.


There is no single national score. Systems are fragmented — local pilots, sectoral blacklists (courts, finance), no unified algorithm
The most consequential piece is mundane: court judgment-debtor blacklists (can’t buy plane/train tickets) — not a sci-fi social ledger
The “score that follows you everywhere” is largely a journalistic composite, not a description of one system



Real, and worth taking seriously: a fragmented but expanding infrastructure of behavioural blacklisting. Mythologised: the unified Black Mirror score.

This slide is deliberately corrective — it’s the week’s best scepticism-training moment (read coverage of authoritarian states critically, same discipline as Week 8’s propaganda material). Good discussion prompt: “why would this story be the one that goes viral in the West?” (answer: it confirms a prior, it’s a great visual, and it’s simpler than the fragmented reality).


Be precise — getting this wrong undercuts the module’s credibility on its most current material.


Add a specific, dated example of a court blacklist consequence (a real documented case) — stronger than the abstract description above. Currency-check every year; this system is still evolving. cc: unverified — no specific case was sourced in this pass; don’t put an invented one on the slide.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Russia: narrative first, walls later

The 2000s: dominate television, leave the internet relatively free
The 2010s: sovereign-internet laws, platform pressure, VPN blocking
Wartime: criminalising speech, throttling, exit of foreign platforms


A regime that walled the garden late — and is still building the wall.

Russia’s approach inverted China’s build order. Where China built the architecture of control from the start of mass internet adoption, the Putin-era regime in the 2000s judged television dominance sufficient and left the internet comparatively open — the internet was a minority medium and a low priority. That changed after the wave of internet-organised protest in 2011–12: the 2010s brought “sovereign internet” legislation, pressure on platforms to localise data and comply with takedown requests, and growing VPN restriction. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the pace accelerated sharply — wartime speech-criminalisation laws, throttling of remaining foreign platforms, and the exit (voluntary or forced) of most major Western platforms from the Russian market.


Your own territory (Russian Politics decks have deeper material on this if you want more depth — POU44172 doesn’t currently carry a dedicated digital-control week, so no duplication risk with that module for this specific angle). The comparative payoff: China and Russia arrived at similar destinations from opposite directions — architecture-first vs. narrative-first.


Currency check, every September: wartime internet-control measures keep moving (new blocking, new platform exits/re-entries). Confirm the current state before teaching. cc: unverified — dates above (2011–12 protest wave, 2022 invasion) are well-established public facts, not newly sourced this pass; the current-state claims (what’s blocked/available right now) are the part that needs a fresh check each year, not the historical sequence.


Ask the room: China’s or Russia’s model looks more durable, and why? No clean textbook answer — let them argue it.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Iran: shutdowns and cat-and-mouse

Nationwide shutdowns during protest waves — the blunt instrument
A large, technically sophisticated population routing around it
Enormous economic cost, imposed on itself


Shutdowns are what you do when you don’t have China’s architecture.

A full or near-full national internet shutdown is a blunt instrument in a way architectural control is not: it is highly visible, immediately reported internationally, and imposes direct economic cost on the very state that orders it (lost e-commerce, banking disruption, remittances blocked). Iran has used nationwide and regional shutdowns repeatedly during major protest waves, betting that short-term disruption to organising is worth the self-inflicted economic and reputational cost. Iran’s population is also comparatively technically literate, which produces a genuine cat-and-mouse dynamic — VPN and circumvention-tool use rises quickly whenever restrictions tighten, unlike in a state with less technical capacity to route around blocks.


Currency check, every September: Access Now’s #KeepItOn shutdown-tracker data makes a good live figure (shutdown count/duration, latest year). Pull the current release; don’t reuse last year’s number. cc: unverified — no specific figure sourced this pass; leave the slide qualitative until a current-year number is pulled.


Iran = “expensive and crude” — corrective to assuming digital authoritarianism means sophistication.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: A fourth case: the middle ground
text:
A fourth case: the middle ground

Kazakhstan — imports China’s surveillance vendors and hardware, but runs Iran-style shutdowns during unrest (January 2022)
Most regimes aren’t purely one model — they shop across the toolkit depending on budget, allies, and what’s actually on offer to buy


The three cases just covered are ideal types. Most real regimes are a blend — worth remembering before the toolkit slide sorts them again.

Added this pass to break up “China / Russia / Iran” reading as an exhaustive menu rather than three points on a continuum — a fourth, hybrid case makes that explicit before the Hellmeier toolkit slide risks re-flattening it into three neat boxes. cc: unverified — the January 2022 unrest and shutdown are well documented in reporting; the claim about Kazakhstan importing Chinese surveillance vendors specifically needs a source check before teaching — flagged, not invented.


Brief, two minutes — not a fourth case to memorise, the point is structural.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Hellmeier’s toolkit, as a frame
Three families of digital control, not a ladder from “weak” to “strong”:

Blocking/architecture — China’s model: build the wall in, make it structural
Shutting down — Iran’s model: blunt, visible, expensive, reactive
Flooding/drowning — Russia (and increasingly everyone)’s model: don’t suppress the signal, bury it


The choice depends on what the regime already has — infrastructure, money, tolerance for economic self-harm — not on how “advanced” it is.

Treating these as a menu rather than a hierarchy matters because it resists the intuitive but misleading story that “more sophisticated” regimes simply progress from shutdowns to blocking to flooding as they modernise. A regime’s choice is closer to a budget constraint than a maturity ladder: architectural control requires sustained investment in infrastructure and cooperative platforms; shutdowns require almost no infrastructure but impose direct, repeated economic cost; flooding requires content-production capacity (paid commentators, bot networks) rather than infrastructure at all. Regimes combine and switch between these depending on what they can afford and what they already have in place.


Verified 2026-09-16 (this pass), web search: the piece titled “The Dictator’s Digital Toolkit” could not be located as a stand-alone article under that exact title. What web search confirms is Hellmeier, “The Dictator’s Digital Toolkit: Explaining Variation in Internet Filtering in Authoritarian Regimes,” Politics & Policy 44(6), 2016, pp. 1158–1191 — same title family, but the confirmed piece is specifically about internet filtering, not the full blocking/shutdown/flooding typology this slide attributes to it. Decision for Noah: either (a) this is the right piece and the three-part typology on this slide is this deck’s own synthesis (in which case say so, don’t attribute the typology itself to Hellmeier), or (b) there is a different, more recent Hellmeier piece (possibly on V-Dem’s Digital Society Project, which Hellmeier is also associated with) that matches the toolkit framing better — worth a library search before this goes on the reading list. Do not present the typology as verbatim Hellmeier without resolving this.


cc: MISATTRIBUTED (2026-09-16 verification pass) — proposal only, not applied. The Hellmeier 2016 Politics & Policy piece is a quantitative study of internet filtering; it does not contain a blocking/shutting-down/flooding typology, so the frame this slide runs on has no source behind it as written. Verified alternative that does supply a real taxonomy of internet control tactics: Eda Keremoğlu & Nils B. Weidmann, “How Dictators Control the Internet: A Review Essay,” Comparative Political Studies 53(10–11) (2020): 1690–1703 (DOI 10.1177/0010414020912278) — confirmed by web search 2026-09-16. This is a proposal for Noah to weigh against option (a)/(b) above, not a swap made in this pass — the reading list still shows Hellmeier per the ground rules for this fix (don’t change reading identity without Noah’s sign-off).


Use this to organise the three cases retrospectively; sets up flooding slide next.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How do we know any of this is real?
text:
How do we know any of this is real?
Firewalls, shutdowns and flooding are hard to observe directly — regimes don’t publish a “censorship report.”

So how does anyone measure digital authoritarianism at all?

Pair chat, 90 sec — guess a method before you answer. Next slide names the actual infrastructure.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Measuring the unmeasurable

V-Dem’s Digital Society Project — expert-coded scores for online censorship, disinformation, and internet shutdowns, country-year
Freedom House’s Freedom on the Net — annual country reports, coded from primary reporting and in-country researchers
Access Now’s #KeepItOn coalition — technical and reported tracking of actual shutdown events, near-real-time, event by event
Technical measurement — network probes (e.g. OONI, the Open Observatory of Network Interference) that directly test what’s actually reachable from inside a country, right now


None of these is perfect — expert coding has bias risk, technical probes miss soft/social forms of control. Triangulating across all four is the discipline.

No single data source fully captures digital authoritarianism, and the methodological caveats differ by source. Expert-coded measures like V-Dem’s Digital Society Project and Freedom House’s Freedom on the Net rely on country specialists’ judgement, which is systematic and comparable across countries but carries the ordinary risks of expert coding (inter-coder disagreement, availability of well-informed local experts in the most closed states). Technical measurement tools such as OONI directly probe what content and services are reachable from vantage points inside a country, which is harder evidence for blocking specifically but says little about softer forms of control such as flooding, platform-level self-censorship, or targeted account suspension. Event-based trackers like Access Now’s #KeepItOn are strong on shutdowns specifically because a shutdown is a discrete, detectable event, but say little about the ongoing, low-visibility forms of control that make up most of the toolkit day to day.


Don’t over-run — point is measurement is hard/multi-method, not a deep dive on any one source.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Flooding, not blocking

Bots and trolls — manufacture the appearance of consensus
Distraction — change the subject rather than forbid it
Doubt — if nothing is verifiable, nothing can be proven against you


Censorship suppresses the signal. Flooding buries it. The second is cheaper — and harder to accuse you of.

The three mechanisms work together rather than separately. Manufacturing the appearance of consensus (coordinated inauthentic accounts posting pro-regime content at scale) makes genuine opposition sentiment look like a fringe minority view even where it isn’t one. Distraction — flooding a contested topic with unrelated content, or manufacturing a rival controversy — works because attention, not information, is the scarce resource online; you don’t need to hide a fact if nobody is looking at it. And manufacturing general doubt about what’s true, rather than pushing one false narrative, is strategically robust in a way outright lying isn’t: a regime that has convinced its population nothing online can be trusted has pre-emptively discredited any future embarrassing leak, not just today’s.


IMG placeholder — could add a bot/troll-farm diagram (accounts → coordinated posting → trending topic) here; no licensed image sourced this pass.


Callback to last week’s Huang/signalling logic: technology changed, mechanism didn’t. Say it out loud.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Two minutes: design the dissident’s counter-toolkit
text:
Two minutes: design the dissident’s counter-toolkit
Pair up. You’re advising a dissident group in a state that mixes all three — some blocking, occasional shutdowns, heavy flooding.

Two minutes: what’s your counter-move for each? What does it cost you?

Real 2 min, then cold-call two pairs. Push past “use a VPN” — it doesn’t fix flooding or transnational reach (next section).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Exile used to mean safety
Increasingly it doesn’t.

Spyware on dissidents’ phones abroad
Harassment of diaspora communities — and of their families back home
Abuse of Interpol notices, coerced returns


Transnational repression names a regime’s use of coercive tools against its own citizens (or former citizens) outside its territory — the practice is old (assassinations of exiled dissidents predate the internet by decades), but digital tools have made it dramatically cheaper and harder to detect. Commercial spyware, most infamously the Pegasus tool, has been documented on the phones of journalists, activists and even heads of state, sold by private firms to governments that use it against targets abroad. Family-based pressure — harassing or detaining relatives still inside the country to coerce an exile’s silence — and abuse of international mechanisms such as Interpol Red Notices to have a state’s own political opponents detained by cooperating foreign governments are the two other major channels documented by Freedom House’s transnational-repression research.


Freedom House transnational-repression data — map or headline stat, latest edition. This section needs the current-year figure; last year’s data will read as stale to a room that follows the news. Also: slot in whatever current case is live when you teach this (there is usually one). Image, w09img/: a Pegasus/NSO Group coverage image or a generic “phone + spyware” graphic — none sourced this pass.


Genuinely novel — isn’t just old logic on new tools.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Not just other people’s problem
The regime’s reach is no longer bounded by its borders — including inside the EU.

Pegasus spyware has been documented on the phones of journalists and officials inside EU member states. Diaspora communities in Dublin are a plausible transnational-repression target, not a purely hypothetical one.

This is the part of the week with the most immediate relevance to students in Dublin specifically: transnational repression is not confined to authoritarian regimes’ own regions. Documented Pegasus spyware cases inside EU member states (several EU governments have opened their own investigations into domestic use or foreign targeting via the tool) show that the infrastructure crosses into liberal-democratic jurisdictions, and diaspora communities from authoritarian-ruled countries living in Ireland are a realistic, not hypothetical, potential target population.


Pick a current example when you teach it — deliberately no single dated case on the slide.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The phone in your pocket
Before you feel too distant from any of this: what does your own phone know about you right now — location history, contact graph, search history, who-you-talk-to-when?

Ask the room: how many of you have location services on for an app you don’t remember granting it to?

Point isn’t “you’re surveilled like a dissident” — infrastructure is the same, stakes/intent differ. Keep analytical, not alarmist. Bridges to AI slide.


Tone check (this pass, per VOICE-AND-REGISTER’s anti-pattern list): read this slide and the one after it specifically for alarmism. Verdict: stays on the right side of it — the slide explicitly distinguishes infrastructure from intent/stakes rather than collapsing student data collection into dissident-level surveillance, and the notes already flag the anti-pattern directly. Left as written.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
What does AI actually change?

Scale — monitoring that once needed analysts now needs none
Synthesis — cheap, plausible, endless content
But not the underlying dilemma: you still can’t tell true loyalty from performed loyalty


Two capabilities are genuinely new rather than merely cheaper versions of old ones. Scale: automated analysis of communications and movement data at a population level no longer requires a proportional number of human analysts, which changes what’s economically feasible for a mid-capacity state, not just a wealthy one. Synthesis: generative tools make plausible, tailored propaganda and disinformation content cheap and fast to produce at volume, lowering the cost of the “flooding” strategy specifically. What doesn’t change is the structural dilemma this whole module is built around: no amount of data tells a ruler with certainty whether a subordinate’s loyalty is genuine or merely performed under observation, because the observed behaviour is itself shaped by the fact of being observed.


Keep this short and sceptical, weight on the last bullet — the module’s spine reasserting itself. Deliberately resisting the “AI changes everything” framing here (anti-pattern: moral panic / hype on tech topics); the honest claim is narrower and more interesting.


Rewrite this slide every single year — it will be the most out-of-date thing in the deck by a wide margin. Check for a genuinely new capability (generative deepfakes in an actual election, AI-assisted network mapping, etc.) before each delivery rather than reusing last year’s bullets.


Short and sceptical, weight on the last bullet. Tools get better; the ruler’s two problems don’t go away.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Does digital authoritarianism actually work?

It has made regimes better at targeting the right people — probably durably so
It has not obviously made them better at knowing what people actually believe, deep down
And it creates new dependencies: on firms, on foreign tech, on engineers who could, in principle, walk away


Verdict for now: a real upgrade to the control toolkit. Not a solution to the power-sharing problem — which is next week’s business.

The new dependency is worth stressing on its own: a regime that has built its control apparatus around specific firms, foreign hardware and software supply chains, and a technically skilled workforce has created a new set of actors whose cooperation it now needs — a vulnerability that a purely coercive, low-tech regime doesn’t have to manage. Export controls, sanctions on surveillance-technology vendors, and the loyalty of the engineers who maintain the system are all now part of the regime’s list of things that can go wrong.


Land on the two-dilemmas frame: surveillance watches the masses, does far less for the colonel down the hall. Hand-off to coups.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Key readings this week

Hellmeier, “The Dictator’s Digital Toolkit: Explaining Variation in Internet Filtering in Authoritarian Regimes,” Politics & Policy 44(6) (2016), pp. 1158–1191
Xu, “To Repress or to Co-opt? Authoritarian Control in the Age of Digital Surveillance,” American Journal of Political Science 65(2) (2021), pp. 309–325


Recommended: Roberts, Censored — selected chapter · Freedom House, Freedom on the Net / transnational-repression data (latest edition)


Both citations checked this pass (web search, 2026-09-16); citation forms now fixed to match, 2026-09-16 follow-up pass.

Xu — confirmed as written. Xu, “To Repress or to Co-opt? Authoritarian Control in the Age of Digital Surveillance,” American Journal of Political Science, Vol. 65, No. 2 (2021), pp. 309–325. DOI: 10.1111/ajps.12514.
Hellmeier — citation itself now confirmed and fixed above: Hellmeier, “The Dictator’s Digital Toolkit: Explaining Variation in Internet Filtering in Authoritarian Regimes,” Politics & Policy 44(6) (2016), pp. 1158–1191. No other/more recent Hellmeier “toolkit” piece was found in two search passes, so this is the reading. What remains unresolved is separate: the piece is about internet filtering, not the blocking/shutdown/flooding typology this deck’s “Hellmeier’s toolkit” slide organises around — see the cc: MISATTRIBUTED note on that slide (proposes Keremoğlu & Weidmann 2020 as an alternative frame; Noah’s call).



Noah: the citation is now settled — no further reference-checking needed. Still open: confirm TCD library access to both pieces before the reading list goes out (PLAN-MT2026.md §6.3), and decide the framing question flagged on the “Hellmeier’s toolkit” slide (keep as this deck’s own synthesis and say so on-slide, or adopt the Keremoğlu & Weidmann framing instead).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
For next week
Week 10 — Coups & the Military

Quinlivan, “Coup-proofing: Its Practice and Consequences in the Middle East,” International Security (1999)
Geddes, Wright & Frantz, How Dictatorships Work — chapter on the military / coups

Think about: all this technology watches the population. Who watches the people with the guns? (Response-paper prompt seed — see cc note.)

What today covered. Digital tools didn’t hand dictators a new strategy — they made the old two-problem toolkit (power-sharing with elites, control of the masses) dramatically cheaper and more precise. Xu’s argument is the week’s sharpest idea: better surveillance lets a regime substitute targeted co-optation for indiscriminate repression, because it finally knows whom to buy. China, Russia and Iran show three different toolkits — architecture, narrative-then-walls, and blunt shutdowns — built from what each regime already had rather than from a shared blueprint, and most real regimes (like Kazakhstan) blend more than one. Hellmeier’s three families — blocking, shutting down, flooding — organise the cases without ranking them by sophistication. Transnational repression is the one genuinely new piece: a regime’s reach is no longer bounded by its own borders. And AI changes scale and synthesis, but not the underlying dilemma every week of this module returns to: you can watch behaviour, but you can never fully verify belief.


Response-paper spec is still unwritten (PLAN-MT2026.md §6.4) — this think-about question is drafted as a plausible response-paper seed, but there’s no format/length/rubric guidance to point students to yet. Flag until that spec exists.

See you next Friday

Pivot back to elite control — no amount of surveillance fixes a disloyal guard.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Protest, Revolution & Breakdown








The regime looked unbreakable — right up until it shattered

Payoff week — repression (Wk4), co-optation (Wk5), propaganda (Wk8) all exist to prevent this. By the end: revolutions are hard to predict not from bad forecasting, but because it’s built into how information works under repression.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Today

Preference falsification — why regimes look stable right up until they don’t
Cascades and thresholds — why 1989 surprised the protesters too, not just the CIA
Focal points and triggers — what actually starts a cascade
How the regime reads (and misreads) protest — it’s guessing as much as you are
What comes after breakdown — the sobering answer


Dense week — say so up front. State explicitly: “the ‘why does nonviolent resistance work’ side is Kneafsey’s Political Violence A — we’re doing the information half.”


Boundary reminder, said out loud on a slide (deliberately), not just in your head: naming the Kneafsey adjacency explicitly on screen does two things — it tells students where to go if they want the Chenoweth & Stephan material, and it pre-empts the “didn’t we cover this already” reaction from anyone taking both modules. Cheap insurance, per the standing courtesy rule in PLAN-MT2026.md §3.
