title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
This week in autocracy


Noah: two or three stories from this week. One line each — headline, country, and the concept it illustrates (elite problem or mass problem?). This slide is the same shape every week, same slot, right after the plan.


Five minutes, no more. Ask the room first: “what happened this week that belongs in this module?” — then show yours. The point is the habit: by teaching week 12 they should be bringing the stories, not you.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Preference falsification
Kuran’s core idea — and the answer to a lot of earlier weeks:

Under repression, people hide their true preferences
Everyone publicly conforms — even those who privately oppose the regime
So no one knows how much hidden opposition really exists — not even the dissidents themselves


Timur Kuran’s term for this is preference falsification: the deliberate public misrepresentation of a privately held view, made rational by the cost of revealing it under repression. It is not lying in the ordinary sense — everyone knows everyone else might be doing it too, which is exactly what makes the regime’s apparent stability so hard to read, from the inside or the outside.


Ties back to Week 4 (repression destroys the ruler’s own information) and Week 8 (propaganda as demoralisation — convincing people their side is alone).


Prior exposure — this is the strongest overlap in the whole module, not a minor one. Comparative Politics A (Weeks 11–12, “Contentious Politics”) already covers Kuran 1991 and preference falsification directly, plus Havel’s “greengrocer” essay and the Tocqueville line about grievances becoming intolerable once redress seems possible. This cohort has almost certainly seen the core idea already, under the same citation. Pitch this as “you’ve met the concept — now we go deeper into the mechanics of the cascade, and into what it means for how the regime itself operates,” not as a fresh reveal. Source: compA/POU22031 Comparative A slides - W11 Thursday.txt.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: The regime looks stable because everyone is pretending
text:
The regime looks stable because everyone is pretending
Including, perhaps, you.

Public conformity doesn’t mean private consent — it means the cost of dissent is currently too high
Nobody has an accurate count of how many people privately agree with them


IMAGE — a simple “private preference vs. public behaviour” two-column diagram, or a classic 1989 crowd photo (Leipzig Monday demonstrations). Drop in w11img/. Currency check not needed — historical images, no live data. Wikimedia Commons has usable Leipzig 1989 photos (search “Montagsdemonstration Leipzig 1989”).


The regime’s strength was partly an illusion built out of everyone’s silence — land this before the twist on the next slide.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The regime is guessing too
Here’s the twist that makes this week the module’s information story, not just a “how protest works” story:

The dictator’s dilemma (Week 4): repression destroys the information a ruler needs to know who’s loyal — informers lie, subordinates report what’s safe to report
Propaganda as signalling (Week 8): spin only works if people can’t compare notes — but that also means the regime can’t easily tell who’s actually persuaded and who’s just performing


So preference falsification doesn’t just fool the public about the public. It fools the regime about the regime’s own support. Everyone is in the dark together.

Repression and propaganda are mass-control tools, but blind the ruler too — that’s why regimes get caught flat-footed by their own citizens.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Spine check: elite tool or mass tool?
text:
Spine check: elite tool or mass tool?
Svolik’s two problems, back again:

Repression, propaganda, co-optation-of-the-public — these are mass-control tools, aimed at preventing exactly the collective action we’re studying today
But protest and cascades are the mass side’s answer — the moment control of the masses fails, not control of elites (that’s coups, Week 10)


Today is what happens when the mass-control toolkit’s side effect — everyone’s silence — stops being enough to hide how much silence there is.

Ask the room: “which problem is this week about?” Mass control, failing. (Week 10’s coups were elite control failing.)

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The big quote

“Revolutions are not planned; they simply happen… [they are] set off by mistakes and miscalculations on the part of authoritarian leaders who could otherwise have continued to rule for a long time.”


Kuran’s argument, distilled: nobody — not the CIA, not Soviet leaders, not the crowds in Leipzig in early 1989 — expected the wall to fall that year


Point stands either way: surprise wasn’t a forecasting failure, it was baked into the information structure.


Currency check on the quote itself, not just data — verify against Kuran 1991 (World Politics, pp. 7–48) before the lecture; if the exact wording doesn’t check out, either find the real line or present it as paraphrase rather than blockquote.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
The cascade
How a stable-looking regime collapses in weeks, sometimes days:

One person’s protest lowers the cost — and the perceived risk — for the next
Each defection reveals a little more hidden opposition → emboldens others
Past some threshold, the dam breaks and the cascade runs on its own


Small spark, sudden avalanche. And — this is the point — impossible to time in advance, from either side of the barricade.

IMAGE — chart. A threshold-model graphic (Granovetter-style): a simple distribution of individual “thresholds” showing how a small shift in the distribution’s shape can flip the outcome from “nothing happens” to “everyone joins.” Worth building with scripts/make_chart.py or matplotlib directly — data is illustrative, not a real dataset. Drop in w11img/.


Granovetter’s threshold models (not required) name the mechanism behind 1989’s speed, if useful. Coming up: elections (Week 6) as the trigger that synchronises the cascade.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Two minutes, in pairs
Discussion device 1 of 3.

Noah: a light personal-anecdote slot — something about a moment (in Russia or elsewhere) where you personally weren’t sure what people around you “really” thought, or a story about the gap between what people said and did. Doesn’t have to be political; the point is just a human-scale version of the concept before the room does the pair exercise below.

Imagine you privately oppose your government, but believe you’re one of only a handful who feel that way. What would it take for you to be the first person to say so in public?

Now: what would it take for you to be the fifth person? The five hundredth?

Actual 2-minute pair discussion, not rhetorical. Listen for “safety in numbers” / “seeing someone else go first” — that’s the threshold concept in their own words. Debrief: “that’s a threshold. Different people have different ones. That’s the whole model.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Focal points: elections as trigger
Tucker: electoral fraud can be the focal point that solves the protesters’ coordination problem.

A stolen election is a wrong everyone witnesses at the same moment, in public — the perfect cascade-starter. It doesn’t create the hidden opposition; it makes it visible to itself, all at once.


So the elections from Week 6 can be the regime’s undoing after all.

Say out loud: “remember why autocrats bother holding elections they could rig? Here’s the risk side — the ritual can be the moment their weakness becomes common knowledge.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Focal points: funerals
Stolen elections aren’t the only kind of focal moment:

A death at the regime’s hands, mourned in public, can reconvene a crowd the state can’t easily ban
Iran 1978–79: 40-day Shia mourning cycles each restarted the cascade — every funeral produced martyrs for the next one


The mourning-cycle mechanism is worth naming on its own: Shia mourning convention marks the 40th day after a death, so each round of protest deaths scheduled the next round of protest automatically, whether or not organisers wanted it to. The regime could suppress one demonstration; it could not suppress a calendar.


Bloody Friday (Jaleh Square, 8 Sep 1978) is the specific date if wanted — keep to the mechanism, not the whole revolution.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Focal points: a single spark
A single act, witnessed by everyone at once — no funeral required.

Mohamed Bouazizi’s self-immolation, Sidi Bouzid, Tunisia, 17 December 2010
Protests in his town within days, across Tunisia within weeks, across the region within a month — the spark for the entire Arab Spring


Same logic as the stolen election and the funeral: a focal point doesn’t create the grievance. It gives everyone who already shares it a moment to discover that they’re not alone.

Bouazizi was a fruit vendor, harassed and humiliated by a municipal inspector who confiscated his cart. Nobody could have predicted that this specific act, rather than any of the countless similar humiliations before it, would be the trigger — that is Kuran’s point about unpredictability applied to the spark itself, not just to the cascade it set off.


Teaching point is unpredictability of the spark, not the biography.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Iran, 2022: a funeral becomes a movement
text:
Iran, 2022: a funeral becomes a movement
Mahsa Amini died in police custody, 16 September 2022, after arrest by the morality police.

Her funeral in Saqqez became the opening protest of the “Woman, Life, Freedom” movement, which spread nationwide within days
Same mechanism as Iran 1978–79’s mourning cycles, four decades apart


cc: unverified. Death date and immediate funeral-protest link are widely reported (BBC, Reuters, Sep 2022) — verify exact wording before presenting as settled fact; the current state of the movement (repression, arrests, any policy change) needs a currency check closer to 27 Nov 2026, not just the 2022 origin.


Note how recent this is — most cases in the deck are decades old. Keep to the mechanism, not a verdict on the movement’s outcome.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Focal points, in one line
A focal point doesn’t create hidden opposition — it makes it visible to itself, all at once, to everyone at the same time.

Recap check: cascade mechanism (falsification, thresholds) vs. triggers (elections, funerals, sparks) — still tracking?

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How does the regime read the room?
text:
How does the regime read the room?
Not well, usually — and that’s the point.

Noah: a Russia-specific focal-point example would land well two slides back (the funerals/single-spark section) if you want one — your Russian Politics deck (POU44172, slides/week11.qmd, “Opposition, Protest, and Civil Society”) covers Bolotnaya Square 2011–12, triggered by a widely-witnessed stolen Duma election (December 2011) — the same “everyone sees the fraud at once” logic as the Tucker slide a few back. Deliberately not built out here already (see the Belarus reuse-flag cc below) to avoid doubling content for students who take both modules; your call whether to add it live.


IMAGE — Stasi surveillance files/archive photo (widely available on Commons, e.g. “Stasi records” or the Runde Ecke museum) as a visual for “the regime tried to measure this and still got it wrong.” Optional; skip if it crowds the slide.


Surveillance and informant networks are supposed to solve this — but Week 4 already showed those channels get distorted by fear and flattery
Security services often discover the scale of opposition at the same moment the opposition discovers it — watching the same crowd everyone else is


Ties the “regime is guessing too” thread through — repression corrupts the ruler’s own sensors.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
1989: even the KGB was blindsided
East German and Soviet intelligence were as caught out as Western intelligence.

Nobody had good numbers, because the numbers didn’t exist yet to be measured — there was nothing to intercept, no plan to find, because no one had decided anything yet.

This is worth taking seriously as a claim about intelligence failure more broadly: the 1989 case is sometimes used (fairly) to argue that “the CIA missed it” stories misdiagnose the problem. It wasn’t a failure of collection or analysis in the usual sense — there was no secret plan to discover, because the cascade was, in Kuran’s account, genuinely undetermined until it happened.


Warn against “the regime always knows” as a lazy essay assumption — it usually doesn’t, and that’s structural, not incompetence.


Noah: your research slot. You work on protest attitudes vs. protest behaviour — the gap between what people say they’d do and what they actually do is close kin to preference falsification, but methodologically sharper (you can measure the gap directly rather than infer it from a surprise revolution). Drop in the framing, the method, and whatever headline finding you’re comfortable sharing at this level. This is the “your lecturer actually studies this” moment for the week — worth more than any borrowed example. Comparative A already cites Dalton/Van Sickle/Weldon on individual- vs. country-level protest predictors (Week 11 Thursday deck) — your work can either extend that thread or deliberately contrast with it (survey-stated intent vs. revealed behaviour).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: How would we even measure hidden opposition?
text:
How would we even measure hidden opposition?
If preference falsification means surveys can’t be trusted at face value, what can political scientists actually do?

Indirect methods — list experiments, randomised response — let respondents reveal a sensitive view without ever stating it directly
After the fact — election results, samizdat, defector testimony, and (now) leaked internal polling are the retrospective evidence base
Kuran’s own answer: mostly, you can’t measure it in advance — that is the argument, not a gap in the argument


List experiments ask respondents how many items on a list make them angry, without saying which — a sensitive item is hidden among neutral ones, and the average difference between treatment and control groups reveals the prevalence of the sensitive view without ever asking anyone to admit to it individually. It is a genuine partial fix for preference falsification in survey research, not a way around Kuran’s underlying point: it estimates a population average, not who, and it still cannot tell you when a threshold will be crossed.


Keep brief — methods aside. Payoff: “we can’t measure it” IS the finding here, not a failure to apologise for.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Live demonstration: could we do this in the room?
text:
Live demonstration: could we do this in the room?
Discussion device 2 of 3 — a live preference-falsification moment.
What if, instead of describing preference falsification, the room demonstrated it?

Concept only — needs careful construction before running live. See cc below for constraints.


Design sketch, needs your judgement before this runs live. The idea: ask students to write down anonymously, on paper, their real opinion on something mildly contested but safe — not politics, something like “is this module’s workload about right?” — then ask them to guess what percentage of the room privately agrees with them. Reveal both distributions. The gap between guessed-consensus and actual-consensus is a live, low-stakes preference-falsification demo. Design constraints: (1) the topic must be genuinely low-stakes — anything that touches politics risks the anonymity assumption not holding, and the pedagogical point is about the mechanism, not about extracting real political opinions from a room of 15–30 people who can often identify each other’s handwriting; (2) test it on a throwaway question before using it live, because a flat result (everyone already knows the room’s real view) kills the demo. If this doesn’t come together in time, the pair-discussion above (two minutes, in pairs) does similar pedagogical work with zero setup — keep that as the fallback, not a downgrade.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: 1989: the cascade in its purest form
text:
1989: the cascade in its purest form

Poland’s Round Table, Hungary’s border opening, Leipzig’s Monday demonstrations, then Berlin — each domino visibly lowered the cost of the next
The Kremlin’s decisive non-decision: Gorbachev signalled Moscow wouldn’t send tanks (unlike 1956, 1968) — removing the one factor that had reliably capped every prior Eastern Bloc cascade
From “unthinkable” to “obvious in hindsight” in about ten weeks


IMAGE — Berlin Wall, November 1989 — the canonical cascade photo. Wikimedia Commons has multiple CC-licensed options (“Berlin Wall 1989” or “Mauerfall 1989”). Drop in w11img/.


Domino sequence for speed: Poland June, Hungary September, Leipzig October, Berlin 9 November. Gorbachev’s non-decision itself shifted everyone’s threshold at once.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Georgia 2003: the Rose Revolution


A rigged parliamentary election (November 2003) is the focal point again — Tucker’s mechanism, a second time, a decade after 1989
Weeks of protest, crowds carrying roses, converge on parliament — Shevardnadze resigns without a shot fired
The template for Ukraine’s Orange Revolution (2004) and Kyrgyzstan’s Tulip Revolution (2005) — a genuine wave, not a one-off


“Colour revolution” became the era’s shorthand for this pattern: a stolen or manipulated post-Soviet election, mass protest organised fast enough to beat the regime’s response, and a peaceful handover. Georgia’s Rose Revolution (2003) is the founding case; Ukraine’s Orange Revolution (2004) and Kyrgyzstan’s Tulip Revolution (2005) followed within two years, each visibly learning from the last.


Contrast with 1989: same mechanism (witnessed fraud as focal point), but faster — Georgia’s Kmara studied Serbia’s 2000 Bulldozer Revolution as a how-to.


Image reused from POU11011’s licensed pool (w08-lec12-img/rose-revolution.jpg, CC BY-SA 3.0, credited in this deck’s w11img/CREDITS.md) rather than refetched — per the brief’s reuse-first rule.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Arab Spring: the cascade that crossed borders
text:
Arab Spring: the cascade that crossed borders

Bouazizi’s death → Tunisia’s Ben Ali gone within a month
Protests spread to Egypt, Libya, Syria, Bahrain, Yemen within weeks — a genuine cross-border diffusion, not just parallel domestic cascades


Social media’s role here is a live methodological debate, not a settled answer this week takes a side on: it plausibly lowered the cost of learning what your neighbours privately thought, which is exactly the information mechanism Kuran’s model needs to travel faster and across borders — but correlation between platform use and protest timing is not proof of that specific causal channel, and the module doesn’t require you to resolve it.


Keep narrow: the trigger and diffusion logic travelled across borders — not “why resistance works” (Kneafsey’s territory).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Same cascade, four different endings

Tunisia → a fragile but real democratic transition
Egypt → a coup and a new authoritarianism (Week 10)
Syria → civil war and regime survival
Libya, Yemen → state collapse


Same information mechanism, wildly different institutional starting points — which is exactly why the cascade and the outcome are two separate questions.

Outcomes depended on separate factors — military cohesion (Wk10), elite unity (Wk3). Bridge into Week 12’s “breakdown doesn’t guarantee democracy.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Assad’s Syria: one push from falling over?
text:
Assad’s Syria: one push from falling over?
The post-Assad commentary said autocracies are brittle. The fifteen years before his fall say otherwise.

Isolated, sanctioned, economically collapsed, ideologically hollow — the regime had every reason to fall apart, for over a decade
Kept alive by external props (Russia, Iran) and sheer survival instinct, not strength
It still took fifteen years of slow destruction to actually end


“Brittle” implies you poke a regime and it breaks. The Assad regime is the counter-example: sanctioned and diplomatically isolated for over a decade, its economy collapsed, its ideology hollowed out to bare survival, and propped up almost entirely by external patrons (Russia, Iran) rather than any real internal strength — and it still took roughly fifteen years of slow destruction before it actually fell in December 2024. The lesson is not that authoritarian regimes never end. It’s that “obviously doomed” and “about to fall” are different claims, and confusing them is exactly the mistake that produced so much premature commentary about Assad’s “inevitable” collapse for over a decade before it happened.


Primes “why didn’t Belarus tip” (next). Line: “always one push from falling over — except when they’re not, for fifteen years.”


Source: Waller, Statecraft, 10 Sep 2026 — “The fall of the Assad regime was very instructive in part by how long it took. This is a regime that was isolated for over a decade, massive sanctions, nobody wanted to touch it, economic collapse and degradation… The word brittle implies that you poke it and it’ll break… Syria had a decade and a half drawn out process of slow destruction.” Paraphrased above, not quoted verbatim on-slide.


Currency check: confirm “fifteen years” framing and Assad’s December 2024 fall date are still accurately described by delivery time (Nov 2026).

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Belarus 2020: the cascade that didn’t tip
text:
Belarus 2020: the cascade that didn’t tip
The counter-case — worth as much airtime as the successes.

August 2020: a stolen election (Lukashenko’s implausible 80%)
Mass protests, hundreds of thousands in Minsk — every ingredient of a 1989-style cascade was present


And yet the regime held. Security forces stayed loyal throughout; Russia backstopped Lukashenko diplomatically and materially; the opposition figure Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya ended up in exile in Lithuania rather than in power. All the public-cascade ingredients of 1989 were present here too — which is exactly what makes the comparison useful.


Currency check required before delivery: confirm the state of Belarusian opposition-in-exile, any developments in Lukashenko’s position, and whether “2020” needs updating to reflect anything since — this is a 2026-live case, not a closed historical one like 1989.


Important: don’t let the week become “and then the dictator always loses.”

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Why didn’t Belarus tip?
Elite cohesion held (Week 3) — the security apparatus never faced the defection cascade that ended East Germany.

A public cascade without an elite one stalls.


You can be as popular as you like. Popularity does not outrank the people holding the rifles.

Public and elite cascades are separate — you need BOTH. Say the callbacks out loud: Week 3 (power-sharing) and Week 10 (security forces’ choice).


Source: Waller, Statecraft, 10 Sep 2026, on why popular support alone doesn’t force a transition: “they can be as popular as they want. But if people start shooting voters in the street, for example… it doesn’t matter all that much.” Compressed above into the on-slide line; not a direct quote.


Reuse flag: Noah’s own Russian Politics deck (POU44172 week11.qmd, “Opposition, Protest, and Civil Society”) has substantial Russia-specific protest material — Bolotnaya 2011–12, Navalny, FBK, civil society figures. This cohort could plausibly also take POU44172 in the same academic year, so deliberately did NOT reuse those examples here; Belarus does the same analytical job (stolen election, cascade, regime survival) without doubling up content across two modules the same students might sit. If you’d rather use a Russia example instead of or alongside Belarus, the material is ready-made in that deck — your call.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Four cascades, one variable that split them
text:
Four cascades, one variable that split them

1989 & Georgia 2003: elite cohesion cracked (Gorbachev’s non-decision; Shevardnadze’s isolation) → the public cascade wasn’t contained
Belarus 2020: elite cohesion held → contained
Arab Spring: elite cohesion split differently case by case — which is why one cascade produced four different endings


Put together, the four cases this week make one argument rather than four separate stories: the information mechanism (preference falsification, thresholds, focal points) explains when a cascade starts and how fast it spreads, but whether it succeeds depends on a completely different variable — elite cohesion (Week 3) and the security forces’ choice (Week 10) — that this week’s mechanism does not itself determine.


Synthesis slide — slow down if time allows. Ties every case back to the mass/elite-control spine before the cold call.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Who decides it?
Discussion device 3 of 3 — cold call.
In the crowd-vs-regime showdown, the security forces’ choice is often decisive.

IMAGE — a security-forces-facing-crowd photo (Tiananmen “Tank Man” is the canonical image but carries its own sensitivities to weigh; an East German Volkspolizei/Leipzig 1989 photo is a safer, still-apt alternative). Your call — this is the slide’s emotional centre, worth picking carefully rather than defaulting.


Shoot the protesters — or defect and join them? Recall Week 10: that single choice can end a regime — or, as Belarus just showed, hold one together.

Callback to Barany (Week 10). Tiananmen vs. East Germany 1989 — same moment, opposite outcomes, down to what security forces chose. Cold-call 2-3 students before revealing.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: So how do autocracies actually end?
text:
So how do autocracies actually end?

Coup / insider removal (Week 10) — still the most common exit
Mass uprising / revolution — dramatic, rarer, and (today’s lesson) unpredictable
Negotiated transition — pacted exits, elite bargains
Incumbent loses an election — and actually leaves


Pull the empirical distribution of exit modes (GWF) if time allows.


IMAGE — chart. GWF’s distribution of autocratic exit modes (coup / popular uprising / election loss / other), from their dataset or the 2014 Perspectives on Politics article’s own figure. Build with scripts/make_chart.py if a comparable OWID/V-Dem series exists, or a simple bar chart from GWF’s published numbers.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Negotiated exits: who’s actually at the table?
text:
Negotiated exits: who’s actually at the table?
Not every regime ends in a cascade or a coup. Some end because both sides decide to talk.

Split the regime into hardliners (want everything to stay the same) and softliners (want reform)
Split the opposition into hard (often ideological — overthrow, full break) and soft (willing to negotiate)
The pact: softliners and soft opposition negotiate with each other, and isolate both sets of extremes


This is the “pacted transition” model, developed from Latin American cases in the 1980s. Rather than the regime collapsing all at once, it divides internally between hardliners who want the status quo preserved and softliners who are willing to countenance reform; the opposition divides in parallel between a hard wing (often ideologically committed to full overthrow) and a soft wing willing to negotiate. The pact happens when the softliners on the regime side and the soft opposition find each other, negotiate directly, and together sideline both extremes — the hardliners who want no change and the hard opposition who want the regime gone entirely and on their terms.


Draw the two-by-two on the board if time: hardliner/softliner × hard/soft opposition. Pact works because it’s the moderates on both sides negotiating, not the extremes.


Source: Waller, Statecraft, 10 Sep 2026 — “if you divide the regime into what the literature calls hardliners and softliners… and then you divide society into the sort of soft opposition and the hard opposition… the key to a pacted transition in the classic model is that the softliners at top and the soft opposition at the bottom negotiate with each other, isolate the other two.” Paraphrased above.


PROPOSAL — recommended reading, Noah’s call: O’Donnell, Guillermo & Philippe Schmitter. 1986. Transitions from Authoritarian Rule: Tentative Conclusions about Uncertain Democracies. Johns Hopkins University Press, ch. 4 — the source of the hardliner/softliner apparatus taught above. Not added to _course.yml; flagging only.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
What the guarantees cost
Gradually freer elections. Gradually, the opposition takes ministerial positions. And in exchange, the outgoing elite gets guarantees.

Usually: amnesty — a promise the old guard won’t be prosecuted for what they did in office
The transition is slow, by design — trust has to be built one step at a time, not declared
The result: the torturer on the bus. A survivor recognises a former torturer riding public transport, years later, free


The mechanics of a pacted transition: elections are gradually made freer and fairer, the opposition is gradually brought into ministerial positions in government, and in exchange regime elites typically receive guarantees — most often amnesty — that they will not be prosecuted for crimes committed while in power. The Argentine case supplies the sharpest illustration of what this actually costs a survivor: a woman who had been tortured during the “Dirty War,” years later, recognises one of her former torturers sitting across from her on a city bus, free, because the negotiated transition let him stay that way. Truth commissions and any real accountability, where they happen at all, typically arrive decades later, after the democracy has consolidated enough to no longer depend on the old elite’s cooperation.


Tell the torturer-on-the-bus story slowly — it’s what makes “nobody is happy” land as real, not abstract. Don’t rush it.


Source: Waller, Statecraft, 10 Sep 2026, relaying the host’s own family story: “I’m half Argentine and there’s a book that I remember very vividly. A woman talking about her experience in the dirty war, including being tortured and then much later in Buenos Aires, she’s on a bus since she realizes that the [passenger] from a real newspaper is one of her former torturers. Because as part of this uneasy transition to democracy, we’ve let those people off. So not everybody is thrilled.” Paraphrased above; the bus/torturer detail is closely drawn from the transcript, cc: verify exact book reference before quoting further.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: Nobody is happy — and it worked anyway
text:
Nobody is happy — and it worked anyway
The pact leaves the old guard unpunished and the survivors unsatisfied.

And still: thirty-plus years of electoral democratic politics followed, in the Latin American cases that ran this model.

Not a happy ending — a working one. Connect to Belarus: a pact needs softliners to believe negotiating is safer than digging in — the calculation Belarus’s forces refused to make.


Source: Waller, Statecraft, 10 Sep 2026 — asked directly whether this counts as a pacted transition working, Waller’s implicit verdict across the segment is that despite nobody being thrilled with the amnesty terms, these transitions produced durable electoral democracies. Paraphrased, not a direct quote.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
After breakdown: what usually follows?
GWF’s sobering finding: most breakdowns do not lead to democracy.

A new strongman, a new single party, or a new junta is the more common sequel.

The one thing to leave them remembering: democratization is a minority outcome, not the default.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Breakdown ≠ democracy
A regime can collapse and be replaced by… another regime.

New autocracy (the “revolving door” — Egypt 2011 → 2013)
Civil war / state failure (Syria, Libya)
Genuine democratization (the harder, rarer path)


Egypt is the cleanest illustration of the revolving door: the 2011 uprising toppled Mubarak, a competitive transition briefly followed, and by 2013 a military coup had installed a new autocracy under Sisi — the same square, a different ruler. Syria and Libya show a different failure mode: the old regime broke down and nothing coherent replaced it, only prolonged civil war and, in Libya’s case, competing governments each claiming legitimacy. Genuine democratization — Tunisia is the Arab Spring’s one clear case — is real but rare, which is the point of this slide.


Cleanest illustration: Arab Spring’s divergent endings — same cascade, three different landing spots.


IMAGE — a small triptych or three thumbnails (Tahrir Square 2011, a Syrian civil-war image, Tunis) illustrating the three divergent outcomes from one starting cascade. Source: Wikimedia Commons, Arab Spring category.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
section: What actually happens, most of the time?
text:
What actually happens, most of the time?
Recall the exit modes from a few slides back — coup, mass uprising, negotiated transition, election loss.

GWF’s own finding: breakdown more often produces a new autocracy than a democracy. Democratization is not the default outcome; it’s one branch among several, and not the most common one.

Currency/citation check: pull GWF’s actual post-WWII breakdown-outcome split (the “% to democracy vs. % to new autocracy” figure) before delivery — don’t eyeball it live. It’s the sobering-data moment; needs the real number, not a paraphrase. Present as a simple stat card, not a wall of text.


One-sentence takeaway: optimism at a dictator’s fall ≠ a democracy being built. Bridges to next week’s mirror question: how does a democracy slide the other way?
